AI.tldr: Cura 1T is a healthcare-specialized LLM trained via a human-gated self-evolution loop, where a training agent iteratively plans capabilities, evaluates failures, and refines data mixtures—achieving top performance on healthcare benchmarks while maintaining general reasoning ability.
AI.motivation: Existing healthcare LLMs are narrow and brittle: improving one capability (e.g., patient consultation, clinical reasoning, EHR tool use, or visual diagnosis) often degrades others. No single model comprehensively covers the full spectrum of high-stakes healthcare communication, multimodal reasoning, interactive diagnosis, and workflow execution.
AI.method: A human-gated self-evolution loop: each round, a training agent (1) plans a target capability, (2) trains the model, (3) evaluates benchmark trajectories, and (4) refines the data mixture based on observed failures. The loop uses targeted synthetic and curated examples rather than a single generic medical-data update.
AI.result: Cura 1T ranks at or near the top among frontier baselines across the healthcare evaluation suite, while remaining competitive on out-of-domain reasoning and agentic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A data-centered, iterative self-evolution approach enables a single healthcare LLM to achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse clinical tasks without catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, addressing the fundamental tension between breadth and depth in medical AI.

title: A Transportable Threshold-Based Framework for Interpretable Classification of Medical Data
summary: Black-box models limit the adoption of artificial intelligence in medicine due to their lack of interpretability and reproducibility. We introduce a statistically grounded framework that provides fully interpretable, rule-based clinical classification using the Bernoulli Naïve Bayes (BNB) model. The method applies supervised $χ^2$-guided statistical binarization to continuous variables, identifying thresholds that maximize association with clinical outcomes within the training data. This transformation allows BNB to operate effectively on continuous medical data without sacrificing its inherent transparency. The approach was evaluated on three benchmark datasets, Pima Indians Diabetes, Wisconsin Breast Cancer, and Heart Failure Prediction, achieving area-under-the-curve (AUC) scores of 0.800 for the Pima analysis, 0.984 for Wisconsin Breast Cancer, and 0.919 for Heart Failure Prediction. In addition to discrimination, probabilistic reliability was assessed using leakage-safe cross-validated calibration analysis including Brier score, calibration intercept/slope, and post-hoc beta calibration, which improved probability calibration across datasets. These results suggest that a statistically interpretable framework can achieve performance comparable to more complex models while providing explicit, clinically meaningful decision rules and calibrated risk estimates. To illustrate this transparency concretely, a complete worked example demonstrates that model inference can be reproduced using only a reference table and basic arithmetic, without access to software or proprietary tools. This work offers a practical approach to supporting trustworthy and generalizable AI in real-world healthcare settings.

AI.tldr: A statistically grounded, fully interpretable clinical classification framework using Bernoulli Naïve Bayes with χ²-guided binarization achieves AUC scores of 0.800–0.984 across three medical datasets while maintaining explicit, reproducible decision rules computable by hand.
AI.motivation: Black-box AI models in medicine suffer from lack of interpretability and reproducibility, limiting clinical adoption. There is a need for transparent models that provide explicit decision rules and calibrated risk estimates without sacrificing predictive performance.
AI.method: The framework applies supervised χ²-guided statistical binarization to continuous variables, identifying thresholds that maximize association with clinical outcomes. These binarized features feed into a Bernoulli Naïve Bayes (BNB) classifier, preserving full transparency. Evaluation includes AUC, leakage-safe cross-validated calibration (Brier score, calibration intercept/slope), and post-hoc beta calibration. A worked example demonstrates inference via reference table and basic arithmetic.
AI.result: AUC scores: 0.800 (Pima Indians Diabetes), 0.984 (Wisconsin Breast Cancer), 0.919 (Heart Failure Prediction). Post-hoc beta calibration improved probabilistic reliability across all datasets. Inference was shown to be reproducible without software tools.
AI.conclusion: A statistically interpretable framework based on BNB with χ²-guided binarization achieves performance comparable to complex black-box models while providing explicit clinical decision rules and calibrated risk estimates, supporting trustworthy and generalizable AI in real-world healthcare.

title: On the Impact of Entropy-based Features
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: Network anomaly detection is increasingly challenging due to the growing diversity and variability of traffic patterns, which are not always well captured by traditional statistical features. In this work, we explore the use of entropy as an additional feature to support supervised network traffic classification. The main idea is to use entropy to represent variability in selected traffic attributes, complementing conventional descriptors rather than replacing them. We integrate the entropy-based feature into a standard machine learning pipeline and evaluate its impact through a direct comparison between models trained with and without this feature. Experiments conducted on a public intrusion detection dataset show consistent improvements in classification performance, while the additional computational cost remains low. The analysis of confusion matrices indicates a reduction in misclassifications, especially in traffic scenarios with higher variability. Overall, the results suggest that entropy-based features offer a simple and practical way to enhance existing anomaly detection pipelines. This approach is particularly attractive in settings where lightweight feature engineering and interpretability are important, making entropy a useful complement to commonly used traffic features.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes augmenting traditional statistical features with entropy-based features to improve supervised network traffic classification for anomaly detection. Experiments on a public intrusion detection dataset show consistent classification gains with minimal computational overhead, particularly reducing misclassifications in high-variability traffic scenarios.
AI.motivation: Traditional statistical features struggle to capture the growing diversity and variability of modern network traffic patterns, limiting the effectiveness of network anomaly detection systems. The authors aim to address this gap by leveraging entropy as a complementary descriptor of traffic attribute variability.
AI.method: The authors introduce entropy as an additional feature representing variability in selected traffic attributes, integrating it into a standard supervised machine learning pipeline. They conduct a controlled comparison by training models both with and without the entropy-based feature, evaluating differences in classification performance on a public intrusion detection dataset. Confusion matrix analysis is used to assess misclassification reduction.
AI.result: Models incorporating the entropy-based feature consistently outperform baseline models without it. Confusion matrix analysis reveals a notable reduction in misclassifications, especially in high-variability traffic scenarios. The additional computational cost of computing entropy remains low.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-based features provide a simple, lightweight, and interpretable enhancement to existing anomaly detection pipelines. The approach is particularly well-suited for settings where low computational overhead and feature interpretability are priorities, making entropy a practical complement to conventional traffic descriptors.

title: RecGPT-V3 Technical Report
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are transforming recommender systems from matching co-occurrence patterns in historical behavior toward reasoning about the intent that drives it. RecGPT-V1 pioneered this paradigm on Taobao by centering user understanding, and RecGPT-V2 scaled it via coordinated multi-agent reasoning; both are deployed in production with consistent gains in user experience and commercial outcomes. However, operating RecGPT at scale reveals three challenges: (1) stateless behavior modeling, where each request reprocesses full user history, wasting computation and discarding prior analysis; (2) a tag-to-item information bottleneck, where natural-language tags form a lossy channel between user understanding and item grounding; and (3) inefficient explicit reasoning, whose lengthy chain-of-thought incurs untenable latency and compute overhead.
  We present RecGPT-V3, a stateful, hybrid-modal recommender that reasons over natural language for open-world knowledge and Semantic IDs (SIDs) for concrete item grounding. A Memory Hub maintains structured, continually evolving user memory that distills long-horizon behavior into condensed units, cutting user-modeling computation by 55.8%. A Hybrid-modal Foundation Model allows the LLM jointly reason over text tags and SIDs, opening a high-bandwidth channel into the item space. Latent Intent Reasoning internalizes verbose rationales into compact learnable latent tokens that remain decodable into readable explanations, lowering output token cost by 200x. Deployed in Taobao's "Guess What You Like" feed, RecGPT-V3 achieves consistent gains in large-scale online A/B tests: IPV +1.28%, CTR +1.00%, TC +1.97%, GMV +3.97%, while cutting end-to-end serving resource consumption by 52.4%.

AI.tldr: RecGPT-V3 introduces a stateful, hybrid-modal recommender system using natural language and Semantic IDs with a Memory Hub, Hybrid-modal Foundation Model, and Latent Intent Reasoning to overcome the computational and latency limitations of prior RecGPT versions, achieving significant gains in both user engagement metrics and serving efficiency.
AI.motivation: Prior RecGPT versions (V1, V2) face three critical scaling challenges: (1) stateless behavior modeling that wastefully reprocesses full user history per request; (2) a tag-to-item information bottleneck where natural-language tags create a lossy channel between user understanding and item grounding; and (3) inefficient explicit reasoning with lengthy chain-of-thought causing untenable latency and compute overhead.
AI.method: RecGPT-V3 introduces three core components: (1) a Memory Hub that maintains structured, continually evolving user memory, distilling long-horizon behavior into condensed units to reduce computation by 55.8%; (2) a Hybrid-modal Foundation Model enabling the LLM to jointly reason over text tags and Semantic IDs (SIDs) for high-bandwidth item-space grounding; and (3) Latent Intent Reasoning that internalizes verbose rationales into compact learnable latent tokens, decodable into readable explanations, reducing output token cost by 200x.
AI.result: In online A/B tests on Taobao's "Guess What You Like" feed, RecGPT-V3 achieved IPV +1.28%, CTR +1.00%, TC +1.97%, GMV +3.97%, while reducing end-to-end serving resource consumption by 52.4%.
AI.conclusion: RecGPT-V3 demonstrates that stateful memory, hybrid-modal reasoning with SIDs, and latent intent reasoning can collectively overcome the scaling bottlenecks of LLM-based recommenders, delivering superior recommendation quality alongside substantial efficiency improvements in a production environment.

title: Verified LLM-Driven Synthesis for Concept Design
summary: Concept Design structures software systems around concepts: user-facing, self-contained units of functionality with a focused purpose. Concepts are composed into applications using synchronization rules called reactions, which specify how actions in one concept trigger actions in others. This paper first gives a formal semantics for concepts and reactions, enabling automatic verification of safety invariants in applications developed with this methodology. It then presents a CEGIS-style, LLM-driven synthesis procedure for generating reaction designs that satisfy such invariants. Because many different designs can satisfy the same invariant, we study two ways of steering synthesis toward the user's intended design: natural-language prompts and positive/negative scenarios. We also propose an LLM-driven scenario elicitation technique to support early design exploration. In an evaluation on three applications and twelve design variants using one LLM configuration, invariant-only synthesis reached verified designs quickly but often produced inconsistent designs across runs, some of which were implausible, showing that invariants alone underconstrain the design task. Scenario-guided synthesis recovered intended designs more consistently than natural-language prompting, although minimal scenarios can lead to overfitting. LLM-driven scenario elicitation, where the user classifies proposed scenarios rather than authoring them from scratch, recovered the intended designs in most variants when enough scenarios were elicited, but missed behaviors and non-determinism prevented reliable coverage in all cases.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes concept-based software design with a semantics for concepts and reactions, enabling automatic invariant verification. It then introduces an LLM-driven CEGIS synthesis procedure for generating reaction designs that satisfy safety invariants, evaluating the effectiveness of natural-language prompts, positive/negative scenarios, and an LLM-driven scenario elicitation technique for steering synthesis toward intended designs.
AI.motivation: Concept-based design structures applications around user-facing functional units (concepts) composed via synchronization reactions. While this methodology is promising, ensuring that composed applications satisfy safety invariants is challenging, and manually designing correct reactions is error-prone. The work aims to automate both verification and synthesis of reaction designs, and to explore how to effectively steer automated synthesis toward the user's intended design when many designs satisfy the same invariant.
AI.method: (1) Formal semantics for concepts and reactions enabling automatic verification of safety invariants. (2) A CEGIS-style (Counter-Example Guided Inductive Synthesis), LLM-driven synthesis procedure for generating reaction designs. (3) Two steering mechanisms: natural-language prompts and positive/negative scenarios. (4) An LLM-driven scenario elicitation technique where users classify proposed scenarios instead of authoring them. Evaluation across three applications with twelve design variants using a single LLM configuration.
AI.result: Invariant-only synthesis reached verified designs quickly but produced inconsistent designs across runs, some implausible — invariants alone underconstrain the design task. Scenario-guided synthesis recovered intended designs more consistently than natural-language prompting, though minimal scenarios risked overfitting. LLM-driven scenario elicitation recovered intended designs in most variants when enough scenarios were elicited, but missed behaviors and non-determinism prevented reliable coverage in all cases.
AI.conclusion: Safety invariants alone are insufficient to reliably guide synthesis toward intended reaction designs — the design space is underconstrained. Scenario-based guidance outperforms natural-language prompting for steering synthesis, and LLM-driven scenario elicitation offers a viable approach to early design exploration, though challenges remain with behavioral coverage and non-determinism.

title: Interactive Mascot: A Scene-Centric Interaction Grammar for Data Visualizations
summary: Scene-centric visualization systems expose semantic components, such as marks, encodings, layouts, and axes, as first-class objects that can be directly manipulated. Existing interaction abstractions, however, are largely based on event streams, signals, and data selections rather than semantic scene components. This mismatch makes interactions involving scene components less natural to specify and limits the expressive power of scene-centric visualization systems. We present Interactive Mascot, a scene-centric interaction grammar for data visualizations. Interactive Mascot extends scene-centric representations for static visualizations by modeling interactive behavior as information flow among four interaction components (trigger, responder, evaluator, and updater) and two forms of context (event context and state context). To realize these semantics, we introduce a dependency-graph execution model that systematically transforms interaction specifications into executable dependency graphs using reusable graph patterns associated with semantic visualization components. We implement Interactive Mascot in the JavaScript library Mascot.js and evaluate its expressiveness, performance, and usability. Interactive Mascot naturally covers Vega-Lite's interaction design space while additionally supporting stateful interactions, direct manipulation of scene components, and freeform selection. It achieves runtime performance comparable to Vega-Lite, and a qualitative user study shows that the grammar is learnable and usable for interaction authoring.

AI.tldr: Interactive Mascot is a scene-centric interaction grammar for data visualizations that models interactive behavior as information flow among four interaction components and two context types, implemented via a dependency-graph execution model in Mascot.js, covering Vega-Lite's design space while adding stateful interactions, direct manipulation, and freeform selection.
AI.motivation: Current visualization systems expose semantic scene components (marks, encodings, axes) as first-class objects, but interaction abstractions remain based on event streams, signals, and data selections rather than these semantic components. This mismatch makes specifying interactions involving scene components less natural and limits expressive power.
AI.method: The authors propose Interactive Mascot, which extends scene-centric representations by modeling interactive behavior as information flow among four interaction components: trigger, responder, evaluator, and updater, plus two context forms: event context and state context. They introduce a dependency-graph execution model that transforms interaction specifications into executable dependency graphs using reusable graph patterns tied to semantic visualization components. The grammar is implemented in the JavaScript library Mascot.js.
AI.result: Interactive Mascot naturally covers Vega-Lite's interaction design space while additionally supporting stateful interactions, direct manipulation of scene components, and freeform selection. It achieves runtime performance comparable to Vega-Lite. A qualitative user study demonstrates that the grammar is learnable and usable for interaction authoring.
AI.conclusion: Interactive Mascot successfully bridges the gap between scene-centric visualization representations and interaction specification, providing a more natural and expressive grammar that matches the expressive power of Vega-Lite while extending it with richer interaction capabilities.

title: EpiNarrate: Agentic Generation of Grounded Narratives from Epidemiological Scenario Projections
summary: Generation of clear and accessible public health narratives is critical for communicating complex epidemiological projections to policymakers and the general public at large. Such narratives require more than simply reporting numbers: projections must be contextualized and quantitatively grounded across multiple dimensions. Further, projections are often derived from large ensemble datasets which combine intervention assumptions, geographic and demographic strata, outcomes, time horizons, and uncertainty quantiles. However, directly using large language models (LLMs) to summarize and contextualize such data often leads to inconsistencies, omissions, and fragile behavior. We introduce an agentic framework (EpiNarrate) for public health report generation that separates structured numerical reasoning from natural-language generation. The framework first extracts scenario axes and organizes them into a partial-order schema, enabling systematic traversal of the underlying multidimensional space. It then constructs an augmented dataset and derives valid quantitative statements through a comparison grammar that enforces semantic and arithmetic consistency. To balance coverage and non-redundancy, we introduce an interestingness-driven selection mechanism based on maximum-entropy principles. Experiments on the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub demonstrate that our model produces narratives with improved factual grounding and broader coverage of salient epidemiological patterns, while preserving the style of expert-written reports.

AI.tldr: EpiNarrate is an agentic framework for generating public health reports that separates structured numerical reasoning from natural-language generation, using a partial-order schema, a comparison grammar, and an interestingness-driven selection mechanism to produce narratives with improved factual grounding and coverage from ensemble epidemiological projections.
AI.motivation: Public health narratives must contextualize complex epidemiological projections across multiple dimensions (scenarios, demographics, time horizons, uncertainty quantiles). Direct use of LLMs for this task leads to inconsistencies, omissions, and fragile behavior, motivating a principled framework that decouples numerical reasoning from text generation.
AI.method: The framework operates in stages: (1) extracts scenario axes and organizes them into a partial-order schema for systematic traversal of the multidimensional space; (2) constructs an augmented dataset and derives quantitative statements using a comparison grammar that enforces semantic and arithmetic consistency; (3) employs an interestingness-driven selection mechanism based on maximum-entropy principles to balance coverage with non-redundancy.
AI.result: Experiments on the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub demonstrate that EpiNarrate produces narratives with improved factual grounding and broader coverage of salient epidemiological patterns compared to baselines, while preserving the style of expert-written reports.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling structured numerical reasoning from natural-language generation, combined with principled traversal and selection mechanisms, enables LLM-based systems to produce more reliable, comprehensive public health narratives from complex ensemble projection data.

title: AnovaX: A Local, Multi-Agent Voice Assistant with LLM Planning, Typed Executors, and Adaptive Recovery
summary: Desktop voice assistants are still dominated by cloud pipelines that ship raw audio off the machine and expose a fixed set of skills. We describe AnovaX, a small local-first assistant that runs entirely on the user's computer and treats the desktop itself as its action surface. A single Python process wires together a wake-word gate, a speech pipeline, an LLM planner (Gemini) that emits a JSON plan of tool calls, a whitelist-and-denylist safety layer, a multi-agent orchestrator that translates each plan into typed child agents on a bounded thread pool, and an adaptive recovery loop that takes over whenever a core step fails. Every tool corresponds to a specialized agent class (AppAgent, TypingAgent, BrowserAgent and six others) with its own timeout, retry policy, and shared-resource locks. A recursive MetaAgent lets the planner delegate a sub-goal back to itself, capped at two levels of nesting. The recovery loop uses a compact ReAct-style prompt and hides Gemini's latency behind speculative execution of read-only tools. A companion Flask server exposes a phone-friendly remote over the local WiFi, mirrors every agent lifecycle event to the phone in real time, and streams the laptop's screen back over MJPEG so the user can watch remote commands land as they run. The point of the project is less to compete with Siri or Alexa than to show that a legible, few-thousand-line assistant is enough to open apps, type into them, run searches, coordinate concurrent actions, recover from single-step failures, and be driven entirely from a phone in another room -- without the LLM ever touching the keyboard.

AI.tldr: AnovaX is a compact, local-first desktop voice assistant that runs entirely on-device, using an LLM planner to orchestrate typed agent classes for desktop control, with speculative execution, multi-agent coordination, failure recovery, and phone-based remote operation — all without the LLM directly touching keyboard input.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that a legible, few-thousand-line voice assistant can achieve rich desktop automation — opening apps, typing, searching, coordinating concurrent actions, and recovering from failures — while running entirely locally and being controllable from a phone, offering an alternative to opaque cloud-dependent assistants that ship raw audio off-device.
AI.method: A single Python process integrates: (1) a wake-word gate and speech pipeline, (2) an LLM planner (Gemini) that outputs JSON tool-call plans, (3) a whitelist/denylist safety layer, (4) a multi-agent orchestrator mapping plans to typed child agents (AppAgent, TypingAgent, BrowserAgent, plus six others) on a bounded thread pool with per-agent timeouts, retry policies, and shared-resource locks, (5) a recursive MetaAgent for bounded two-level sub-goal delegation, (6) an adaptive ReAct-style recovery loop with speculative execution of read-only tools to hide LLM latency, and (7) a Flask server for phone-based WiFi remote control with real-time agent lifecycle event mirroring and MJPEG screen streaming.
AI.result: The system successfully demonstrates that a few-thousand-line assistant can open applications, type into them, run searches, coordinate concurrent multi-agent actions, recover from single-step failures, and be driven remotely from a phone — with speculative execution effectively hiding Gemini's latency during recovery.
AI.conclusion: A local-first, transparently architected assistant with typed agents and adaptive recovery is viable for practical desktop automation, challenging the dominance of cloud-dependent voice assistant pipelines while maintaining safety constraints (LLM never directly touches the keyboard) and offering remote phone control.

title: Regularity-Aware Stochastic MGDA with Adaptive Conflict-Avoidant Update Direction Control
summary: Multi-objective learning (MOL) aims to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously. The multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) is a workhorse that iteratively updates along a common descent or conflict-avoidant (CA) direction across objectives. In stochastic settings, however, the vanilla stochastic MGDA method, SMG, lacks a fast convergence rate because mini-batch sampling introduces noise in the gradients. This causes bias in the update direction, which is controlled by the CA direction continuity. In this paper, we show that the CA direction is $1/2$-Holder continuous with respect to the Jacobian matrix, and the exponent $1/2$ cannot be improved in the worst case. This leads to a suboptimal convergence rate for vanilla stochastic MGDA in prior works. Nevertheless, under additional regularity conditions, we show this can be improved to Lipschitz continuity. Based on this insight, we propose a stochastic multi-objective regularity-aware (MoRe) method that exploits the Lipschitz continuity of the CA direction when the subproblem is regular, and switches to a fixed scalarization weight otherwise. Intuitively, the proposed algorithm employs CA direction update when the gradient conflict is large, and linear scalarization update otherwise. Theoretically, our method improves the convergence rate of SMG in the nonconvex setting from $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(T^{-1/4})$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(T^{-1/2})$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic factors. Meanwhile, we also establish the per-iterate conflict-avoidance guarantees. Empirically, experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in multi-task performance and verify convergence behavior consistent with the established theoretical rate.

AI.tldr: Stochastic multi-objective optimization suffers from slow convergence due to noisy gradients biasing the conflict-avoidant (CA) direction. The authors prove the CA direction is 1/2-Hölder continuous (tight), but becomes Lipschitz under regularity conditions. They propose MoRe, which exploits this to switch between CA updates and linear scalarization, improving the convergence rate from O(T^{-1/4}) to O(T^{-1/2}) in nonconvex settings.
AI.motivation: Vanilla stochastic MGDA (SMG) converges slowly because mini-batch gradient noise biases the CA direction. Prior works achieved only O(T^{-1/4}) rates. The authors identify that the root cause lies in the continuity properties of the CA direction mapping and seek to understand and exploit this to design a faster algorithm.
AI.method: First, the authors prove the CA direction is 1/2-Hölder continuous w.r.t. the Jacobian matrix (tight worst-case bound). Under additional regularity conditions (when the minimal-norm element in the convex hull of gradients is unique and a constraint qualification holds), they show Lipschitz continuity. Based on this insight, they propose MoRe (Multi-objective Regularity-aware method): when the subproblem is "regular" (Lipschitz regime), it follows the CA direction; otherwise, it falls back to a fixed linear scalarization. This is implemented by checking gradient conflict magnitude — large conflict triggers CA updates, small conflict triggers scalarization.
AI.result: The proposed MoRe method improves the nonconvex convergence rate from O(T^{-1/4}) to O(T^{-1/2}) (up to logarithmic factors). Per-iterate conflict-avoidance guarantees are also established. Empirical experiments confirm the theoretical rate and demonstrate improved multi-task performance.
AI.conclusion: The CA direction's continuity properties fundamentally govern stochastic MOL convergence. By identifying when Lipschitz continuity holds and designing a regularity-aware switching mechanism, MoRe achieves provably faster convergence while maintaining conflict avoidance, advancing the state of the art in stochastic multi-objective optimization.

title: Improving Network Anomaly Detection via Choquet-Integral-Based Feature Aggregation
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: This work investigates a generalized Choquet-integral-based feature aggregation framework to improve anomaly detection in high-dimensional network traffic data. The approach combines adaptive weighting with incremental feature selection to address feature redundancy. Using Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers, we evaluate models trained with both raw and Choquet-aggregated features under varying feature subset sizes. The proposed aggregation achieves up to $7\%$ higher accuracy while reducing data volume by $77.5\%$ (from $214$~MB to $48$~MB), without degrading precision and recall. Results averaged over multiple stratified repetitions indicate that Choquet-based aggregation yields statistically significant gains ($p < 0.05$) in scenarios with limited feature availability, highlighting its suitability for real-time intrusion detection under bandwidth and feature-availability constraints.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Choquet-integral-based feature aggregation method for network anomaly detection that improves accuracy by up to 7% while reducing data volume by 77.5%, with statistically significant gains under constrained feature availability.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional network traffic data suffers from feature redundancy, and real-time intrusion detection systems face bandwidth and feature-availability constraints that demand efficient, compact representations without sacrificing detection performance.
AI.method: A generalized Choquet-integral-based feature aggregation framework that combines adaptive weighting with incremental feature selection. Features are aggregated via fuzzy measures (Choquet integral) to capture inter-feature interactions. Evaluated using Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers on both raw and Choquet-aggregated features across varying feature subset sizes, with stratified repeated experiments and statistical significance testing.
AI.result: Up to 7% accuracy improvement; data volume reduced by 77.5% (214 MB → 48 MB); precision and recall preserved; statistically significant gains (p < 0.05) under limited feature availability.
AI.conclusion: Choquet-based aggregation is well-suited for real-time intrusion detection under bandwidth and feature-availability constraints, offering compact yet discriminative feature representations with statistically significant performance gains.

title: PCTD: Preference-Guided Counterfactual Task Decomposition for Agent Tool Retrieval
summary: Task decomposition aims to transform ambiguous instructions into executable atomic subtasks, thereby guiding high-precision tool retrieval. However, our analysis reveals that directly adopting tool retrieval metrics, i.e., Recall or NDCG, as rewards for task decomposition can easily induce reward hacking in reinforcement learning-based methods. Specifically, models tend to maximize retrieval matching through strategies such as repetitive decomposition. This spurious correlation between the shallow features of decomposition results and retrieval metric impairs generalization in Out-of-Domain (OOD) scenarios involving unseen tools. To address this issue, we propose PCTD, a Preference-guided Counterfactual Task Decomposition framework. PCTD quantifies the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking through a counterfactual reward, thereby cutting off spurious correlations at their source. Meanwhile, it introduces a preference reward to impose fine-grained structural supervision on logical coherence and atomicity, encouraging the model to generate high-quality decompositions. In addition, we construct MTDTool, the task decomposition benchmark specifically designed for mobile multi-turn interactions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PCTD alleviates repetitive decomposition and surpasses SOTA methods in retrieval, decomposition quality, and OOD generalization.

AI.tldr: To prevent reward hacking (e.g., repetitive decomposition) in RL-based task decomposition for tool retrieval, PCTD uses a counterfactual reward to measure causal gain and a preference reward for structural quality, outperforming SOTA on retrieval, decomposition quality, and OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing methods use retrieval metrics (Recall, NDCG) directly as rewards for training task decomposition models via reinforcement learning. However, this creates a spurious correlation: models exploit shallow features like repetitive decomposition to artificially maximize retrieval matching, harming Out-of-Domain (OOD) generalization when encountering unseen tools. A reward mechanism that captures genuine causal contribution rather than superficial matching is needed.
AI.method: PCTD (Preference-guided Counterfactual Task Decomposition) has two key components: (1) A counterfactual reward that quantifies the marginal causal gain of a decomposition on retrieval ranking, severing spurious correlations at the source. (2) A preference reward that provides fine-grained structural supervision on logical coherence and atomicity. The authors also construct MTDTool, a benchmark for task decomposition in mobile multi-turn interactions.
AI.result: PCTD alleviates the repetitive decomposition problem and surpasses state-of-the-art methods on retrieval performance, decomposition quality, and OOD generalization. Extensive experiments validate these improvements.
AI.conclusion: By replacing naive retrieval-metric rewards with counterfactual and preference-based rewards, PCTD effectively mitigates reward hacking in task decomposition for tool retrieval, yielding robust and generalizable decompositions, especially in OOD settings.

title: GapForge: Directed Compiler Fuzzing via Coverage-Gap Analysis
summary: Modern compiler codebases (e.g., GCC and LLVM) are large and complex, making comprehensive coverage across diverse code regions highly challenging. Most existing test generation techniques ignore characteristics of the target code, producing test programs that exercise only a limited subset of it. Consequently, substantial compiler regions remain insufficiently tested, leaving persistent long-tail coverage gaps that survive across releases. Even existing white-box techniques achieve limited coverage on large-scale compilers. To improve compiler coverage, especially for hard-to-reach edge regions, we present GapForge, a targeted LLM-based test generation technique that reasons about coverage gaps. Unlike program-driven techniques that generate diverse inputs without modeling which regions they exercise, and unlike whole-file summarization that yields coarse guidance, GapForge treats coverage gaps as explicit region-level targets in three steps. First, it prioritizes files via coverage-driven scoring that favors large, undercovered files. Second, it pairs each uncovered line span with its enclosing covered context and performs path-difference analysis to infer fine-grained triggering requirements: the program structures and compilation options needed to reach the uncovered region. Third, it synthesizes prompts from these requirements and previously failed prompts, using coverage feedback to guide next-round selection. On GCC 14.3.0 and LLVM 19.1.0, GapForge significantly outperforms eight state-of-the-art techniques. Within 72 hours, it achieves 68.13% and 69.11% coverage on core compiler modules in GCC and LLVM, surpassing the white-box technique WhiteFox by 24,736 and 19,798 additional lines, respectively. Moreover, GapForge discovers 12 real-world compiler failures (5 in GCC, 7 in LLVM), including 8 crashes and 4 miscompilations, with each component contributing to its performance.

AI.tldr: GapForge is an LLM-based test generation technique that explicitly targets compiler coverage gaps by analyzing uncovered line spans with their enclosing context, inferring triggering requirements, and iteratively refining prompts using coverage feedback. It significantly outperforms existing techniques on GCC and LLVM, achieving ~68-69% core module coverage and discovering 12 real-world compiler bugs.
AI.motivation: Modern compilers (GCC, LLVM) are large and complex codebases with persistent long-tail coverage gaps. Existing test generation techniques—both black-box and white-box—fail to model which code regions are exercised, leaving substantial under-tested regions that survive across releases. A targeted approach is needed to reason about and close these specific coverage gaps.
AI.method: GapForge operates in three steps: (1) Coverage-driven file prioritization—scores and ranks files favoring large, undercovered ones. (2) Path-difference analysis—pairs each uncovered line span with its enclosing covered context to infer fine-grained triggering requirements (program structures and compilation options needed to reach the gap). (3) LLM-based prompt synthesis—generates prompts from these requirements and previously failed prompts, using coverage feedback for iterative next-round selection.
AI.result: On GCC 14.3.0 and LLVM 19.1.0 within 72 hours, GapForge achieves 68.13% and 69.11% line coverage on core compiler modules, outperforming 8 state-of-the-art techniques. It surpasses WhiteFox by 24,736 (GCC) and 19,798 (LLVM) additional covered lines. GapForge also discovers 12 real-world compiler failures: 8 crashes and 4 miscompilations (5 in GCC, 7 in LLVM).
AI.conclusion: GapForge demonstrates that treating coverage gaps as explicit region-level targets, combined with path-difference analysis and LLM-driven iterative prompt synthesis, is highly effective for improving compiler test coverage. Each component contributes to its performance, enabling the discovery of real-world bugs in hard-to-reach compiler regions.

title: CASAband: Easy-to-Wear Textile Wristband using Shape Memory Alloy Actuators for Spatial and Temporal Haptic Feedback
summary: Haptic interfaces for the wrist and forearm offer an attractive alternative to hand-worn devices as they are simple to wear, leave the hands free for interaction with the real world, and interfere minimally with natural arm motions. To be useful in real-world settings, however, such devices must balance functionality, wearability and comfort, all while being fully untethered with minimal mass and volume. In this work, we present CASAband, a haptic wristband that integrates compliant amplified shape memory alloy actuators (CASA) into a multi-layered textile wristband to deliver spatial and temporal haptic feedback. CASAband operates completely untethered, generates no noise, and has a total mass of 63 g. The device incorporates four actuators that can generate up to 1.7 N of blocked force and 3.2 mm of free displacement with an operating bandwidth ranging from 1.34-6.59 Hz depending on the applied voltage. We conducted a perceptual study and determined that users could identify the location of a single haptic cue around their wrist and discriminate among several patterned cues with over 90% accuracy on average, highlighting that CASAband can be a suitable wearable interface to deliver information for real-world guidance and navigation tasks. To highlight the potential use cases for CASAband, we conducted two demonstrations: a pick and place task where the user relied only on haptic communication from a moderator, and an outdoor pedestrian navigation task where the user relied only on directional cues on the wrist. CASAband is one of the first haptic interfaces that balances the tradeoff between form and function and presents new opportunities for haptic feedback in the real world

AI.tldr: CASAband is a 63g untethered textile wristband using compliant amplified shape memory alloy actuators (CASA) to deliver silent, spatial haptic feedback with >90% user accuracy in cue identification, demonstrated in pick-and-place and outdoor navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing haptic wrist/forearm devices struggle to simultaneously achieve wearability, comfort, full untethered operation, and minimal mass/volume while maintaining functional haptic performance for real-world use.
AI.method: The authors developed CASAband, a multi-layered textile wristband integrating four CASA actuators. They characterized actuator performance (blocked force up to 1.7 N, free displacement up to 3.2 mm, bandwidth 1.34–6.59 Hz depending on voltage), conducted a perceptual study measuring user accuracy in localizing single cues and discriminating patterned cues, and performed two real-world demonstrations (collaborative pick-and-place and outdoor pedestrian navigation).
AI.result: Users identified single haptic cue locations and discriminated patterned cues with over 90% average accuracy. The device operates untethered, silently, at 63 g total mass, with four actuators delivering up to 1.7 N blocked force and 3.2 mm free displacement.
AI.conclusion: CASAband successfully balances form and function as a wearable haptic interface, demonstrating viability for real-world guidance and navigation applications where hands-free, silent, and comfortable haptic communication is needed.

title: SkillCorpus: Consolidating and Evaluating the Open Skill Ecosystem for Real-World LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills, SKILL.md files that package reusable procedural knowledge for an LLM agent, are a popular mechanism for extending agent capabilities. Public repositories now host them in large and growing numbers, yet these artifacts are fragmented, redundant, and uneven in quality, and their value in practice is unclear. A core question remains open, namely how to consolidate this open-source SKILL.md ecosystem into a single usable corpus, and what bounds its benefit on real-world agent tasks. We present SkillCorpus, a framework that aggregates, curates, matches, and evaluates the open skill ecosystem at scale. It filters ~821,000 crawled skills through a multi-stage pipeline into 96,401 skills organised by a 16-class taxonomy and three quality facets (utility, robustness, safety), and pairs them with a fine-tuned retrieval-and-selection stack that matches task-relevant skills. We evaluate end-to-end across three benchmarks (SkillsBench, GDPVal, QwenClawBench), two harnesses, and two open backbones with a frontier robustness check. Integrating SkillCorpus yields consistent gains across all three benchmarks, largest on SkillsBench (+7.5 pp). An operational analysis traces the gains to a coverage boundary and a harness boundary. SkillCorpus is, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end account of when a curated, retrieval-served community corpus improves real agent tasks, and where it does not. The dataset, models, and code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: SkillCorpus is a framework that aggregates ~821,000 crawled open-source agent skills, curates them into 96,401 high-quality skills via a multi-stage pipeline with taxonomy and quality scoring, and pairs them with a retrieval-and-selection stack to serve task-relevant skills to LLM agents, yielding consistent benchmark gains (up to +7.5 pp on SkillsBench).
AI.motivation: The open-source SKILL.md ecosystem is growing rapidly but suffers from fragmentation, redundancy, and uneven quality. It remains unclear whether consolidating these skills into a single usable corpus can measurably benefit real-world agent tasks, and what the practical boundaries of such benefit are.
AI.method: SkillCorpus uses a multi-stage pipeline: (1) crawling ~821,000 skills from public repositories; (2) filtering and curating them into 96,401 skills; (3) organizing them by a 16-class taxonomy and scoring along three quality facets (utility, robustness, safety); (4) a fine-tuned retrieval-and-selection stack that matches task-relevant skills to agent queries. Evaluation uses three benchmarks (SkillsBench, GDPVal, QwenClawBench), two harnesses, and two open backbones with a frontier robustness check.
AI.result: Integrating SkillCorpus yields consistent performance gains across all three benchmarks, with the largest improvement on SkillsBench (+7.5 pp). An operational analysis identifies two key boundaries: a coverage boundary and a harness boundary that explain where and why the corpus helps or does not.
AI.conclusion: SkillCorpus provides the first end-to-end account of how a curated, retrieval-served community skill corpus can improve real agent tasks, delineating both its benefits and limitations. The dataset, models, and code will be publicly released.

title: Precise but Uncoupled: Reviewer Precision Does Not Guarantee Critique Uptake in Multi-Agent Math Reasoning
comment: 48 pages, 20 figures, 25 tables. Public release website: https://huggingface.co/spaces/AgentsSci/scientific-agent-protocol-traces-site
summary: Many math- and science-oriented agent systems use hierarchical designs with specialized reviewer roles, assuming that a dedicated review stage should help turn wrong candidates into correct ones. We test this assumption on 4,181 verifier-grounded Omni-MATH problems using matched gpt-oss-120b actors. Collaboration adds little on the easiest tiers, but from tier 4 onward the gains open sharply; in this harder regime, broadcast-style peer discussion reaches higher final accuracy than a planner-executor-reviewer pipeline (PER). We ask whether this gap is explained by reviewer quality or by whether critique changes the next answer the protocol carries forward. It is not explained by reviewer precision alone: PER's reviewer is more precise than broadcast's (0.861 vs. 0.644), yet evaluator-verified useful critique is much less likely to change the next candidate and produces lower reviewer-guided repair. These results show that reviewer detection quality and critique uptake are empirically separable. Within matched PER interventions, forcing explicit acknowledgment lowers final accuracy, while embedding reviewer guidance directly in the solver's working context partially improves follow-through without closing the gap. Overall, reviewer-centric evaluation can overstate system quality: a protocol may spot errors well yet still fail to solve more problems if it does not act on those critiques.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether dedicated reviewer stages in hierarchical agent systems improve problem-solving accuracy. Testing on 4,181 Omni-MATH problems with gpt-oss-120b, the authors find that reviewer precision and critique uptake are empirically separable: a reviewer can detect errors well but fail to improve outcomes if the system doesn't act on critiques. Broadcast-style peer discussion outperforms planner-executor-reviewer pipelines on harder problems, despite lower reviewer precision.
AI.motivation: Many math and science agent systems assume that specialized reviewer roles improve correctness by catching and correcting errors. The authors challenge this assumption by testing whether reviewer quality actually translates into better final answers, and whether alternative collaboration protocols (broadcast peer discussion vs. hierarchical PER) differ in their ability to convert critique into improved solutions.
AI.method: The experiment uses 4,181 verifier-grounded Omni-MATH problems with matched gpt-oss-120b actors. Two protocols are compared: a planner-executor-reviewer (PER) pipeline and broadcast-style peer discussion. The authors analyze reviewer precision, critique uptake (whether critique changes the next candidate), and reviewer-guided repair rates. They also test interventions: forcing explicit acknowledgment of reviewer feedback and embedding reviewer guidance directly in the solver's working context.
AI.result: Collaboration adds negligible benefit on easy tiers, but from tier 4 onward gains diverge sharply. Broadcast peer discussion achieves higher final accuracy than PER on harder problems. PER's reviewer is more precise (0.861 vs. 0.644), yet evaluator-verified useful critique is less likely to change the next candidate and produces lower reviewer-guided repair. Forcing explicit acknowledgment lowers accuracy, while embedding reviewer guidance in the solver's context partially improves follow-through but does not close the accuracy gap.
AI.conclusion: Reviewer-centric evaluation can overstate system quality: a protocol may spot errors well yet still fail to solve more problems if it does not act on those critiques. Reviewer detection quality and critique uptake are empirically separable dimensions, and protocol design must account for both to achieve effective error correction.

title: AI Trading: Evaluating Large Language Models for Technical Market Analysis
comment: Master's research paper, Georgia Institute of Technology. 31 pages, 4 figures
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for processing the heterogeneous information environments of modern financial markets. This paper presents a systematic, comparative evaluation of five prominent LLMs: GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 70B, and the domain-specialized FinGPT, with respect to their capacity for technical market analysis. The evaluation spans four structured tasks: candlestick pattern recognition from OHLCV data, directional signal generation (BUY/SELL/HOLD), backtesting of signal quality through a simulated execution pipeline, and financial report comprehension. Our experimental framework employs rigorous quantitative metrics, including Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, Sortino ratio, information coefficient, F1-score, and BLEU score. Findings from simulated backtesting indicate that GPT-4 Turbo achieves the highest annualized return and Sharpe ratio among general-purpose models, while FinGPT demonstrates competitive risk-adjusted performance due to domain-specific fine-tuning. Both models outperform a passive S&P 500 benchmark under the tested conditions. The study identifies persistent failure modes across all evaluated models, including numerical hallucination, context-window limitations, and inconsistent performance in sideways market regimes. We conclude that while LLMs hold genuine promise within AI trading systems, robust deployment requires careful task decomposition, rigorous backtesting protocols, and domain-aware fine-tuning strategies.

AI.tldr: A comparative evaluation of five LLMs (GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 70B, FinGPT) on technical market analysis tasks shows GPT-4 Turbo leads in risk-adjusted returns during backtesting, while FinGPT excels through domain-specific fine-tuning. All models exhibit numerical hallucination, context-window limitations, and struggles in sideways markets, indicating that robust deployment requires task decomposition and rigorous backtesting.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly applied to financial markets, yet there lacks a systematic, quantitative comparison of their technical analysis capabilities. The authors aim to fill this gap by rigorously benchmarking both general-purpose and domain-specialized models across well-defined trading-relevant tasks.
AI.method: Five LLMs (GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 70B, FinGPT) are evaluated on four structured tasks: (1) candlestick pattern recognition from OHLCV data, (2) directional signal generation (BUY/SELL/HOLD), (3) simulated backtesting of signal quality, and (4) financial report comprehension. Quantitative metrics include Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, Sortino ratio, information coefficient, F1-score, and BLEU score.
AI.result: GPT-4 Turbo achieved the highest annualized return and Sharpe ratio among general-purpose models. FinGPT showed competitive risk-adjusted performance due to domain-specific fine-tuning. Both outperformed a passive S&P 500 benchmark. Across all models, persistent failures were identified: numerical hallucination, context-window constraints, and degraded performance in sideways market regimes.
AI.conclusion: LLMs hold genuine promise for AI trading systems, but robust deployment demands careful task decomposition, rigorous backtesting protocols, and domain-aware fine-tuning strategies to mitigate known failure modes.

title: FLINT: Fingerprinting Federated Learning Architectures from 5G PHY-Layer Side Channels
summary: Federated Learning (FL) over 5G cellular networks protects raw data but remains vulnerable to side-channel leakage. Prior fingerprinting attacks assume packet-level network visibility, an assumption that does not hold at the 5G Physical (PHY) layer, where user payloads are encrypted and Radio Network Temporary Identifiers (RNTIs) may change over time. However, we demonstrate that PHY-layer scheduling metadata broadcast over the Physical Downlink Control Channel (PDCCH) preserves architecture-associated temporal patterns. We introduce FLINT, a novel black-box fingerprinting framework that infers FL model architecture families, including CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers, using only coarse PHY-layer observations. FLINT overcomes the lack of network-layer visibility by decoding PDCCH scheduling information, mapping changing RNTIs to physical user devices, and applying multi-view temporal modeling to distinguish architecture-specific training behavior. This leakage is security-critical because knowledge of a client's model architecture can transform passive reconnaissance into targeted downstream exploitation. Extensive experiments on an over-the-air srsRAN-based 5G testbed demonstrate that FLINT achieves a macro F1-score of 0.930 for architecture-family classification. To our knowledge, FLINT is the first work to fingerprint AI/ML model architectures using lower-layer 5G side-channel information obtainable by any protocol-aware adversary.

AI.tldr: FLINT is a black-box attack that fingerprints FL model architecture families (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) by exploiting PHY-layer PDCCH scheduling metadata in 5G networks, achieving 0.930 macro F1-score without needing packet-level visibility.
AI.motivation: Prior FL fingerprinting attacks rely on packet-level network visibility, which is unavailable at the encrypted 5G PHY layer. This paper addresses the open question of whether lower-layer side-channel information—specifically PDCCH scheduling metadata—can still leak model architecture information despite encryption and changing RNTIs.
AI.method: FLINT operates in three stages: (1) decoding PDCCH Downlink Control Information (DCI) to extract scheduling metadata; (2) mapping dynamically changing RNTIs to persistent physical devices via temporal correlation heuristics; (3) applying multi-view temporal modeling to classify architecture-specific traffic patterns into CNN, RNN, and Transformer families.
AI.result: Evaluated on an over-the-air srsRAN-based 5G testbed, FLINT achieves a macro F1-score of 0.930 for architecture-family classification, demonstrating robust leakage despite PHY-layer encryption and RNTI reassignment.
AI.conclusion: PHY-layer side-channel leakage constitutes a realistic and critical threat to FL privacy in 5G networks. Knowledge of a client's model architecture enables targeted downstream attacks, and any protocol-aware adversary can mount FLINT without network-layer visibility.

title: From Skill Extraction to Multistakeholder Recommendation: A Two-Stage Framework for Bias Governance in Skills-Based Job Matching
comment: Accepted to BIAS Conference 2026 in Leiden, The Netherlands
summary: AI-based labor-market systems or platforms can affect access to job opportunities prior to organizational candidate rankings or hiring decisions. Such applications warrant caution, as biases in skill extraction, profile formation, and candidate-job matching may contribute to unfair treatment of candidates. In this paper, we propose a two-stage framework for detecting and governing bias in skills-based job matching. Stage 1, skill extraction and profile formation, addresses how candidates provide skills and preferences to the system, how the system extracts and structures this information, and the bias risks this entails, with a focus on chatbot-based elicitation. Stage 2, multistakeholder candidate-job recommendation, would embed this information in a recommender system in which candidate, company, and regulatory objectives are represented by separate agents, each producing an independent candidate-job ranking; these rankings would be combined through social choice-based aggregation into a single, auditable recommendation. The two stages are connected by a shared distinction between hard constraints, which require correction before processing continues, and soft constraints, which are logged to inform later decisions. Following an AI Act-aligned assessment methodology (based on the Fraunhofer AI Assessment Catalog), we propose using distributional auditing and counterfactual testing to produce a Stage 1 bias inventory sorted into hard and soft constraints, with the latter informing fairness thresholds for Stage 2. The same logic would apply to Stage 2: fairness metrics crossing predefined thresholds would trigger an adapted recommendation process, while smaller deviations would be logged as bias reports and persistent fairness states.

AI.tldr: Proposes a two-stage framework for detecting and governing bias in AI-based skills-based job matching: Stage 1 addresses bias in skill extraction and profile formation via chatbot elicitation, distinguishing hard/soft constraints; Stage 2 uses multi-agent recommender systems with social choice aggregation to balance candidate, company, and regulatory objectives. Both stages employ distributional auditing and counterfactual testing aligned with the EU AI Act.
AI.motivation: AI-based labor-market platforms can introduce unfair treatment of candidates through biases in skill extraction, profile formation, and candidate-job matching, occurring before organizational hiring decisions. Existing systems lack systematic mechanisms to detect, categorize, and govern these biases across the full matching pipeline, necessitating a structured governance framework aligned with emerging AI regulations like the EU AI Act.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: Stage 1 — chatbot-based skill elicitation and profile formation where biases are detected via distributional auditing and counterfactual testing, then classified into hard constraints (requiring correction) and soft constraints (logged for downstream use). Stage 2 — a multi-stakeholder recommender system where candidate, company, and regulatory agents independently rank candidate-job pairs, aggregated via social choice mechanisms into a single auditable recommendation. Fairness thresholds derived from Stage 1's soft constraints govern Stage 2: threshold violations trigger adapted recommendations, minor deviations are logged as bias reports. The methodology follows the Fraunhofer AI Assessment Catalog, aligned with the AI Act.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework rather than empirical results. It contributes a structured, auditable pipeline connecting skill extraction bias detection to multi-stakeholder recommendation governance, with operationalizable mechanisms (hard/soft constraint taxonomy, distributional auditing, counterfactual testing, social choice aggregation) designed for AI Act compliance.
AI.conclusion: A two-stage governance framework with shared constraint logic can systematically detect and mitigate bias in skills-based job matching platforms, providing auditability and regulatory alignment. The hard/soft constraint distinction enables both mandatory corrections and persistent fairness monitoring, while multi-agent social choice aggregation balances competing stakeholder interests transparently.

title: Making Agent-Mediated Contributions Governable: A Project-Level Governance Manifest for Open-Source AI Collaboration
summary: Generative AI and coding agents are intensifying a central governance tension in open-source software (OSS): they scale contribution generation faster than maintainers can assess risk, evidence, and accountability. Existing responses improve agent-readability and traceability, but project rules must also organize contribution-specific risk, evidence, accountability, and review-gate states. We theorize this organizational arrangement as project-side governability infrastructure. A diagnostic audit of 50 GitHub repositories finds widespread general governance artifacts, observable agent-readability, and fragmented AI-governance cues, but no project-wide arrangement that coordinates shared rules, preparation obligations, verification rights, and maintainer decision authority across AI-mediated contribution workflows. We develop the Agent Governance Manifest (AGM) as a repository-hosted boundary resource and bidirectional governance contract linking contributor-side evidence preparation with maintainer-side verification. In a controlled reviewer-side evaluation with 15 participants and 75 task-level outputs, AGM-supported materials improved exact risk-label recovery (37/38 vs. 15/37) and perceived review support (6.14 vs. 3.27 on a 1-7 scale). In a contributor-side feasibility check, 15 participants completed 45 tasks; all final packages represented the core governance state correctly, and 41 passed strict structural validation. The study develops a three-layer framework of agent-readability, traceability, and governability, theorizes agent-mediated contributions as governable boundary objects, and advances compliance-enabling digital innovation governance while preserving maintainer decision authority.

AI.tldr: Generative AI coding agents create contributions faster than open-source maintainers can assess risk, evidence, and accountability. The paper audits 50 GitHub repos, finds fragmented AI governance, and proposes the Agent Governance Manifest (AGM) — a repository-hosted boundary resource that links contributor evidence preparation with maintainer verification. Evaluations show AGM improves risk-label recovery and perceived review support while preserving maintainer decision authority.
AI.motivation: Generative AI and coding agents are scaling contribution generation in open-source software faster than maintainers can perform adequate risk assessment, evidence evaluation, and accountability attribution. Existing solutions focus narrowly on agent-readability and traceability but fail to provide project-wide organizational arrangements that coordinate governance rules, preparation obligations, verification rights, and maintainer decision authority across AI-mediated contribution workflows. This governance gap threatens the integrity and sustainability of open-source projects.
AI.method: The study proceeds in four phases: (1) Theorization of project-side governability infrastructure as an organizational arrangement coordinating risk, evidence, accountability, and review-gate states. (2) A diagnostic audit of 50 GitHub repositories examining general governance artifacts, agent-readability, and AI-governance cues. (3) Design and development of the Agent Governance Manifest (AGM) as a repository-hosted boundary resource and bidirectional governance contract. (4) Two empirical evaluations: a controlled reviewer-side evaluation with 15 participants across 75 task-level outputs measuring risk-label recovery and perceived review support; and a contributor-side feasibility check with 15 participants completing 45 tasks assessing governance state representation and structural validation.
AI.result: The diagnostic audit revealed widespread general governance artifacts and observable agent-readability but no project-wide arrangement coordinating AI-mediated contribution workflows. In the reviewer-side evaluation, AGM-supported materials significantly outperformed baseline: exact risk-label recovery was 37/38 versus 15/37, and perceived review support scored 6.14 versus 3.27 on a 1–7 scale. In the contributor-side feasibility check, all 45 final packages correctly represented the core governance state, and 41 of 45 passed strict structural validation.
AI.conclusion: The paper develops a three-layer framework comprising agent-readability, traceability, and governability, and theorizes agent-mediated contributions as governable boundary objects. The AGM advances compliance-enabling digital innovation governance by structuring risk, evidence, and accountability obligations while preserving maintainer decision authority. The study demonstrates that project-side governability infrastructure is both feasible and effective for managing the governance tension introduced by generative AI in open-source software ecosystems.

title: Physiological Prior-Driven Label Enhancement for Cross-Subject EEG Emotion Recognition
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based emotion recognition captures affective neural signals with high temporal precision, but cross-subject variability and label noise remain critical challenges to its practical healthcare deployment. Existing label-denoising methods lack physiological grounding, while physiology-informed approaches rely on hand-crafted hyperparameters. To bridge these two paradigms, we propose PhyDA, a plug-and-play, tuning-free framework that unifies neurophysiological priors with data-driven label refinement. PhyDA comprises two modules. Since cross-subject variability renders global thresholds suboptimal, the Physiological Noise Quantifier (PhyNQ) exploits a spectral slope} to produce a subject-specific noise score, providing a neurophysiologically interpretable quality assessment {that naturally adapts to each individual. The Data-Adaptive Label Refiner (DALR) directly adopts this noise score as the contamination ratio to drive a label refinement pipeline that requires no additional neural network training, thereby directly mitigating the impact of inter-subject label noise. Extensive experiments on three public datasets (DEAP, SEED, SEED-IV) across seven backbone architectures under strict leave-one-subject-out cross-validation demonstrate that PhyDA consistently and significantly outperforms both general and EEG-tailored label-denoising baselines, achieving average accuracy gains of 2.76%, 2.66%, and 3.32%, respectively. Visualization further confirms its neurophysiological interpretability and practical robustness. The source code is available at: https://github.com/HongyuZhu-s/PhyDA.

AI.tldr: PhyDA is a tuning-free, plug-and-play framework for EEG emotion recognition that unifies neurophysiological priors with data-driven label refinement, using a spectral-slope-based subject-specific noise quantifier and a training-free label refiner to mitigate cross-subject label noise, achieving significant accuracy gains across multiple datasets and architectures.
AI.motivation: EEG-based emotion recognition suffers from two critical challenges: (1) cross-subject variability that undermines generalization, and (2) label noise in affective annotations. Existing label-denoising methods lack physiological grounding, while physiology-informed approaches depend on hand-crafted hyperparameters that do not adapt to individual differences. There is a need to bridge these two paradigms.
AI.method: PhyDA introduces two modules: (1) Physiological Noise Quantifier (PhyNQ), which computes a spectral slope to generate a subject-specific noise score, offering a neurophysiologically interpretable quality assessment that adapts to each individual; and (2) Data-Adaptive Label Refiner (DALR), which directly adopts this noise score as the contamination ratio to drive label refinement without requiring additional neural network training. The framework is plug-and-play and tuning-free.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on DEAP, SEED, and SEED-IV datasets across seven backbone architectures under strict leave-one-subject-out cross-validation show PhyDA consistently and significantly outperforms both general and EEG-tailored label-denoising baselines, with average accuracy gains of 2.76%, 2.66%, and 3.32% respectively. Visualization confirms neurophysiological interpretability and practical robustness.
AI.conclusion: PhyDA successfully bridges physiology-informed and data-driven label-denoising paradigms, providing an interpretable, tuning-free solution that adapts to individual subjects' noise characteristics and significantly boosts EEG emotion recognition performance without requiring additional model retraining.

title: Process Reward Informed Tree Rollout for Effective Multi-Turn RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key approach for training LLM agents, yet popular methods such as GRPO/RLOO rely on multiple independently sampled complete trajectories for advantage estimation. In long-horizon agentic tasks, such a uniform rollout strategy can waste budget on uninformative dead-end attempts, while promising intermediate states do not receive sufficient exploration. The multi-turn structure of agentic trajectories, with interleaved actions and observations, naturally supports organizing a trajectory group as a tree, where each turn serves as a decision point for exploration. This perspective reframes effective exploration as the problem of deciding where to branch. We propose Process-Scorer Guided Adaptive Tree Rollout (PATR), a quality-aware rollout framework for multi-turn agent RL. PATR uses task-appropriate process feedback to score partial trajectories, selectively branches from promising states, reuses shared prefixes, and conservatively stops degenerate paths to reduce wasted sampling. The resulting rollout groups remain compatible with standard policy optimization while providing more efficient exploration under the same training budget. We evaluate PATR on FrozenLake and the challenging SWE-Bench, which is largely unexplored by prior tree-rollout agent RL methods. Experiments show that PATR improves performance by up to +5.0 points on SWE-Bench and +9.3 points on FrozenLake, highlighting process-guided tree rollouts as an effective strategy for scalable multi-turn RL.

AI.tldr: PATR introduces a tree-structured rollout strategy for multi-turn agent RL that uses process feedback to selectively branch from promising states, reuse shared prefixes, and stop degenerate paths early, improving exploration efficiency under fixed training budgets.
AI.motivation: Standard RL methods like GRPO/RLOO sample complete trajectories independently, which wastes budget on dead-end paths and under-explores promising intermediate states in long-horizon agentic tasks. The multi-turn structure of agent interactions naturally suits tree-based exploration, but existing methods lack a principled way to decide where to branch.
AI.method: PATR organizes trajectory groups as trees where each turn is a decision point. It uses a process scorer to evaluate partial trajectories, branches from high-scoring intermediate states, reuses shared prefixes across rollouts, and conservatively terminates low-quality paths. The resulting rollout groups remain compatible with standard policy optimization (GRPO/RLOO).
AI.result: PATR achieves up to +5.0 points improvement on SWE-Bench and +9.3 points on FrozenLake compared to baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of process-guided tree rollouts for scalable multi-turn RL.
AI.conclusion: Process-guided adaptive tree rollouts are an effective and scalable strategy for improving exploration in multi-turn agent RL, particularly for long-horizon tasks where uniform trajectory sampling is inefficient.

title: DrawingVQA: A Real-World Benchmark for Multi-Depth Visual-Textual Reasoning on Construction Drawings
summary: We introduce DrawingVQA, the first benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on real-world construction drawings -- a core media in architecture, civil, and many other engineering practices. Unlike natural images or schematic floor plans, construction drawings fuse abstract geometry, symbolic notation, tabular data, annotations, and domain-specific text, forming a uniquely complex visual-textual domain core to engineering workflows. DrawingVQA bridges this gap with 33 "Issued for Construction" drawings and 92 expertly curated question-answer pairs, spanning three reasoning depths: perceptual understanding, contextual interpretation, and domain-expert reasoning. To evaluate model capabilities, we present a dual categorization framework to jointly analyze performance across seven construction-engineering and four MLLM capability dimensions -- the first to explicitly map engineering workflows to AI reasoning competencies. Evaluations of state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal a substantial gap between model and expert performance, particularly at higher reasoning depths. This benchmark lays a foundation for domain-specialized multimodal reasoning to allow for advancement on integration of AI-driven understanding and real-world engineering workflows.

AI.tldr: DrawingVQA is the first benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on real-world construction drawings, featuring 33 drawings and 92 QA pairs across three reasoning depths. It introduces a dual categorization framework mapping engineering workflows to AI reasoning competencies, revealing significant performance gaps between models and human experts.
AI.motivation: Construction drawings are a fundamentally distinct visual-textual domain combining abstract geometry, symbolic notation, tables, annotations, and domain text — yet no benchmark exists to evaluate MLLMs on this medium critical to architecture, civil, and engineering workflows.
AI.method: DrawingVQA comprises 33 "Issued for Construction" drawings and 92 expert-curated QA pairs across three reasoning depths (perceptual understanding, contextual interpretation, domain-expert reasoning). A dual categorization framework jointly evaluates performance along seven construction-engineering dimensions and four MLLM capability dimensions.
AI.result: State-of-the-art MLLMs show a substantial performance gap compared to expert human performance, particularly at higher reasoning depths requiring domain-expert reasoning.
AI.conclusion: DrawingVQA establishes a foundation for domain-specialized multimodal reasoning, highlighting the need for AI systems that can integrate understanding of complex engineering drawings into real-world workflows.

title: qZACH-ViT: Quantization-Aware Intrinsic Explanations with Recursive Attribution-Stabilized Optimization
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Includes executable mixed-precision ONNX INT8 deployment validation across 210 checkpoints
summary: Compact medical-image classifiers need efficiency and interpretable evidence, yet these goals are often addressed separately. We introduce qZACH-ViT, a quantization-aware extension of the zero-token (CLS-token-free), position-free ZACH-ViT backbone with recursive intrinsic patch-level class evidence. We also introduce Recursive Attribution-Stabilized Optimization (RASO), which norm-matches classification and attribution gradients and removes attribution components that conflict with classification. We evaluate four controlled conditions on seven MedMNIST datasets using 50 training images per class and ten fixed seeds, completing 280 runs. All 210 qZACH-ViT checkpoints are converted to executable mixed-precision ONNX INT8 graphs containing 16 signed INT8 MatMulInteger projections with INT32 accumulation. Deployed mixed-precision INT8 qZACH-ViT with Adam improves the FP32 ZACH-ViT baseline mean on all seven datasets, with a mean paired gain of 0.0313 in the dataset-specific primary metric; qZACH-ViT with RASO yields a mean gain of 0.0368. Across 964,920 source-to-INT8 test comparisons, prediction agreement is 99.9751\%, with a mean absolute primary-metric change of 0.000133 and a maximum of 0.004386. Across 3,600 matched intrinsic maps, mean cosine similarity is 0.999955, mean rank correlation is 0.9944, and mean top-10\% overlap is 0.9692. ONNX artifacts are 70.0\% smaller than source checkpoints and provide $1.41\times$ and $2.39\times$ end-to-end CPU speedups with one and four threads. RASO significantly reduces sufficiency error and improves input-noise stability over Adam with the same attribution loss, but does not dominate every predictive or explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) metric. These results establish qZACH-ViT as a deployable compact intrinsically explainable model and RASO as a targeted stability-oriented optimization procedure.

AI.tldr: qZACH-ViT is a quantized, zero-token Vision Transformer that produces intrinsic patch-level explanations. Combined with the proposed RASO optimizer, it achieves mixed-precision INT8 deployment with near-identical predictions and explanations to FP32, while improving accuracy and delivering significant model compression and CPU speedups.
AI.motivation: Compact medical-image classifiers require both computational efficiency (for deployment) and interpretable evidence (for trust/clinical adoption), but these goals are typically pursued independently.
