The authors aim to unify them in a single deployable model that retains intrinsic explainability after quantization.
AI.method: The authors propose qZACH-ViT, a quantization-aware extension of ZACH-ViT (a CLS-token-free, position-free ViT with recursive intrinsic patch-level evidence). They also introduce RASO (Recursive Attribution-Stabilized Optimization), which aligns classification and attribution gradient norms while removing attribution components conflicting with classification. Models are trained on 50 images/class across seven MedMNIST datasets (280 runs), then converted to ONNX INT8 mixed-precision graphs using 16 signed INT8 MatMulInteger projections with INT32 accumulation.
AI.result: qZACH-ViT with Adam improves over FP32 ZACH-ViT baseline on all seven datasets (mean gain 0.0313); with RASO, mean gain is 0.0368. INT8 prediction agreement vs. source is 99.9751% (over 964,920 comparisons). Attribution map similarity: mean cosine 0.999955, mean rank correlation 0.9944, top-10% overlap 0.9692. ONNX artifacts are 70% smaller, with 1.41× (1-thread) and 2.39× (4-thread) CPU speedups. RASO significantly improves sufficiency error and input-noise stability vs. Adam with same attribution loss, but does not dominate all predictive or XAI metrics.
AI.conclusion: qZACH-ViT is established as a deployable, compact, intrinsically explainable model suitable for medical imaging. RASO provides targeted stability-oriented optimization. The work bridges the gap between efficient deployment and interpretability, showing that INT8 quantization can preserve both predictive performance and explanation fidelity.

title: From Neural Intent to Cryptographic Authorization: Governing Agentic Workflows
summary: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven and agentic workflows is transforming traditional government and enterprise systems into language-based, tool-using and increasingly autonomous infrastructures. Conventional key management services authenticate who may invoke a cryptographic primitive, but remain agnostic to which workflow steps are authorized at runtime: an authenticated agent can still be hijacked by direct or indirect prompt injection into executing malicious actions that satisfy identity checks yet violate user intent. We present \emph{Neural Cryptographic Services} (NCS), an active security governance plane grounded in a neural-symbolic design and interposed between LLM agents and privileged tools. Under NCS, an untrusted neural planner compiles natural-language instructions into structured plan drafts but holds no execution authority. Execution is instead gated by a deterministic symbolic controller operating over an offline-signed, hash-chained instruction stream. NCS verifies the signature, incrementally validates the hash chain, releases exactly one instruction payload at a time, and enforces strict binding between the agent's proposed tool parameters and the verified payload. Mismatched or out-of-order tool calls are rejected fail-closed, while previously verified states are retained for post-hoc auditing. We evaluate NCS on AgentDojo and a custom argument-hijacking benchmark. NCS drives attack success rates to near zero while preserving acceptable utility on benign workflows. NCS thus reframes agent security from asking whether a model's intent complied to asking whether a proposed dispatch matches a cryptographically authorized step.

AI.tldr: Neural Cryptographic Services (NCS) introduces a security governance plane that interposes a deterministic symbolic controller between LLM agents and privileged tools. The controller executes only cryptographically signed, hash-chained instruction streams, rejecting any tool call whose parameters do not match the verified payload — reducing prompt injection attack success to near zero while preserving benign workflow utility.
AI.motivation: Conventional key management services authenticate agent identity but are agnostic to runtime workflow authorization — an authenticated LLM agent can be hijacked via prompt injection into executing malicious actions that satisfy identity checks yet violate user intent. There is a need for security that binds tool invocation to cryptographically authorized workflow steps.
AI.method: NCS employs a neural-symbolic architecture: an untrusted neural planner compiles natural-language instructions into structured plan drafts, while a deterministic symbolic controller gates execution using an offline-signed, hash-chained instruction stream. The controller verifies signatures, incrementally validates the hash chain, releases one instruction payload at a time, and enforces strict binding between the agent's proposed tool parameters and the verified payload. Mismatched or out-of-order calls are rejected fail-closed, with verified states retained for post-hoc auditing.
AI.result: Evaluated on AgentDojo and a custom argument-hijacking benchmark, NCS drives attack success rates to near zero while preserving acceptable utility on benign workflows.
AI.conclusion: NCS reframes agent security from assessing whether a model's intent complied with policy to assessing whether a proposed dispatch matches a cryptographically authorized step, providing a robust defense against prompt injection in agentic workflows.

title: RECAP: Feedback-Driven Streaming Semantic User Profiles for Short-Video Recommendation
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at RecSys 2026
summary: Language-based user profiles convert long behavioral histories into explicit semantic representations for recommendation. However, most profile generators are optimized in an open loop: they may summarize past behavior fluently, but are not directly trained to improve future recommendation. We study this problem in real-world short-video recommendation, where user behaviors continuously arrive as streams and profiles must be incrementally updated under limited capacity. This requires maintaining a consistent bounded profile state and constructing profile-targeted semantic feedback from industrial implicit behavior logs. We propose RECAP, an offline closed-loop framework for optimizing streaming structured semantic profiles with historical recommendation feedback. RECAP maintains each profile as a bounded structured memory by combining LLM-based semantic updates with deterministic lifecycle and capacity control. RECAP constructs profile-targeted semantic feedback by filtering label-consistent behavior pairs with an LLM judge and training a dual-tower evaluator whose matching score serves as a GRPO reward. Experiments on Kuaishou short-video data show that RECAP improves uAUC by 0.0084 and Recall@2000 by about 4.9% over the base generator. Further analyses confirm the benefits of feedback construction and policy optimization, and show more grounded refinement and user-level abstraction in profile updates. A seven-day online A/B test further shows a statistically significant 0.139% improvement in average application usage time per user.

AI.tldr: RECAP is an offline closed-loop framework that optimizes streaming structured semantic user profiles for short-video recommendation by using LLM-based profile updates with GRPO reinforcement learning, where rewards come from a dual-tower evaluator trained on label-consistent behavior pairs. It improves uAUC, recall, and real-world user engagement on Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Current language-based user profile generators are optimized in an open loop — they produce fluent summaries of past behavior but are not directly trained to improve future recommendation performance. In real-world short-video platforms, user behaviors arrive as streams requiring incremental profile updates under capacity constraints, demanding consistent bounded profile states and profile-targeted semantic feedback from implicit industrial behavior logs.
AI.method: RECAP maintains each user profile as a bounded structured memory using LLM-based semantic updates combined with deterministic lifecycle and capacity control. Profile-targeted semantic feedback is constructed by filtering label-consistent behavior pairs with an LLM judge. A dual-tower evaluator is trained on these pairs, and its matching score serves as the reward signal for GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to refine the profile generator in a closed loop.
AI.result: On Kuaishou short-video data, RECAP improves uAUC by 0.0084 and Recall@2000 by approximately 4.9% over the base generator. Analyses confirm benefits from feedback construction and policy optimization, with more grounded refinement and user-level abstraction in profile updates. A seven-day online A/B test shows a statistically significant 0.139% improvement in average application usage time per user.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop optimization of streaming semantic user profiles using RECAP yields significant improvements in both offline metrics and online user engagement, demonstrating the value of directly training profile generators with recommendation feedback rather than relying on open-loop fluency objectives alone.

title: READU: Inconsistency-Driven Just-in-Time Detection and Repair of README Bugs
summary: Repository-level documentation, such as READMEs, is often the first point of contact between users and a repository. When this documentation is incorrect, users may encounter runtime errors or waste their time debugging. We call such mistakes in repository-level documentation README bugs. Addressing README bugs is challenging because documentation mixes prose with code, its connection to the source of truth is loose, and finding a bug still leaves developers to craft a repair. This paper presents READU, an inconsistency-driven technique for just-in-time detection and repair of README bugs. The key insight behind READU is that README bugs often manifest as inconsistencies between documentation and another source of truth: either repository-internal facts, such as source code, or repository-external facts, such as external dependencies. READU applies a high-recall commit filter, runs internal and external consistency checkers in parallel, uses an alert judge to remove false positives, and automatically synthesizes documentation patches. On 6,000 recent commits from six popular repositories including Linux and Spring Boot, READU detects 244 true positives with 75% precision, while consuming less than $0.01 and less than one minute per commit, on average. Of these true positives, READU correctly repairs 217. We report 66 found README bugs, of which (so far) 44 are confirmed and 26 are fixed.

AI.tldr: READU is a technique that detects and automatically repairs README bugs by identifying inconsistencies between documentation and sources of truth (source code or external dependencies). Evaluated on 6,000 commits across six major repositories, it detected 244 true bugs with 75% precision and correctly repaired 217, all at minimal cost.
AI.motivation: Repository-level documentation (READMEs) is the first contact point for users, but bugs in it cause runtime errors and wasted debugging time. Fixing README bugs is hard: documentation interleaves prose and code, its connection to source code is loose, and even after finding a bug, developers must manually craft a repair.
AI.method: READU is an inconsistency-driven, just-in-time technique with four stages: (1) a high-recall commit filter to select suspect commits, (2) parallel internal consistency checkers (comparing README against source code) and external consistency checkers (comparing against external dependencies), (3) an alert judge that prunes false positives, and (4) automatic synthesis of documentation patches.
AI.result: On 6,000 recent commits from six popular repositories (including Linux and Spring Boot), READU detected 244 true positives at 75% precision, repaired 217 correctly, with average cost under $0.01 and under one minute per commit. Of 66 reported bugs, 44 are confirmed and 26 fixed.
AI.conclusion: Inconsistency-driven analysis effectively detects and repairs README bugs at scale. READU demonstrates that automated, just-in-time documentation bug fixing is practical, inexpensive, and yields high confirmation and fix rates from real-world repositories.

title: Visualization Autocomplete: Visualization Authoring via Stepwise Design Recommendations
comment: IEEE VIS 2026 & IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)
summary: When domain experts create charts, the bottleneck is rarely the data, but knowing the optimal next step in chart design. The visualization design space is vast, and while domain experts can recognize a good design when they see it, it is often challenging to determine the exact path to get there. To address this, we present VISAUTOCOMPLETE, a system inspired by text autocompletion that reconceptualizes visualization design as a sequential process, recommending concrete next steps at each stage of the authoring process based on common practices. Users can intervene at any step, or delegate multiple steps to the system and select one from the design recommendations. To support responsive interaction, we distill the translation logic of a large language model (LLM) into a single function that receives the current chart state and recommended transition as input and returns the updated chart specification as output. We evaluate the system against a LLM vibecoding, Microsoft Excel, and TaskVis, an automated chart recommendation engine, on chart quality and approachability. Our results show that VisAutocomplete outperforms all baselines in the articulacy of complex chart authoring, while remaining on par with LLM in approachability.

AI.tldr: VISAUTOCOMPLETE reimagines visualization design as a sequential autocomplete process, using a distilled LLM function to recommend next design steps. It outperforms baselines (LLM vibecoding, Excel, TaskVis) on complex chart authoring while matching LLM approachability.
AI.motivation: Domain experts struggle not with data, but with navigating the vast visualization design space to determine optimal next steps. The gap between recognizing good design and knowing how to achieve it motivated an autocomplete-inspired approach.
AI.method: The system frames visualization authoring as a sequential process, offering concrete next-step recommendations at each stage. Users can accept, intervene, or delegate multiple steps. For responsiveness, LLM translation logic is distilled into a single function that maps current chart state and recommended transition to an updated chart specification.
AI.result: VisAutocomplete outperformed LLM vibecoding, Microsoft Excel, and TaskVis on the articulacy of complex chart authoring, while remaining comparable to LLM vibecoding on approachability.
AI.conclusion: Sequential, autocomplete-style interaction with distilled LLM logic offers a promising paradigm for visualization authoring, balancing expressiveness and ease of use more effectively than fully automated or fully manual approaches.

title: On the Structure of Address in Multi-Party Dialogue: From Discrete Labels to Continuous Levels
summary: In multi-party dialogues between a dialogue system and multiple users, identifying to whom an utterance is addressed is a key challenge. Prior work has typically treated addressee detection as a multi-class classification task, selecting a single label representing an individual participant or the group. This formulation assumes that address is inherently discrete and has primarily been used for predicting turn-taking. In this paper, we revisit this assumption by analyzing address as a continuous phenomenon. Using a multi-party human dialogue corpus annotated by multiple annotators, we construct both binary address labels derived from majority-vote addressee labels and continuous address levels inferred from annotator judgments using a latent-variable model. We then examine how these representations relate to turn-taking as well as listener behaviors, including gaze and backchannels. Our results show that, in addition to turn-taking, both gaze and backchannels are associated with address. Furthermore, models using continuous address levels achieve better predictive fit than those using discrete labels, suggesting that address may exhibit graded structure. Finally, we discuss the future directions of addressee detection research based on the findings of this study.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the conventional discrete treatment of addressee detection in multi-party dialogues, proposing instead that addressee status is a continuous/graded phenomenon. Using annotated corpus data, the authors demonstrate that continuous address representations better predict listener behaviors (gaze, backchannels) and turn-taking than discrete majority-vote labels.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats addressee detection as a multi-class classification problem with discrete labels (individual or group), implicitly assuming addressee status is categorical. This assumption may oversimplify the nuanced, graded nature of how attention and address are distributed among multiple participants in dialogue.
AI.method: Using a multi-party human dialogue corpus with multiple annotators, the authors construct two representations: (1) binary address labels via majority-vote addressee annotations, and (2) continuous address levels inferred through a latent-variable model applied to annotator judgments. They then statistically model the relationship between these address representations and three behavioral signals: turn-taking, listener gaze, and backchannel responses, comparing model fit across discrete vs. continuous formulations.
AI.result: Both gaze and backchannels are significantly associated with addressee status, beyond just turn-taking. Critically, models employing continuous address levels achieve superior predictive fit compared to those using discrete labels, providing empirical evidence that addressee status exhibits graded structure rather than being strictly categorical.
AI.conclusion: Addressee detection should be reformulated as a continuous rather than discrete phenomenon. The authors recommend future research adopt graded representations of address to better capture the nuanced distribution of attention in multi-party dialogue systems.

title: Do Coding Agents Need Executable World Models, Simplification, and Verification to Solve ARC-AGI-3?
summary: Our previous ARC-AGI-3 agent bundled executable world modeling, scheduled simplification, and exact replay verification, leaving unclear which idea accounted for its performance. We address this attribution question with four nested Codex-based agents: a textual baseline; a flexible-interface executable world model without replay verification; the same executable model with scheduled simplification; and a fixed-interface verification treatment that retains simplification and requires exact reproduction of recorded observations. The main study evaluates all four agents with gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.5 at high and xhigh reasoning effort on the public ARC-AGI-3 games. Exploratory follow-ups evaluate the textual and verification variants with gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh and max. The most robust result is that every agent variant improves with a stronger model and with greater reasoning effort. Within each model-effort setting, differences among variants are smaller than anticipated, while the effects of individual components vary across settings. Requiring a persistent executable deliverable is not universally beneficial: the textual variant outperforms the flexible-interface executable variant in both gpt-5.5 settings. Simplification improves performance in three of the four model-effort settings, with the weakest setting as the only exception. The complete verification treatment ranks first in all four settings, although it uses substantially more resources. In the gpt-5.6-sol follow-up, the verification variant fully solves every public game at both reasoning efforts, achieves about 99% RHAE, and uses fewer than half the total actions of the human baseline. Because the model postdates these games and held-out performance remains untested, this result should be interpreted as saturation of the public set only.

AI.tldr: This paper disentangles the contributions of three techniques in an ARC-AGI-3 agent—executable world modeling, scheduled simplification, and exact replay verification—by ablating them across four nested agents and multiple GPT model/reasoning-effort settings. The key finding is that exact replay verification consistently ranks first, but component effects vary by setting, and executable world models are not universally beneficial over textual baselines.
AI.motivation: A prior ARC-AGI-3 agent bundled three techniques together, making it impossible to attribute performance gains to any single component. The authors seek to isolate the causal contribution of each component through a controlled ablation study.
AI.method: Four nested Codex-based agents are constructed: (1) a textual-only baseline; (2) a flexible-interface executable world model without replay verification; (3) the same executable model augmented with scheduled simplification; (4) a fixed-interface verification agent that adds exact replay verification (requiring exact reproduction of recorded observations) on top of simplification. The main study evaluates all four agents using gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.5 at high and xhigh reasoning effort on public ARC-AGI-3 games. Exploratory follow-ups test the textual and verification variants with gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh and max effort.
AI.result: Every agent variant improves with stronger models and greater reasoning effort. Within each model-effort setting, inter-variant differences are smaller than expected, and component effects vary across settings. The textual variant outperforms the flexible-interface executable variant under gpt-5.5, indicating executable deliverables are not universally beneficial. Scheduled simplification improves performance in three of four settings. The full verification treatment ranks first in all four settings but consumes substantially more resources. With gpt-5.6-sol, the verification variant fully solves every public game, achieves ~99% RHAE, and uses fewer than half the actions of the human baseline—though this is acknowledged as saturation of the public set only, with held-out performance untested.
AI.conclusion: Exact replay verification is the most robustly beneficial component, though it incurs high resource costs. Executable world modeling alone can underperform a textual baseline, and scheduled simplification generally helps but not universally. The public ARC-AGI-3 set appears saturated by the strongest model configuration, and held-out evaluation is necessary for genuine generalization claims.

title: From hyperplanes to hyperellipsoids: characterizing the inherent interpretability of linear and single-qubit mixed-state binary classification models
summary: We characterize and compare the inherent interpretability offerings of a standard linear model with a single qubit mixed state model for the task of supervised binary classification. A side by side comparison reveals that a single qubit mixed state model for binary classification is just the ``ellipsoid version" of standard linear model classification. More precisely, rather than learning a hyperplane to classify data, we learn a hyperellipsoid. We discuss the consequences of the geometric inductive biases of both models, as well as how each model contains a different feature importance inductive bias. This short characterization offers an accessible route to quantum machine learning (ML) ideas for readers who have zero background in quantum and are only familiar with linear classification in ML. In support of ML pedagogy, we encourage instructors to utilize this piece to smoothly introduce quantum ML ideas into the undergraduate ML classroom.

AI.tldr: A single-qubit mixed state model for binary classification is shown to be the "ellipsoid version" of standard linear classification — learning a hyperellipsoid rather than a hyperplane — revealing how the two models differ in their geometric and feature-importance inductive biases.
AI.motivation: To provide an accessible bridge between classical linear classification and quantum machine learning by characterizing the inherent interpretability differences between a standard linear model and a single-qubit mixed state model, targeting readers with no quantum background.
AI.method: Side-by-side comparison and characterization of the geometric and feature-importance inductive biases of a standard linear model versus a single-qubit mixed state model for supervised binary classification.
AI.result: The single-qubit mixed state model is precisely the "ellipsoid version" of linear classification: it learns a hyperellipsoid instead of a hyperplane. Each model embodies distinct inductive biases — the linear model learns a separating hyperplane, while the quantum model learns a hyperellipsoid, leading to different feature importance interpretations.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a concise, pedagogy-oriented characterization that smoothly introduces quantum ML concepts into the undergraduate machine learning classroom by framing them in familiar linear classification terms.

title: Do Agents Dream of False Memories? Black-box Visual Attacks on Long-term Memory in Multimodal AI Agents
summary: Multimodal AI agents increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory to ground generation in past visual and textual episodes. We show that unconditional trust in visual data creates a critical vulnerability. We propose Lucid, a black-box adversarial framework that compromises multimodal memory pipelines under a strictly image-bounded threat model, requiring no access to the target MLLM, target retrieval encoder, or the text channel. Lucid crafts imperceptible perturbations to enable two distinct failure modes based on the availability of historical context: (1) Memory poisoning, an in-context attack where the adversarial image replaces a benign one whose content is reinforced by prior textual context, reliably corrupting visual recall and steering the agent toward attacker-chosen narratives; (2) Memory injection, an out-of-context attack where the adversarial image replaces a benign one in a conversation turn devoid of prior textual grounding, causing the agent to generate attacker-influenced responses with no corrective signal from memory. We evaluate Lucid across various conversation domains and five black-box memory architectures, including graph-structured, LLM-summarized, and commercially deployed systems. Lucid achieves 61.6% ASR on poisoning and 58.4% ASR on injection, exposing a structural vulnerability in multimodal memory pipelines.

AI.tldr: Lucid is a black-box adversarial framework that attacks multimodal memory pipelines using imperceptible image perturbations, achieving two failure modes—memory poisoning (61.6% ASR) and memory injection (58.4% ASR)—without access to the target model, encoder, or text channel.
AI.motivation: Multimodal AI agents increasingly depend on persistent long-term memory combining visual and textual data, but unconditional trust in visual inputs creates an unexamined security vulnerability. The authors aim to expose and systematically evaluate this structural weakness.
AI.method: Lucid operates under a strictly image-bounded threat model (no access to the target MLLM, retrieval encoder, or text). It crafts imperceptible adversarial perturbations for two attack modes: (1) Memory poisoning — in-context attacks where an adversarial image replaces a benign one reinforced by prior textual context; (2) Memory injection — out-of-context attacks where an adversarial image replaces a benign one in turns lacking prior textual grounding. Evaluation spans multiple conversation domains and five black-box memory architectures, including graph-structured, LLM-summarized, and commercial systems.
AI.result: Lucid achieves 61.6% Attack Success Rate on memory poisoning and 58.4% ASR on memory injection across five black-box memory architectures, demonstrating a consistent and exploitable vulnerability in multimodal memory pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Unconditional reliance on visual data in multimodal memory systems constitutes a structural vulnerability that adversarial images can exploit, enabling both in-context memory corruption and out-of-context response manipulation with high success rates.

title: What Do Chinese-Language Generative Search Engines Cite and Surface? A Large-Scale Empirical Study
comment: 49 pages, 15 figures. Tao Zhen and Yue Liu contributed equally and share first authorship; Gege Zhang and Yixuan Niu contributed equally and share second authorship
summary: Generative AI question-answering systems increasingly mediate information access, shifting content visibility from ranked search results to retrieval, citation, and presentation in generated answers. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of Chinese-language generative search across the Web and App interfaces of four mainstream platforms. The controlled design covers eight platform interfaces, 614 queries, and three replications per query-platform-interface combination. From 214,119 raw records, we construct a cleaned citation-level dataset of 160,860 records and analyze citation behavior, source attribution, entity exposure, and cross-interface consistency. Five findings emerge. First, brands in the citation pool were selectively surfaced in answers: the overall brand-selection rate was 8.3%, and 12.4% of retrieved sources containing contact information contributed contact information to answers. Second, content fit, cross-source occurrence count, and semantic role were relatively important in predictive models, whereas the 5118-Baidu Composite Quality Score was not the leading predictor for any examined outcome. Third, among cited pages with publication dates, fitted half-lives were approximately 39 days for high-timeliness queries and 68 days for low-timeliness queries. Fourth, approximately 13% of brand exposures could not be matched to the contemporaneous citation pool, and approximately 71% of contact-information exposures could not be matched to the crawled body text. Fifth, source sets differed systematically between the App and Web interfaces of the same platform. These results characterize how Chinese-language generative search systems select, attribute, and surface information and show that interface type is an important dimension of analysis.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of four Chinese-language generative search platforms (Web and App interfaces, 614 queries, 160,860 citation records) reveals selective brand surfacing (8.3% selection rate), limited predictive value of Baidu's quality score, recency bias with ~39–68 day half-lives, substantial unattributed entity exposure, and systematic cross-interface inconsistency.
AI.motivation: Generative AI QA systems are transforming how information is accessed, shifting from traditional ranked results to AI-generated answers with citations. Despite the growing dominance of these systems, there is a lack of large-scale empirical research on how Chinese-language generative search platforms select, attribute, and surface information—particularly regarding brand exposure, source attribution fidelity, recency bias, and cross-interface consistency.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled empirical study across four mainstream Chinese-language generative search platforms, spanning eight platform-interface combinations (Web and App). Using 614 queries with three replications per query-platform-interface combination, they collected 214,119 raw records and constructed a cleaned citation-level dataset of 160,860 records. They analyzed citation behavior, source attribution, entity exposure (brands and contact information), and cross-interface consistency using descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and half-life estimation for content recency.
AI.result: Five key findings: (1) brands were selectively surfaced—8.3% overall brand-selection rate, and 12.4% of sources with contact info contributed that info to answers; (2) content fit, cross-source occurrence count, and semantic role were relatively important predictors, while Baidu's 5118 Composite Quality Score was not the leading predictor for any outcome; (3) fitted citation half-lives were ~39 days for high-timeliness queries and ~68 days for low-timeliness queries; (4) ~13% of brand exposures and ~71% of contact-information exposures could not be matched to the contemporaneous citation pool or crawled body text; (5) source sets differed systematically between App and Web interfaces of the same platform.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal that Chinese-language generative search systems exhibit selective, non-transparent information surfacing behaviors, with significant unattributed entity exposure and systematic cross-interface inconsistency. Interface type emerges as a critical dimension for analyzing generative search systems, and conventional quality signals (like Baidu's composite score) may not drive citation selection as expected.

title: In the Driver's Seat: A Multi-Company Study on the Reality of Autonomous Driving System Testing
summary: Autonomous driving systems (ADS) are rapidly advancing and increasingly deployed in real-world applications. This creates growing demands for effective testing to ensure system functionality and safety. However, ADS testing remains complex and lacks well-established standards for scenario selection, performance evaluation, and acceptance criteria. To better understand current ADS testing practices and challenges, we conducted an interview study with experts working on ADS development and testing in nine companies from six different countries. Through thematic analysis, we synthesized industrial testing practices, challenges, potential solutions, future trends, and proposed an evidence-centered closed-loop testing framework for ADS testing. Our findings show that current practices primarily focus on scenario-based and X-in-the-loop testing approaches, supported by diverse tools, metrics, benchmarks, and testing strategies. The participants highlighted major challenges related to scenario realism, scenario coverage, simulation fidelity, and acceptance criteria, while also discussing potential solutions such as the use of AI, world models, and end-to-end approaches. Furthermore, participants envisioned future ADS testing to become more automated, data-driven, and transparent across the industry. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive industry-grounded overview of ADS testing, proposes an evidence-centered closed-loop testing framework to provide actionable guidance for ADS testing, and outlines important directions for future research and practice.

AI.tldr: An interview study across nine companies in six countries examining autonomous driving systems (ADS) testing practices, revealing challenges in scenario realism, coverage, simulation fidelity, and acceptance criteria, while proposing an evidence-centered closed-loop testing framework and identifying trends toward automation, data-driven methods, and AI integration.
AI.motivation: ADS testing lacks well-established standards for scenario selection, performance evaluation, and acceptance criteria. As ADS deployment grows, there is a pressing need to understand current industrial practices, challenges, and potential solutions to guide more effective and standardized testing approaches.
AI.method: The authors conducted a semi-structured interview study with ADS development and testing experts from nine companies across six countries. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to synthesize industrial practices, challenges, solutions, and future trends. Based on findings, the authors proposed an evidence-centered closed-loop testing framework.
AI.result: Current practices center on scenario-based testing and X-in-the-loop (e.g., MiL, SiL, HiL) approaches, supported by diverse tools, metrics, and benchmarks. Key challenges identified include insufficient scenario realism, limited scenario coverage, simulation fidelity gaps, and unclear acceptance criteria. Participants highlighted AI, world models, and end-to-end approaches as promising solutions, and envisioned future testing becoming more automated, data-driven, and transparent.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers a comprehensive industry-grounded overview of ADS testing, introduces an evidence-centered closed-loop testing framework for actionable guidance, and outlines key directions for future research, emphasizing the shift toward automated, data-driven, and transparent testing practices across the industry.

title: Understanding Fortunetelling with Large Language Models in China: User Practices, Perceptions, and Impacts on Beliefs and Decisions
summary: Fortunetelling is a cultural practice for navigating uncertainty, often associated with people's beliefs and decisions. Fortunetelling with recent large language models (LLMs) introduces new opportunities and risks. This paper conducts qualitative studies to understand users' practices, perceptions, and impacts of LLM fortunetelling in China. We first analyze 1,045 posts on Chinese social media, yielding a comprehensive taxonomy of the diverse foretold topics (e.g., career, romance), emotion reactions (e.g., surprise, worry), and perceived credibility (e.g., doubt, trust) of LLM fortunetelling. Then, we conduct interviews with 20 users of LLM fortunetelling. The findings indicate that users treat LLM fortunetelling as a tool less for accurate prediction but more for emotional support. While the fortunetelling results rarely change users' initial beliefs or decisions, they are associated with subtle mindset shifts, with some users reporting small behavioral adjustments. We discuss implications for gaining benefits from LLM fortunetelling.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study of LLM-based fortunetelling in China, analyzing 1,045 social media posts and 20 user interviews. Users primarily seek emotional support rather than accurate predictions; results rarely change core beliefs but may prompt subtle mindset shifts and minor behavioral adjustments.
AI.motivation: Fortunetelling is a culturally significant practice for navigating uncertainty. The emergence of LLM-based fortunetelling introduces both new opportunities and risks, yet users' actual practices, perceptions, and the psychosocial impacts remain underexplored.
AI.method: A two-phase qualitative study: (1) content analysis of 1,045 posts from Chinese social media to develop a taxonomy of foretold topics, emotional reactions, and perceived credibility; (2) semi-structured interviews with 20 active users of LLM fortunetelling.
AI.result: The taxonomy revealed diverse fortunetelling topics (career, romance, etc.), emotional reactions (surprise, worry, etc.), and credibility perceptions (doubt, trust, etc.). Interview findings show users value LLM fortunetelling primarily for emotional support rather than prediction accuracy. Results rarely alter users' existing beliefs or decisions but are associated with subtle mindset shifts and occasional small behavioral adjustments.
AI.conclusion: LLM fortunetelling functions as a tool for emotional support rather than a decision-making instrument. The authors discuss implications for designing and regulating LLM fortunetelling to maximize benefits while mitigating risks.

title: Adaptive Multi-Step Lookahead Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel text generation by iteratively refining masked tokens, offering a promising alternative to autoregressive decoding. Recent lookahead-based decoding methods improve the accuracy--efficiency trade-off by exploring future decoding states before committing token updates. However, existing approaches mainly rely on shallow one-step lookahead, which optimizes immediate information gain but can be suboptimal for longer-horizon decoding trajectories. Meanwhile, we find that a naive extension for deeper lookahead is also ineffective, as fixed-depth rollout introduces additional computation and cannot adapt to heterogeneous intermediate decoding states. Thus, in this work, we propose AdaLook, an adaptive lookahead framework for DLM decoding. AdaLook dynamically determines whether to continue rollout based on candidate-score variance and further enables branch expansion when intermediate rollout states require additional exploration. This design avoids unnecessary deep rollout while allowing the decoder to re-trigger lookahead from informative intermediate states. Experiments on various benchmarks and models demonstrate that AdaLook achieves a better accuracy--decoding steps trade-off than existing one-step lookahead decoding methods.

AI.tldr: AdaLook proposes an adaptive lookahead framework for masked diffusion language models that dynamically determines rollout depth based on candidate-score variance, outperforming fixed one-step lookahead methods on the accuracy–decoding steps trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing lookahead-based decoding for masked DLMs relies on shallow one-step lookahead, which is suboptimal for long-horizon trajectories. Naive deeper lookahead (fixed-depth rollout) is also ineffective due to added computation and inability to adapt to heterogeneous intermediate states.
AI.method: AdaLook dynamically controls rollout depth using candidate-score variance as an adaptive stopping criterion and enables branch expansion to trigger additional exploration from informative intermediate states.
AI.result: Experiments across benchmarks and models show AdaLook achieves a superior accuracy vs. decoding steps trade-off compared to existing one-step lookahead methods.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive lookahead with variance-based depth control and branch expansion effectively addresses the limitations of both shallow and fixed-depth lookahead, yielding more efficient DLM decoding.

title: Beyond a Joke: Multi-Angle Reasoning for Detecting and Explaining Harmful Humor in Memes
summary: Internet memes intertwine visual cues, textual content, and cultural context, making them particularly challenging to interpret in scenarios where humor, sarcasm, and harmful intent coexist. These complexities highlight the need for explainable meme understanding systems that can provide reliable and structured reasoning to support both accurate classification and human interpretability. However, existing multimodal classifiers either overlook these interdependencies or provide only limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce MAR-12, a novel framework that leverages Vision Language Models (VLMs) for meme detection and understanding in settings where humorous and hateful elements may coexist. The framework first interprets each meme through twelve structured perspectives derived from humor and hate theories. It then applies a role-aware soft-gated attention mechanism to learn how much each perspective should contribute, followed by a prototype-based classifier for the final prediction. Finally, explanations are synthesized using both perspective-specific reasoning and learned attention weights, ensuring transparent and context-grounded justifications. We evaluate MAR-12 on the PrideMM and Memotion datasets, where it achieves up to 80.3% accuracy for humor detection and 75.9% accuracy for hate detection, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, both human and GPT-4-based evaluations confirm that MAR-12 produces coherent and persuasive explanations, particularly for memes in which humorous and harmful cues co-occur.

AI.tldr: MAR-12 is a VLM-based framework that interprets memes through 12 structured perspectives grounded in humor and hate theories, uses role-aware soft-gated attention and prototype-based classification, and generates transparent explanations. It achieves SOTA results on PrideMM and Memotion datasets (up to 80.3% humor accuracy, 75.9% hate accuracy) with coherent explanations validated by human and GPT-4 evaluations.
AI.motivation: Internet memes combine visual, textual, and cultural cues, making interpretation difficult when humor, sarcasm, and harmful intent coexist. Existing multimodal classifiers either ignore these interdependencies or offer limited interpretability, creating a need for explainable systems that provide structured, reliable reasoning for both accurate classification and human understanding.
AI.method: The MAR-12 framework uses Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret each meme through twelve structured perspectives derived from humor and hate theories. A role-aware soft-gated attention mechanism learns the contribution weight of each perspective, and a prototype-based classifier produces the final prediction. Explanations are synthesized by combining perspective-specific reasoning with the learned attention weights for context-grounded justifications.
AI.result: MAR-12 achieves up to 80.3% accuracy for humor detection and 75.9% accuracy for hate detection on the PrideMM and Memotion datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Both human evaluation and GPT-4-based evaluation confirm that the framework generates coherent and persuasive explanations, especially for memes where humorous and harmful cues co-occur.
AI.conclusion: MAR-12 demonstrates that grounding meme understanding in structured theoretical perspectives and making the reasoning process transparent via attention-guided explanations significantly improves both classification performance and interpretability, particularly in the challenging setting where humor and hate coexist.

title: Stochastic Reset Pathfinding: Path-Level Regret for Cascading Bandits over Graph Paths
summary: We introduce Stochastic Reset Pathfinding (SRP), an episodic learning problem on a known directed graph with unknown stationary edge success probabilities. In each episode, the agent commits to a source-to-goal path, and any edge failure during execution resets it to the source. SRP captures settings such as entanglement distribution in quantum repeater networks, payment routing on the Lightning Network, and delivery in unreliable mesh networks. We show that the global-reset structure makes the optimal policy open-loop, placing SRP within the combinatorial cascading bandit (CCB) framework. We propose a Log-Dijkstra meta-algorithm with UCB (PathUCB) and Thompson Sampling (PathTS) instantiations. Our main technical result is a path-level regret bound for PathUCB that decomposes regret over suboptimal paths via a per-path complexity C(pi) combining each edge's prefix and suffix reliability. The bound is complementary to the edge-level CCB bound and more informative on structured graphs with polynomially many source-to-goal paths. Experiments on quantum-network, layered-DAG, grid-world, and Erdos-Renyi domains support the theory and show that PathTS typically achieves the best empirical performance among the algorithms tested. We then exhibit an adversarial instance on which PathTS fails to converge, consistent with a known exponential obstruction for combinatorial Thompson Sampling on multiplicative-reward problems. We recommend PathTS as the practical default while cautioning that adversarial instances exist.

AI.tldr: SRP is a pathfinding problem where edge failures reset the agent to the source. The optimal policy is open-loop, placing it in the combinatorial cascading bandit framework. The authors propose PathUCB and PathTS algorithms, prove a path-level regret bound for PathUCB, and show empirically that PathTS performs best, though an adversarial counterexample shows it can fail to converge.
AI.motivation: Modeling sequential pathfinding under uncertainty where failure on any edge forces a complete restart — motivated by quantum repeater networks, Lightning Network payment routing, and unreliable mesh network delivery.
AI.method: Frames SRP as a combinatorial cascading bandit (CCB) problem with open-loop optimal policies. Proposes Log-Dijkstra — a meta-algorithm that uses logarithmic transformation of edge probabilities to apply shortest-path methods — instantiated with UCB (PathUCB) and Thompson Sampling (PathTS). Derives a path-level regret bound using per-path complexity C(π) based on prefix and suffix reliability.
AI.result: PathUCB achieves a path-level regret bound that decomposes over suboptimal paths via per-path complexity, complementary to existing edge-level CCB bounds and more informative on graphs with polynomially many source-to-goal paths. PathTS empirically outperforms baselines across quantum-network, layered-DAG, grid-world, and Erdős-Rényi domains. An adversarial instance is constructed where PathTS fails to converge, consistent with known exponential obstructions for combinatorial Thompson Sampling on multiplicative rewards.
AI.conclusion: PathTS is recommended as the practical default algorithm for SRP, with the caveat that adversarial instances can cause non-convergence. The path-level regret analysis provides novel structural insights beyond edge-level CCB bounds.

title: Beyond Detection: Agentic Attack Synthesis and Simulation for Smart Contracts
summary: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose severe financial risks, yet existing security tools largely stop at vulnerability detection, offering limited support for explaining whether reported flaws are exploitable, how attacks unfold, and what concrete damage they cause. To bridge this gap, we propose KASS (Knowledge-Augmented Attack Synthesis and Simulation), a multi-agent framework for executable smart contract exploit verification. KASS decomposes automated exploit generation into planning, generation, and testing stages, and integrates three complementary mechanisms: retrieval-augmented planning over real-world audit knowledge, formal generation and validation constraints that bind attack plans to executable proof-of-concept tests, and a hierarchical dual-loop refinement process that repairs code-level errors while triggering strategy-level replanning when attack assumptions fail. We evaluate KASS on 104 SmartBugs-Curated contracts across four vulnerability categories. Experimental results show that KASS successfully generates executable exploits for 94.23% of tested contracts; this rate is higher than previously reported results for REX and AdvSCanner on comparable SmartBugs-Curated subsets, and higher than our reproduced Claude Code baseline under the same evaluation protocol. On 11 real-world CVE-tagged contracts, KASS successfully validates 9 cases. Beyond exploit generation, KASS produces structured attack plans that document exploitation flows, quantify potential asset losses, and serve as semantic false positive filters for static analysis tools.

AI.tldr: KASS is a multi-agent framework that automatically generates executable smart contract exploits by combining retrieval-augmented planning, formal constraints, and hierarchical dual-loop refinement. It achieves 94.23% exploit generation success on 104 SmartBugs-Curated contracts and validates 9/11 real-world CVEs, while also producing structured attack plans useful for false positive filtering.
AI.motivation: Existing smart contract security tools only detect vulnerabilities but fail to explain exploitability, attack mechanics, or financial impact. There is a gap between vulnerability detection and practical exploit verification, leaving developers uncertain about which reported flaws pose real threats.
AI.method: KASS decomposes exploit generation into three stages (planning, generation, testing) within a multi-agent framework. It employs: (1) retrieval-augmented planning that leverages real-world audit knowledge; (2) formal generation and validation constraints linking attack plans to executable proof-of-concept tests; and (3) a hierarchical dual-loop refinement process that handles both code-level error repair and strategy-level replanning when attack assumptions fail.
AI.result: KASS achieves 94.23% executable exploit generation on 104 SmartBugs-Curated contracts across four vulnerability categories, outperforming prior results from REX and AdvSCanner on comparable subsets and a reproduced Claude Code baseline. On 11 real-world CVE-tagged contracts, KASS successfully validates 9. It also generates structured attack plans documenting exploitation flows and quantifying potential asset losses.
AI.conclusion: KASS demonstrates that knowledge-augmented multi-agent systems can effectively bridge the gap between vulnerability detection and practical exploit verification, offering both higher exploit generation rates than prior work and actionable attack documentation that aids in false positive triage.

title: Scientific Claim-Source Retrieval Revisited: A Comparative Study of Style Transfer and Re-Ranking
summary: Scientific claims shared on social media are often difficult to verify and may contribute to the spread of misinformation. To address this challenge, automated fact verification systems require scientific claim-source retrieval, the task of identifying the source publication underlying a given claim. However, claims often differ substantially from their source publications in language, style, and specificity, making retrieval challenging. We present a comparative study of scientific claim-source retrieval on the CheckThat! 2026 benchmark across sparse and dense retrieval models. Our results show that translating claims into English outperforms both original and bilingual claim representations, while incorporating publication metadata provides additional retrieval gains by capturing indirect source references. In addition, we analyze four style transfer approaches and find that they improve retrieval performance for most models, although the optimal style depends on the underlying retrieval objective. Finally, we investigate similarity- and signal-based re-ranking approaches, introducing three novel re-ranking models based on attribution, entity overlap, and verification-based reasoning. Verification-based re-ranking yields additional gains beyond semantic similarity and achieves the best overall performance with an MRR@5 of 0.758.

AI.tldr: This paper tackles scientific claim-source retrieval—matching social media claims to their original publications—and finds that translating claims to English, using publication metadata, and applying verification-based re-ranking significantly improves retrieval performance, achieving a top MRR@5 of 0.758 on the CheckThat! 2026 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Scientific claims on social media are hard to verify and fuel misinformation. Automated fact-verification systems need to retrieve the source publication for a given claim, but claims diverge substantially from source texts in language, style, and specificity, making this retrieval task difficult.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comparative study on the CheckThat! 2026 benchmark, evaluating sparse and dense retrieval models. They test: (1) claim translation into English versus original/bilingual representations, (2) incorporation of publication metadata, (3) four style transfer approaches to bridge the claim–source gap, and (4) similarity- and signal-based re-ranking methods, introducing three novel re-rankers based on attribution, entity overlap, and verification-based reasoning.
AI.result: Translating claims to English outperforms both original-language and bilingual representations. Publication metadata yields additional retrieval gains. Style transfer improves most models, though optimal style is objective-dependent. Among re-ranking approaches, verification-based re-ranking surpasses pure semantic similarity and achieves the best overall MRR@5 of 0.758.
AI.conclusion: Effective scientific claim-source retrieval benefits from a multi-pronged strategy: English-only translation, metadata enrichment, style transfer, and particularly verification-based re-ranking, which together push state-of-the-art performance for this task.

title: Agentic Synthesis against Counterexample-Supplemented Sketches
comment: 32 pages, 5 displayed figures (4 distinct screenshots). Includes the CatSynth artifact supplement. Code and captured experiment artifacts: https://github.com/open-horizon-labs/counterexample-supplemented-sketches
summary:
Coding agents can fix a failing example without preserving the domain rule that made it fail, so later generations can repeat the same plausible mistake. We present agentic synthesis against counterexample-supplemented sketches, a repository-native method for systems whose governing policy is discovered during implementation. A human starts with a partial, code-shaped sketch, and a coding agent generates the first implementation. When a concrete failure exposes missing or mistaken policy, an operator explicitly approves the corrected behavior and rule. The agent then revises the sketch and repairs or regenerates code and prompt surfaces for that one counterexample. The full archive preserves provenance; a selected regression set gates each revision before the next candidate is revealed; and periodic clean regeneration tests whether the evolved sketch, rather than prompt history or accumulated examples, carries the learned policy.
  We demonstrate the method with CatSynth, a synthetic browser application and captured coding-agent experiment. In one open-world run with GPT-5.4-mini, 8 of 14 frozen candidate cases became counterexamples. The rebuild controls inherited that promotion schedule, and all three paths passed the 8 accepted cases. Rebuilding from the evolved sketch passed 19 of 21 withheld cases, compared with 15 of 21 when rebuilding from the initial sketch and replaying all accepted examples. Retaining code across counterexamples required 9 Developer calls and 719 lines of cumulative artifact churn, versus 15 calls and 2,394 lines for replay-all, and passed 18 of 21 withheld cases. These results provide inspectable evidence that the evolved sketch carried reviewed policy and that retaining code reduced rework in this run; with one model and one reveal order, they do not establish general superiority or correctness beyond the encoded checks.

AI.tldr: Coding agents often fix bugs by patching symptoms without learning the underlying domain rules, leading to repeated mistakes. The authors propose agentic synthesis against counterexample-supplemented sketches — a method where a human-provided sketch evolves as the agent encounters failures, with operators explicitly approving corrections. Experiments with CatSynth show that the evolved sketch better preserves learned policy than replaying all examples, while reducing developer calls and code churn.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can superficially fix failing examples without internalizing the domain rule that caused the failure, resulting in later generations repeating the same mistake. Existing approaches lack a systematic mechanism for capturing discovered policy during iterative code generation, particularly for systems whose governing rules emerge during implementation rather than being fully specified upfront.
AI.method: The method, agentic synthesis against counterexample-supplemented sketches, operates as follows: (1) A human provides a partial, code-shaped sketch. (2) A coding agent generates an initial implementation. (3) When a concrete failure reveals missing or mistaken policy, an operator explicitly approves the corrected behavior and rule. (4) The agent revises the sketch and repairs/regenerates code and prompt surfaces for that one counterexample. (5) A full archive preserves provenance; a selected regression set gates each revision; and periodic clean regeneration tests whether the evolved sketch (rather than prompt history or accumulated examples) carries the learned policy.
AI.result: In an open-world run with GPT-5.4-mini on CatSynth (a synthetic browser application), 8 of 14 frozen candidate cases became counterexamples. Rebuilding from the evolved sketch passed 19/21 withheld cases, versus 15/21 when rebuilding from the initial sketch and replaying all accepted examples. Retaining code across counterexamples required 9 Developer calls and 719 lines of cumulative artifact churn, versus 15 calls and 2,394 lines for replay-all, and passed 18/21 withheld cases.
AI.conclusion: The results provide inspectable evidence that the evolved sketch carried reviewed policy and that retaining code reduced rework in this specific run. However, with only one model and one reveal order, the experiment does not establish general superiority or correctness beyond the encoded checks.

title: Can't Stop: How Context and Individual Traits Influence Effectiveness of Different Gradual Interventions for Infinite Scrolling on Short-Form Video Platforms
summary: Infinite scrolling on short-form video platforms like TikTok encourages prolonged engagement and post-usage regret. Interventions aim to mitigate such behavior, but their effectiveness may depend on the interplay between intervention type, contextual factors, and individual traits. In a 7-day within-subject randomized field study (N=104), we compared a baseline pop-up and two gradually intensifying design frictions (visual and haptic). We evaluated behavioral changes and user experience using objective and subjective measures. Results showed that the pop-up was initially effective but quickly lost impact, whereas the visual gradual intervention sustained subjective ratings the longest. Bayesian modeling revealed that self-regulation traits moderate how participants responded to the three intervention types. For participants with low impulsivity, the type of intervention had little influence on its subjective effectiveness. For participants with high impulsivity, however, differences between intervention types were substantial, with the explicit baseline pop-up being most effective compared to the novel gradual interventions. Contextual factors, in contrast, showed little influence. These findings suggest that intervention modality and individual differences in self-regulation shape intervention effectiveness.

AI.tldr: A 7-day field study (N=104) compared three interventions (baseline pop-up, visual gradual friction, haptic gradual friction) to reduce infinite scrolling on short-form video platforms. The pop-up quickly lost impact, while visual gradual friction sustained subjective ratings longest. Self-regulation traits moderated effectiveness: for high-impulsivity users, the explicit pop-up was most effective; for low-impulsivity users, intervention type mattered little. Contextual factors showed minimal influence.
AI.motivation: Infinite scrolling on short-form video platforms (e.g., TikTok) promotes prolonged, regretful engagement. While interventions exist to curb such behavior, their effectiveness likely depends on the interplay between intervention design (type), contextual factors, and individual differences—yet this interplay remains poorly understood, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: A 7-day within-subject randomized field study with 104 participants compared three intervention types: a baseline pop-up and two gradually intensifying design frictions (visual and haptic). Both objective behavioral measures and subjective user experience ratings were collected. Bayesian modeling was applied to examine how self-regulation traits and contextual factors moderated intervention effectiveness.
AI.result: The baseline pop-up was initially effective but quickly lost impact. The visual gradual intervention sustained subjective effectiveness ratings the longest. Bayesian modeling showed that self-regulation traits significantly moderated responses: for low-impulsivity participants, intervention type had little influence; for high-impulsivity participants, the explicit pop-up was substantially more effective than the gradual interventions. Contextual factors showed little influence overall.
AI.conclusion: Intervention modality and individual differences in self-regulation jointly shape intervention effectiveness for curbing infinite scrolling. One-size-fits-all approaches are suboptimal; tailoring interventions to users' impulsivity levels may improve outcomes. Explicit, attention-capturing interventions may be necessary for high-impulsivity users, whereas gradual frictions may suffice for others.

title: Better Starts, Better Ends: Bootstrapped Iterative Self-Reasoning Distillation for Compressed Reasoning
summary: Large reasoning models often solve problems through long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, yet much of this computation is spent on redundant derivations, repeated self-verification, and detours that do not improve the final answer. Existing on-policy self-distillation methods reduce this cost by matching a student model to a concise copy of itself on prefixes sampled from the student's own rollouts. We show that this objective has an initialization bottleneck. Since supervision is applied only to visited prefixes, training from a verbose base model places the KL loss on contexts that are often noisy, redundant, or already off track. In such regions, a concise teacher can provide only local corrections, while the student continues to explore trajectories that an efficient reasoner should avoid. In this paper, we propose BIRD(Bootstrapped Iterative Self-Reasoning Distillation), a two-stage self-reasoning distillation method that improves the rollout distribution before on-policy training. BIRD first samples concise solutions from the base model under a brevity instruction, keeps only answer-correct traces, and performs a lightweight prompt-switch SFT step. The traces are generated with the brevity instruction but learned under the original task prompt, turning instruction-induced conciseness into a default reasoning behavior. Starting from this warm model, BIRD then applies on-policy reverse-KL distillation with a concise self-teacher, now on cleaner and more informative prefixes. Across Qwen3 series models, BIRD achieves a stronger accuracy-efficiency trade-off than prompting and cold-start on-policy distillation on MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. On Qwen3-8B, it improves MATH-500 accuracy from 86.2% to 92.0% while reducing the average response length from 3,099 to 1,115 tokens. These results highlight prefix support as a central factor in efficient reasoning distillation.

AI.tldr: BIRD is a two-stage self-distillation method that first bootstraps concise reasoning behavior via prompt-switch SFT on brevity-instructed correct traces, then applies on-policy reverse-KL distillation on cleaner prefixes, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation methods suffer from an initialization bottleneck: when training from a verbose base model, the KL loss is applied to noisy, redundant, or off-track prefixes where a concise teacher can only provide local corrections, while the student continues exploring inefficient trajectories.
AI.method: BIRD operates in two stages: (1) Bootstrap stage — sample concise solutions under a brevity instruction, filter for answer-correct traces, then perform prompt-switch SFT (trained under the original task prompt but using brevity-instructed traces), converting instruction-induced conciseness into default reasoning behavior; (2) On-policy distillation stage — apply reverse-KL distillation with a concise self-teacher on the cleaner, more informative prefixes from the warm model.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B, BIRD improves MATH-500 accuracy from 86.2% to 92.0% while reducing average response length from 3,099 to 1,115 tokens. Across Qwen3 series models, BIRD achieves a stronger accuracy-efficiency trade-off than prompting and cold-start on-policy distillation on MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Prefix support is a central factor in efficient reasoning distillation. By improving the rollout distribution before on-policy training, BIRD enables more effective and stable distillation of concise reasoning models.

title: From Black Box to Executable Logic: Explainable Reinforcement Learning through Prolog Expert Systems
summary: A trained deep reinforcement learning policy is a black box, and we ask whether it can be made explainable by rewriting it as an executable logic program that reproduces its behaviour and that a person can read, a logic engine can run, and an optimizer can edit. We present a three-stage post-hoc transformation that extracts a frozen proximal policy optimization teacher, induces an ordered rule list from its decisions in the manner of classical relational learning, and emits the result as a Prolog program whose every decision is executed by an off-the-shelf logic engine; a subsequent expansion stage edits the rule base and accepts an edit only when policy evaluation certifies a return increase. We prove four guarantees. A return-loss bound makes the distilled program a machine-checkable certificate in a finite Markov decision process, and the expansion loop improves monotonically and terminates. For the continuous-observation setting we answer whether the conversion is possible at all: the propositional threshold instantiation converts the network to arbitrary fidelity as the resolution B grows, with disagreement O(1/B) and a return gap that closes at the same rate, and a matching lower bound shows the cost is exponential in the observation dimension for an oblique decision boundary. Empirically, on a two-room key-and-door task with 16,944 reachable states the expanded Prolog program attains exact optimal return in every seed and, in a budget-capped regime, exceeds the stochastic teacher on exact return in ten of ten seeds. On three continuous-control tasks the emitted program substitutes the network, matching the neural teacher within noise on Acrobot with eleven clauses and recovering about 97% of its return on CartPole, while on the finer-control LunarLander it recovers only partially, exactly the ceiling the exponential lower bound predicts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a three-stage method to transform a trained deep RL policy into a human-readable, executable Prolog program with formal guarantees. The approach distills a neural policy into an ordered rule list via relational learning, emits it as a logic program, and iteratively refines it using policy evaluation. The authors provide theoretical bounds on return loss, monotonic improvement, and fidelity limits in continuous domains. Empirically, the method achieves exact optimal return on a discrete task and closely matches the teacher on simple continuous-control tasks, with performance degrading on finer-control problems as predicted by the exponential lower bound.
AI.motivation: Deep RL policies are opaque black boxes. The authors aim to make them explainable by converting them into executable logic programs that humans can read, logic engines can run, and optimizers can edit, while preserving or improving performance.
AI.method: A three-stage post-hoc transformation: (1) extract a frozen PPO teacher policy; (2) induce an ordered rule list from teacher decisions using classical relational learning techniques; (3) emit the rules as a Prolog program executable by a standard logic engine. An expansion stage follows that edits the rule base, accepting edits only when policy evaluation certifies a return increase. For continuous observations, a propositional threshold instantiation converts the network with fidelity O(1/B) as resolution B grows.
AI.result: Four theoretical guarantees: a return-loss bound making the distilled program a machine-checkable certificate in finite MDPs; monotonic improvement and termination of the expansion loop; O(1/B) disagreement and return gap for continuous settings; and an exponential lower bound in observation dimension for oblique decision boundaries. Empirically, on a two-room key-and-door task (16,944 states) the expanded Prolog program achieves exact optimal return and exceeds the stochastic teacher under budget caps. On continuous-control: matches teacher within noise on Acrobot (11 clauses), recovers ~97% return on CartPole, but only partially on LunarLander, consistent with the theoretical bound.
AI.conclusion: Neural RL policies can be faithfully converted into interpretable, executable logic programs with formal performance guarantees. The approach works well for discrete and simple continuous domains, but finer-grained continuous control faces inherent exponential barriers predicted by the lower bound, establishing a principled ceiling on what such transformations can achieve.

title: Who Became Financially Vulnerable After COVID-19? A Population-Level Machine Learning Analysis Using MEPS Data
summary:
The cost of healthcare remains a concern in the United States and may have been influenced by disruptions associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines healthcare financial vulnerability before and after the pandemic using Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data from 2019 and 2021. High financial burden was defined as out-of-pocket healthcare expenditures exceeding 10% of family income. Survey-weighted subgroup analyses were performed to obtain nationally representative estimates across demographic and socioeconomic groups.
  Descriptive analyses were complemented by interpretable logistic regression and machine learning models. Logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios, while random forest and gradient boosting models were used to evaluate predictive performance. Temporal generalization assessed whether models trained on pre-pandemic data remained predictive when applied to post-pandemic observations.
  Financial vulnerability was strongly associated with poverty status, insurance coverage, and prescription drug spending. Subgroup analyses indicated persistent disparities across population groups, with some evidence of increased burden among vulnerable populations in 2021. Despite these differences, models trained on pre-pandemic data exhibited only modest reductions in predictive performance when evaluated on post-pandemic data, suggesting that the principal predictors of healthcare financial vulnerability remained relatively stable over time.
  These findings provide a population-level assessment of healthcare financial vulnerability during the COVID-19 period and demonstrate the value of combining interpretable statistical modeling with machine learning for population health research. The results may support future population health surveillance, risk stratification, and healthcare policy research aimed at reducing financial barriers to care.

AI.tldr: Using MEPS data from 2019 and 2021, this study examines healthcare financial vulnerability (defined as out-of-pocket spending >10% of family income) before and after COVID-19. It finds persistent disparities linked to poverty, insurance coverage, and prescription drug costs, with models trained on pre-pandemic data still predictive post-pandemic, suggesting stable risk factors.
AI.motivation: Healthcare costs remain a major concern in the United States, and the COVID-19 pandemic may have exacerbated financial vulnerability. The study aims to assess whether the pandemic disrupted pre-existing patterns of healthcare financial burden and whether pre-pandemic predictive models retain validity in the post-pandemic period.
AI.method: The study uses Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data from 2019 (pre-pandemic) and 2021 (post-pandemic). High financial burden is defined as out-of-pocket expenditures exceeding 10% of family income. Survey-weighted subgroup analyses provide nationally representative estimates. Logistic regression estimates adjusted odds ratios, while random forest and gradient boosting models assess predictive performance. Temporal generalization evaluates whether models trained on 2019 data maintain accuracy when applied to 2021 data.
AI.result: Financial vulnerability was strongly associated with poverty status, insurance coverage, and prescription drug spending. Subgroup analyses revealed persistent disparities, with some evidence of increased burden among vulnerable populations in 2021. Models trained on pre-pandemic data showed only modest reductions in predictive performance on post-pandemic data, indicating relative stability in the principal predictors of healthcare financial vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a population-level assessment of healthcare financial vulnerability during COVID-19 and demonstrates the utility of combining interpretable statistical models with machine learning for population health research. Results may inform health surveillance, risk stratification, and policy efforts aimed at reducing financial barriers to care.

title: Natural Backdoor Attacks on Speech Recognition Models
comment: This is the authors' manuscript of a chapter published in Machine Learning for Cyber Security, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 13655, pp. 597-610 (2023)
summary: With the rapid development of deep learning, its vulnerability has gradually emerged in recent years. This work focuses on backdoor attacks on speech recognition systems. We adopt sounds that are ordinary in nature or in our daily life as triggers for natural backdoor attacks. We conduct experiments on two datasets and three models to validate the performance of natural backdoor attacks and explore the effects of poisoning rate, trigger duration and blend ratio on the performance of natural backdoor attacks. Our results show that natural backdoor attacks have a high attack success rate without compromising model performance on benign samples, even with short or low-amplitude triggers. It requires only 5% of poisoned samples to achieve a near 100% attack success rate. In addition, the backdoor will be automatically activated by the corresponding sound in nature, which is not easy to be detected and will bring severer harm.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates natural backdoor attacks on speech recognition systems using everyday environmental sounds as triggers. With only 5% poisoned training data, the attack achieves near 100% success rate while maintaining benign performance, even with short or low-amplitude triggers.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models are increasingly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. The authors aim to expose a more stealthy and realistic threat vector in speech recognition — using naturally occurring sounds (rather than artificial patterns) as backdoor triggers, making the attack harder to detect and more dangerous in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose natural backdoor attacks where ordinary sounds from nature or daily life serve as triggers. They embed these acoustic triggers into training samples with a certain poisoning rate, trigger duration, and blend ratio. Experiments are conducted on two datasets and three models to evaluate attack success rate and benign accuracy under varying poisoning parameters.
AI.result: Natural backdoor attacks achieve near 100% attack success rate with only 5% poisoned samples, without degrading performance on benign inputs. The attack remains effective even when triggers are short or have low amplitude. The backdoor is automatically activated by corresponding natural sounds, making it highly stealthy.
AI.conclusion: Natural backdoor attacks pose a severe and stealthy threat to speech recognition systems. Their ability to use common environmental sounds as triggers, combined with high success rates at low poisoning levels and resilience to short/low-amplitude triggers, highlights an urgent need for robust defenses.

title: Trans-Domain Digital Twin: Conceptual Foundations, Architecture, and Research Outlook
