AI.tldr: This paper evaluates five energy system optimization tools (REMix, MTRESS, COMANDO, OEMOF, HOMER PRO) against a set of comparison criteria to determine their suitability for different optimization scenarios. REMix excels in investment path optimization, COMANDO handles atypical components best, OEMOF is the top open-source choice for standard problems, and HOMER PRO is ideal for rapid synthesis optimization by non-programmers. MTRESS could not be fully assessed due to insufficient information.
AI.motivation: Selecting the most appropriate software tool for energy system optimization is challenging due to the diverse objectives and requirements across different energy systems. There is a need for systematic comparative guidance to help practitioners and researchers match tools to specific optimization scenarios, contributing to the broader goal of a carbon-neutral future.
AI.method: The authors conducted an extensive review of literature, documentation, tutorials, and example models for five preselected tools (REMix, MTRESS, COMANDO, OEMOF, HOMER PRO). They developed a set of comparison criteria and performed a qualitative evaluation of each tool against these criteria to characterize their respective strengths and ideal use cases.
AI.result: Four of five tools were successfully analyzed: REMix is best for investment path optimization; COMANDO excels with atypical components; OEMOF is the best open-source tool for standard optimization problems; HOMER PRO suits rapid synthesis optimization, particularly for users with limited programming experience. MTRESS could not be evaluated due to insufficient accessible information.
AI.conclusion: No single tool is universally optimal; the choice depends on the specific requirements of the energy system optimization problem. The paper provides a structured comparison to guide tool selection, while acknowledging the limitation that MTRESS remains unassessed and highlighting the importance of transparent documentation for such evaluations.

title: Conditional Reliability of Toxicity Signals for Multilingual and Code-Mixed Abuse Detection
summary: Moderation systems increasingly rely on external toxicity tools, but those tools are unreliable under code-mixing, transliteration, slang, and language mismatch. We study the \emph{conditional reliability} of toxicity priors in Indian multilingual and code-mixed short text: English toxicity, Indic abuse, and rule-based severity cues can be useful evidence, but only in some linguistic and abuse-severity contexts. We propose ToxGate, a trust-fusion head that conditions each auxiliary signal on the encoder representation before adding it to the prediction state. Across three short-text abuse datasets, four transformer encoders, and five seeds per setting, ToxGate improves over matched plain encoders in 10 of 12 in-domain settings and 7 of 8 transfer settings. The largest and most interpretable gains occur in high-risk moderation slices, including explicit slurs, violent threats, and cross-dataset transfer. The broader lesson is that moderation systems should treat external toxicity tools and priors as conditional evidence rather than fixed features or ground truth, in focused ablations, source-specific gating gives the strongest results in transfer, severe-abuse slices, and high-risk triage.

AI.tldr: ToxGate improves abuse detection in code-mixed and multilingual Indian short texts by conditioning external toxicity signals (English toxicity, Indic abuse, severity cues) on the encoder representation via a trust-fusion head. It yields consistent gains over plain encoders, especially in high-risk slices like slurs and threats, and in cross-dataset transfer.
AI.motivation: External toxicity detection tools are unreliable in code-mixed, transliterated, slang-heavy, and language-mismatched settings common in Indian social media. Existing approaches treat these auxiliary signals as fixed features or ground truth, ignoring that their reliability varies by linguistic context and abuse severity.
AI.method: ToxGate, a trust-fusion head that conditions each auxiliary toxicity signal (English toxicity scores, Indic abuse predictions, rule-based severity cues) on the transformer encoder's contextual representation before adding it to the prediction state. This gating mechanism lets the model dynamically decide how much to trust each external signal based on the input context.
AI.result: ToxGate improves over matched plain encoders in 10 of 12 in-domain settings and 7 of 8 transfer settings across three short-text abuse datasets, four transformer encoders, and five seeds. Gains are largest and most interpretable in high-risk slices: explicit slurs, violent threats, and cross-dataset transfer. Source-specific gating performs best in transfer, severe-abuse slices, and high-risk triage.
AI.conclusion: Moderation systems should treat external toxicity tools as conditional evidence rather than fixed features or ground truth. Context-aware fusion via gating provides robust, interpretable improvements, particularly for high-stakes moderation decisions.

title: Neuro-Symbolic AI for LEED compliance: Document-Centric Benchmarking, Deterministic Numeric Checking, and When Multimodal Hurts
summary: LEED v4.1 BD+C certification remains a document-intensive process that requires reviewers to read hundreds of pages of project evidence and apply credit-specific threshold logic by hand. This paper investigates whether small, locally deployed language models can perform meaningful screening of LEED documentation and how deterministic symbolic components should share that work. A neuro-symbolic pipeline is introduced that aligns project PDFs to LEED credit sections, retrieves evidence with credit-aware keyword signatures, verifies compliance with a locally hosted 4-billion-parameter language model, and applies a LEED-specific numeric checker to quantitative thresholds. Experiments on four university buildings (484 PDFs, 153 credit-level decisions) show that a 4-billion-parameter model (gemma3:4b) is the strongest text-only core verifier, achieving 67.3% accuracy and outperforming a larger 8-billion-parameter model (llama3.1:8b) in this task. The deterministic numeric checker corrects arithmetic errors on key quantitative credits, moving EA-p2 from 50% to 100% accuracy and improving several other credits when required values are reliably extracted. At the same time, the full neuro-symbolic configuration achieves 61.6% overall accuracy, trailing the best text-only baseline due to extraction failures and conservative behavior on qualitative categories. Systematic ablations show that adding low-resolution drawing images (150-300 dpi) consistently reduces accuracy, and that prompt effectiveness depends on the building's ground-truth PASS rate: rubric prompts perform best on documentation-rich projects, while chain-of-thought prompts perform best on documentation-lean projects. Within the specific scope of LEED v4.1 BD+C compliance verification over raw project documentation, this pipeline and its baselines provide an initial reproducible reference point for both accuracy and failure modes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a neuro-symbolic pipeline for automating LEED v4.1 BD+C certification compliance verification, combining a small local language model (gemma3:4b) with deterministic symbolic components. Tested on 484 PDFs across four university buildings, the system achieves 67.3% text-only accuracy with the 4B model — surprisingly outperforming an 8B model — and demonstrates that a numeric checker can fully correct certain quantitative credits (e.g., EA-p2 from 50% to 100%), though the full neuro-symbolic pipeline drops to 61.6% due to extraction failures on qualitative categories.
AI.motivation: LEED v4.1 BD+C certification is heavily document-intensive, requiring manual review of hundreds of pages of project evidence and application of credit-specific thresholds. Automating even a screening-level review could reduce reviewer burden, but it is unclear whether small, locally deployable language models are capable of this task and how symbolic reasoning should complement them.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic pipeline with four stages: (1) alignment of project PDFs to LEED credit sections, (2) credit-aware keyword signature retrieval, (3) compliance verification using a locally hosted 4B-parameter language model (gemma3:4b), and (4) a LEED-specific deterministic numeric checker for quantitative thresholds. Systematic ablations compare model sizes (4B vs 8B), prompt strategies (rubric vs chain-of-thought), and the effect of low-resolution drawing images (150–300 dpi). Evaluation covers 153 credit-level decisions across four university buildings.
AI.result: The 4B gemma3:4b model achieved 67.3% accuracy as the best text-only verifier, outperforming llama3.1:8b (8B parameters). The deterministic numeric checker raised EA-p2 from 50% to 100% accuracy and improved several other quantitative credits. However, the full neuro-symbolic pipeline reached only 61.6% overall accuracy, trailing the text-only baseline due to extraction failures and conservative handling of qualitative categories. Adding low-resolution drawing images (150–300 dpi) consistently degraded accuracy. Prompt strategy effectiveness was project-dependent: rubric prompts excelled on documentation-rich projects, while chain-of-thought prompts worked better on documentation-lean projects.
AI.conclusion: Small, locally deployed language models show promise for LEED compliance screening, but the neuro-symbolic integration introduces fragility at the extraction stage, particularly for qualitative credits. The work establishes an initial reproducible benchmark for both accuracy and failure modes in automated green building certification review, highlighting the need for more robust evidence extraction before symbolic components can reliably contribute.

title: ADS-C: Antidistillation Sampling for Classification
summary: Knowledge distillation enables an adversary to replicate a proprietary classifier by querying its prediction interface and training a surrogate on the returned probability vectors. Antidistillation sampling, proposed for large language models, counters this threat with an input-dependent, gradient-directed perturbation of the served distribution; its transfer to classification has not been studied. Adapting the defense to classification, we show its behavior is governed by the distribution of the teacher's per-input confidence margins. Because well-trained classifiers are severely overconfident, the direct transfer exhibits an inert window: below a closed-form-predictable threshold, it affects neither attacker nor defender; beyond it, the defense undergoes a phase transition and degrades the teacher faster than the attacker's student. Temperature softening rescales the transition in closed form, and every temperature configuration lies on the same unfavorable trade-off curve. Our method, ADS-C, composes the perturbation under a closed-form, per-input margin budget that provably preserves every served top-1 prediction, so the defended teacher's accuracy equals the undefended teacher's identically. Under this guarantee the distilled student still loses 17.4 percentage points on CIFAR-100, 29.6 on CIFAR-10, and 13.3 on Tiny-ImageNet; matching this degradation with the unmodified defense costs 27.5, 32.9, and 22.2 points of teacher accuracy. Because served labels are unchanged, a hard-label attacker gains nothing, while the defended soft output trains a student up to 29.7 points below that floor: the incentive to distill served probabilities is not merely removed but reversed. To our knowledge, ADS-C is the first antidistillation defense for classification whose utility cost is exactly zero.

AI.tldr: ADS-C is a novel antidistillation defense for classification that applies a margin-budgeted, gradient-directed perturbation to softmax outputs. It provably preserves every top-1 prediction (zero accuracy cost to the teacher) while degrading student accuracy by 13–30 percentage points, reversing the incentive to distill.
AI.motivation: Model extraction via knowledge distillation allows adversaries to steal proprietary classifiers by querying prediction APIs. Prior antidistillation defenses for LLMs perturb output distributions but, when naively transferred to classification, exhibit an "inert window" and trade off teacher accuracy against student degradation. The authors aim to design a defense for classification with provably zero utility cost to the teacher.
AI.method: ADS-C adapts gradient-directed, input-dependent perturbation (antidistillation) to classification. The key innovation is a closed-form, per-input margin budget derived from the teacher's confidence margin distribution. This budget provably guarantees that the top-1 prediction is never altered. The authors also analyze the phase-transition behavior of the unmodified defense, characterize it via temperature softening, and show all configurations lie on a Pareto-inferior trade-off curve compared to ADS-C.
AI.result: ADS-C achieves zero teacher accuracy degradation by construction. Under this guarantee, student accuracy drops by 17.4 pp on CIFAR-100, 29.6 pp on CIFAR-10, and 13.3 pp on Tiny-ImageNet. Matching these student degradation levels with the unmodified defense costs 27.5, 32.9, and 22.2 teacher accuracy points, respectively. Hard-label attackers gain nothing since top-1 predictions are unchanged.
AI.conclusion: ADS-C is the first antidistillation defense for classification with exactly zero utility cost. By preserving top-1 predictions, it not only removes but reverses the distillation incentive: the student trained on defended soft outputs performs up to 29.7 points below the hard-label baseline.

title: The Language of Security: How Prompt Syntax Shapes Secure Code Generation in Open LLMs
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for source code generation despite their outputs often exhibiting security vulnerabilities. Prior work shows that prompt engineering can mitigate such risks, yet (1) they focused on high-level prompting strategies, neglecting recent evidence that fine-grained syntactic variations can substantially alter model behavior; and (2) predominantly evaluate proprietary LLMs, limiting the applicability of their findings in industrial settings where self-hosted, open models are preferred for privacy, compliance, and deployment control. In this paper, we study how fine-grained syntactic constituents of prompts influence the security of open LLM-generated code. Using a parser-driven approach, we systematically generate syntactic variants of security-relevant code generation prompts and evaluate their impact on code security across multiple open LLMs and programming languages. Our results show that specific syntactic elements, such as constraints, guards, conditions, and concept bindings, and their position within the prompt consistently affect the likelihood of generating insecure code. These findings identify prompt syntax as a concrete security control surface and provide actionable guidance for reducing vulnerability risk in LLM-assisted development.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how fine-grained syntactic variations in prompts (e.g., constraints, guards, conditions, concept bindings, and their positional placement) affect the security of code generated by open-source LLMs, using a parser-driven systematic approach across multiple models and programming languages.
AI.motivation: Prior work on prompt engineering for secure code generation focused on high-level prompting strategies and proprietary LLMs, neglecting (1) evidence that fine-grained syntactic variations significantly alter model behavior, and (2) the practical needs of industrial settings where self-hosted open models are preferred for privacy, compliance, and deployment control.
AI.method: A parser-driven approach that systematically generates syntactic variants of security-relevant code generation prompts. These variants manipulate specific syntactic constituents (constraints, guards, conditions, concept bindings) and their positions within prompts. The impact on code security is then evaluated across multiple open LLMs and programming languages.
AI.result: Specific syntactic elements—constraints, guards, conditions, and concept bindings—along with their positional placement within prompts, consistently affect the likelihood of LLMs generating insecure code.
AI.conclusion: Prompt syntax constitutes a concrete security control surface. The findings provide actionable guidance for reducing vulnerability risk in LLM-assisted software development by strategically designing prompt syntax.

title: An MLIR-Based Compilation Method for Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become the dominant workload on modern AI accelerators, yet deploying them on specialized hardware still faces two core challenges: how to import a trained model into a compiler-friendly intermediate representation, and how to efficiently schedule the autoregressive inference loop under limited on-chip memory. This paper presents an MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) based compilation method for large language models, illustrated using two dialects of operators, TopOp and TpuOp. TopOp serves as a high-level graph dialect that is independent of both the source framework and the target chip, and is responsible for expressing model semantics; TpuOp serves as the target hardware dialect, carrying chip-related decisions such as quantization, layer groups, and memory layout. A model is first represented as TopOp, then lowered layer by layer to TpuOp, and finally a deployable binary is generated. In addition, each Transformer layer is split into three stages for static compilation: prefill, prefill_kv (prefill with historical key-value cache), and decode, so as to accommodate the different computational characteristics of prompt-parallel processing and per-token generation. The method has been implemented in the TPU-MLIR compiler{https://github.com/sophgo/tpu-mlir} and the LLM-TPU deployment project\footnote{https://github.com/sophgo/LLM-TPU}, supporting a variety of generative models including the Qwen, Llama, InternVL, and MiniCPM-V series, as well as multiple quantization and deployment forms such as GPTQ, AWQ, and AutoRound.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TPU-MLIR, an MLIR-based compilation framework for deploying LLMs on specialized AI accelerators. It introduces a two-dialect lowering pipeline (TopOp → TpuOp) and a three-stage static compilation strategy (prefill, prefill_kv, decode) tailored for autoregressive inference under constrained on-chip memory.
AI.motivation: Deploying large language models on specialized AI hardware faces two core challenges: (1) importing trained models into a compiler-friendly intermediate representation, and (2) efficiently scheduling the autoregressive inference loop under limited on-chip memory. Existing compilation flows lack a principled, layered approach to handle both source-framework and target-chip independence while accommodating the distinct computational patterns of prompt processing versus token-by-token generation.
AI.method: The authors propose an MLIR-based compilation method with two operator dialects: TopOp (a high-level, framework- and chip-agnostic graph dialect for model semantics) and TpuOp (a target-hardware dialect carrying quantization, layer groups, and memory layout decisions). Models are first expressed in TopOp, then progressively lowered to TpuOp, and finally compiled to deployable binaries. Furthermore, each Transformer layer is partitioned into three static compilation stages — prefill, prefill_kv (prefill with historical KV cache), and decode — to separately optimize for prompt-parallel processing and per-token generation. The method is implemented in the open-source TPU-MLIR compiler and LLM-TPU deployment project.
AI.result: The approach has been implemented and open-sourced, supporting a range of generative models including Qwen, Llama, InternVL, and MiniCPM-V series, along with multiple quantization schemes (GPTQ, AWQ, AutoRound). The three-stage static compilation successfully accommodates divergent computational characteristics across the autoregressive inference lifecycle.
AI.conclusion: The MLIR-based two-dialect lowering pipeline combined with three-stage static compilation provides an effective solution for deploying LLMs on specialized accelerators with limited on-chip memory, offering broad model and quantization support.

title: ToolVerse: Unlocking Massive Environments and Long-Horizon Tasks for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: While LLM agents demonstrate strong reasoning abilities in compact and well-defined scenarios, they struggle to maintain robustness and effectiveness when faced with large-scale, diverse, and dynamic real-world environments that demand seamless tool integration. To address this gap, we introduce ToolVerse, a comprehensive framework that scales up agentic RL environments and enables agents to perform complex long-horizon reasoning in Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) tasks. First, ToolVerse automatically builds the massive executable agent training environments from nearly 400 real-world Model Context Protocols (MCPs) that contain about 4500 tools. Second, we propose a task design strategy based on a tool dependency graph, utilizing Dynamic Unlocking Sampling Algorithm to generate long-horizon tasks, and produce GUST (Graph Unlocking Sampling Tasks) dataset. Third, to alleviate the credit assigment problem in long-horizon agentic RL, we propose a fine-grained Turn-Aware Relative Advantage algorithm. We conduct extensive Agentic RL training using ToolVerse and evaluate our framework on serveral agentic benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly strengthens LLMs' capabilities in long-horizon tool use, achieving a marked performance boost and showcasing robust reasoning within dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: ToolVerse is a framework that automatically builds large-scale RL training environments from ~400 real-world MCPs (~4500 tools), generates long-horizon tasks via a graph-based Dynamic Unlocking Sampling Algorithm, and proposes a Turn-Aware Relative Advantage algorithm to address credit assignment in agentic RL, significantly improving LLMs' long-horizon tool-use capabilities.
AI.motivation: LLM agents perform well in compact, well-defined scenarios but fail to maintain robustness in large-scale, diverse, dynamic real-world environments requiring seamless tool integration. There is a gap in scaling up agentic RL environments for Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) tasks.
AI.method: 1) ToolVerse automatically constructs massive executable agent training environments from nearly 400 Model Context Protocols (MCPs) containing ~4500 tools. 2) A task design strategy leveraging a tool dependency graph with a Dynamic Unlocking Sampling Algorithm generates long-horizon tasks, producing the GUST (Graph Unlocking Sampling Tasks) dataset. 3) A fine-grained Turn-Aware Relative Advantage algorithm is proposed to mitigate the credit assignment problem in long-horizon agentic RL.
AI.result: Extensive agentic RL training using ToolVerse and evaluation on multiple agentic benchmarks demonstrate that the framework significantly strengthens LLMs' long-horizon tool-use capabilities, achieving marked performance improvements and robust reasoning in dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: ToolVerse effectively bridges the gap between LLM agents and real-world tool-integrated reasoning by providing a scalable training framework, novel task generation, and improved RL credit assignment, yielding substantial gains in agentic performance.

title: Deep Learning Approaches for Sleep Apnea Classification from Polysomnographic EEG Signals
summary: Sleep apnea diagnosis via polysomnography remains resource intensive and relies on time consuming manual data analysis and scoring. Recent work has demonstrated that central nervous system effects of sleep apnea events can be detected through electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. However, most work uses a single feature type on various datasets combined with different classification algorithms. In this work, we present a comprehensive comparison of deep learning architectures and feature representations for automated sleep apnea detection from multichannel EEG on a single dataset of pediatric subjects. We evaluate Vision Transformers and Graph Attention Networks across distinct signal representations: raw temporal signals, short-time Fourier transform spectrograms, coherence based graphs, and two topological data analysis (TDA) derived features. Using age and sex matching of our train and test sets, we train on 2410 pediatric subjects and test on 575 pediatric subjects. We achieve a best test AUC of 0.750 using a vision transformer based model trained on TDA features. Stratified analysis across patient demographics (age, sex, AHI severity) and sleep stages (N1, N2, N3, REM) reveals significant performance variation. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of EEG based automated OSA screening while highlighting essential challenges for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive comparison of deep learning architectures and EEG feature representations for automated pediatric sleep apnea detection, finding Vision Transformers trained on topological data analysis features achieve the best performance (AUC 0.750), with significant variation across demographics and sleep stages.
AI.motivation: Polysomnography-based sleep apnea diagnosis is resource-intensive and time-consuming. While EEG signals can detect central nervous system effects of sleep apnea, prior work lacks systematic comparison of deep learning architectures and feature types on a unified dataset, limiting progress toward clinically deployable automated screening.
AI.method: The authors train and evaluate models on a large pediatric EEG dataset (2410 training, 575 test subjects) with age/sex matching. They compare: (1) architectures — Vision Transformers and Graph Attention Networks; and (2) five feature representations — raw temporal signals, STFT spectrograms, coherence-based graphs, and two topological data analysis (TDA) features. Stratified analysis is performed across age, sex, AHI severity, and sleep stages (N1, N2, N3, REM).
AI.result: The best performance is AUC 0.750 using a Vision Transformer trained on TDA features. Performance varies significantly across patient demographics and sleep stages, revealing both the feasibility of EEG-based automated OSA screening and key challenges for clinical translation.
AI.conclusion: EEG-based deep learning can feasibly screen for pediatric OSA, but substantial performance heterogeneity across subpopulations and sleep stages must be addressed before reliable clinical deployment.

title: Code-Poisoning Property Inference Attacks
summary: The flourishing code hosting platforms and coding agents enable even beginners with private data to build tailored Machine Learning (ML) models using available code quickly. The training data for ML models, often regarded as private property (e.g., clinical records, transaction information), is at significant risk of information leakage. Property Inference Attacks (PIAs), as a significant type of privacy attack, aim to expose global property information of the training set. In this paper, we present Code-Poisoning Property Inference Attack (CPPIA), the first code-level PIA, which overcomes four limitations of existing works: insufficient attack performance, severe degradation of model accuracy, high computational overhead, and failure under defenses. We consider malicious code providers from code hosting platforms (GitHub) and coding agents (Codex). Upon downloading the poisoned code, data holders train models with their private data without professional auditing, subsequently releasing label-only APIs to the public. The adversary embeds the properties into secret samples during training and queries the trained model on these samples later to leak privacy. CPPIA offers 100\% attack accuracy without degrading model accuracy. It is also computationally lightweight and requires no shadow models. We evaluate the attack performance across four datasets, eight model architectures, eighteen properties, and under three defense mechanisms, demonstrating the universality and effectiveness of CPPIA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CPPIA, a code-level property inference attack where malicious code providers inject poisoned code that embeds secret property-tied samples during training. The adversary later queries the model's label-only API on these secret samples to infer global training data properties with 100% accuracy, without degrading model utility or requiring shadow models.
AI.motivation: Existing property inference attacks suffer from four key limitations: insufficient attack accuracy, significant degradation of target model accuracy, high computational overhead (requiring shadow models), and failure under common defenses. The rise of code hosting platforms and coding agents allows adversaries to distribute poisoned training code that unsuspecting data holders (e.g., clinicians, financial analysts) will execute on private data without professional auditing, creating a realistic threat vector.
AI.method: The adversary (malicious code provider on GitHub or via coding agents like Codex) crafts poisoned training code that, when executed, embeds property-correlated secret samples into the training process. These secret samples are designed such that the trained model's predictions on them reveal global properties of the private training set. After the data holder releases a label-only API, the adversary queries the model on these secret samples and statistically analyzes the outputs to infer properties. The method is code-level (poisoning occurs in the training script, not data), requires no shadow models, and is computationally lightweight.
AI.result: CPPIA achieves 100% attack accuracy across four datasets, eight model architectures, and eighteen properties, without degrading the target model's accuracy. It remains effective under three defense mechanisms. The attack is computationally lightweight and eliminates the need for shadow models.
AI.conclusion: CPPIA demonstrates a practical, powerful, and stealthy privacy threat against ML models trained by non-experts using third-party code. It exposes a critical vulnerability in the ML supply chain where code-level poisoning can reliably leak global properties of private training data through label-only model APIs.

title: How Much Human Label Variation Does Formal Semantic Structure Explain?: Group-Level Effects and Item-Level Ceilings in NLI
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Code and preregistered analysis log: https://github.com/oudeis01/nli-hlv-structure
summary: Human label variation in natural language inference is increasingly treated as signal rather than noise, but how much of it formal semantic structure explains has not been measured directly. We measure it on the 3,113 SNLI and MNLI items of ChaosNLI, using a rule-based operator and monotonicity tagger validated against MED (0.883 agreement at the edit site, 0.807 on the sentence-level summary our analyses consume), three preregistered analysis blocks, and full reporting of negative results. Three bounds emerge. First, a group-level boundary: hypotheses that are not purely upward monotone show reliably higher label entropy (Cliff's delta = -0.284), and rank-based tests defend the effect against operator-presence and length reductions, though a bounded-outcome sensitivity check weakens the regression form of the length defense. Second, an item-level ceiling: the same formal profiles explain only 3.3 to 3.6 percent of entropy variance and reach a median-split AUC of 0.606, too weak to identify high-disagreement items. Third, composition invariance: across the boundary, three high-powered preregistered contrasts on validated error shares and explanation-type shares (VariErr, LiTEx) all return null results. In this sample, formal semantic structure shifts how much annotators disagree by a small amount and does not detectably change what they disagree about. ChaosNLI-S/M consists of items selected for low original agreement, and every claim is conditioned on that scope. All analyses were preregistered in a version-controlled research log, whose audit trail, including one corrected interpretation rule, the paper discloses.

AI.tldr: This paper measures how much formal semantic structure explains human label variation in NLI, finding a small but reliable effect on disagreement magnitude (group-level boundary) but near-zero explanatory power for identifying high-disagreement items, and no detectable effect on what annotators disagree about.
AI.motivation: Human label variation in NLI is increasingly treated as informative signal, but the extent to which formal semantic structure (specifically monotonicity properties) accounts for this variation has never been directly quantified. The authors aim to fill this gap with rigorous, preregistered measurement.
AI.method: The authors analyze 3,113 SNLI/MNLI items from ChaosNLI using a rule-based monotonicity tagger (validated against MED with 0.883 edit-site agreement, 0.807 sentence-level agreement). They conduct three preregistered analysis blocks: (1) a group-level comparison of label entropy between upward-monotone and non-upward-monotone hypotheses, (2) item-level variance-explained and classification analyses, and (3) composition-invariance tests using VariErr and LiTEx error-share and explanation-type contrasts.
AI.result: Three bounds emerge: (1) Group-level boundary — hypotheses that are not purely upward monotone show reliably higher label entropy (Cliff's delta = -0.284), robust to operator-presence and length reductions. (2) Item-level ceiling — formal profiles explain only 3.3–3.6% of entropy variance and achieve a median-split AUC of 0.606, too weak for practical identification of high-disagreement items. (3) Composition invariance — three preregistered contrasts all return null results, indicating formal structure does not detectably change what annotators disagree about.
AI.conclusion: Formal semantic structure exerts a small, statistically reliable influence on how much annotators disagree in NLI, but explains very little variance and does not alter the qualitative nature of disagreement. All claims are conditioned on ChaosNLI's scope of low-agreement items. The study demonstrates the value of preregistered, negative-result-transparent analysis in computational semantics.

title: S1-Omni: A Unified Multimodal Reasoning Model for Scientific Understanding, Prediction, and Generation
summary: We present S1-Omni, a unified multimodal reasoning model for scientific understanding, prediction, and generation. AI for Science (AI4S) has advanced significantly through domain-specific models, tool-augmented LLMs, and scientific language models. However, model capabilities remain highly fragmented, limiting the joint modeling of heterogeneous data, scientific laws, and expert knowledge. S1-Omni addresses this gap by consolidating these capabilities into a single, coherent scientific reasoning model. The architecture of S1-Omni is built upon three core components: unified representation of scientific data, natural-world knowledge alignment, and decoding for domain-specific tasks. First, S1-Omni maps natural-language instructions and scientific objects, including CIF, SMILES, protein sequences, spectra, and scientific images, into a shared representation space. Second, it incorporates scientific laws and expert knowledge into data construction and training, enabling the model to reason from scientific evidence. Third, it performs task-specific decoding to support a broad range of applications, including property prediction, spectrum-to-molecular generation, protein site and structure prediction, and scientific image generation and editing. S1-Omni is trained on S1-Omni-Corpus, which covers 200 scientific tasks and contains millions of reasoning samples, and is evaluated on over 60 scientific benchmarks. It outperforms GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro on most benchmarks and matches or surpasses domain-specific models on several benchmarks. Overall, S1-Omni provides a practical path toward unified scientific modeling.

AI.tldr: S1-Omni is a unified multimodal reasoning model for AI for Science that consolidates heterogeneous data types, scientific laws, and expert knowledge into a single architecture. It supports property prediction, molecular generation, protein structure prediction, and scientific image tasks, outperforming GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro on over 60 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI4S models are highly fragmented, with domain-specific models, tool-augmented LLMs, and scientific language models operating in isolation. This fragmentation limits the joint modeling of heterogeneous scientific data (CIF, SMILES, protein sequences, spectra, images), scientific laws, and expert knowledge. There is a need for a unified model that can reason across these modalities and tasks.
AI.method: S1-Omni employs a three-component architecture: (1) Unified representation — mapping natural language instructions and scientific objects (CIF, SMILES, protein sequences, spectra, images) into a shared representation space; (2) Natural-world knowledge alignment — incorporating scientific laws and expert knowledge into data construction and training; (3) Task-specific decoding — enabling diverse applications such as property prediction, spectrum-to-molecular generation, protein site/structure prediction, and scientific image generation/editing. The model is trained on S1-Omni-Corpus, spanning 200 scientific tasks with millions of reasoning samples.
AI.result: S1-Omni outperforms GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro on most of over 60 scientific benchmarks and matches or surpasses domain-specific models on several benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: S1-Omni demonstrates a viable path toward unified scientific modeling by consolidating fragmented AI4S capabilities into a single coherent model, achieving strong performance across diverse scientific reasoning tasks.

title: Inpainting Insights: Elevating Visual XAI with Photorealistic Perturbations
comment: Preprint accepted at XAIE4 (ICPR 2026). 15 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code available at: https://github.com/jo01123/LILI and https://github.com/m-chaves/LIME
summary: The increasing complexity of state-of-the-art machine learning models has made their behavior progressively harder to interpret, spurring rapid advancements in the field of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Among many methods proposed, perturbation-based approaches play a major role. By systematically altering (perturbing) input features, these approaches measure the impact on the model's predictions. For image data, traditional perturbation techniques, often involve replacing pixel values e.g., with a pre-defined color. However, such approaches, but also more refined deterministic techniques, generate unrealistic out-of-distribution samples and often leave visible artifacts, which can mislead the model and compromise explanation quality. In this work, we adjust LIME, a widely used perturbation-based method, to demonstrate how generative inpainting can improve perturbation-based explanations for images. We achieve photorealistic perturbed samples that align better with the original data distribution and enhance explanation quality.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts LIME to use generative inpainting for creating realistic perturbed image samples, improving the quality of perturbation-based explanations by avoiding out-of-distribution artifacts.
AI.motivation: Traditional perturbation-based XAI methods for images use techniques like replacing pixels with predefined colors, which produce unrealistic, out-of-distribution samples with visible artifacts that can mislead the model and degrade explanation quality. More refined deterministic approaches still suffer from similar issues.
AI.method: The authors modify LIME, a widely-used perturbation-based explanation method, by incorporating generative inpainting to produce perturbed samples. Instead of crude pixel replacement, inpainting fills occluded or altered regions with photorealistic content that remains consistent with the original data distribution.
AI.result: The generative inpainting approach produces photorealistic perturbed samples that better align with the original data distribution, resulting in enhanced explanation quality compared to traditional perturbation techniques.
AI.conclusion: Generative inpainting offers a meaningful improvement over traditional perturbation strategies for image-based XAI, enabling more faithful and reliable explanations by mitigating distribution-shift artifacts.

title: Refusal is Not Safety! Benchmarking Latent Safety Risks of LLM-Driven Content Humorization
summary: Safety defenses for large language models (LLMs) have been extensively studied, with existing approaches focusing on attack detection and refusal mechanisms. Such fixed-form direct refusal strategies may introduce the risk of prefix injection attacks. Recent work has explored a new direction that leverages humor as an indirect refusal mechanism to mitigate over-refusal in jailbreak scenarios and reduce prefix injection risks. However, this approach implicitly assumes that humorous responses are safe. Whether humorization itself introduces safety risks remains unexplored. To address this issue, we conduct an exploratory study involving over 30,000 real-world agent interaction records and 45 stand-up comedians, revealing practical safety concerns in LLM-based content humorization. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textsc{HumorSafe}, a novel framework for evaluating latent safety risk propagation during humorization. \textsc{HumorSafe} enables LLMs to learn harmful humorization patterns and use them to transform benign content into humorous content with safety risks. Across five frontier LLMs, we find that LLMs can introduce stereotypes and toxicity during humorization. We further propose \textsc{HumorPIA}, a prompt injection attack that exploits latent risks in humor-based defenses. \textsc{HumorPIA} preserves the appearance of safe humorous refusal while covertly injecting harmful content, allowing latent risks to evade existing detection mechanisms. Experiments show that it increases toxicity by 3.14$\times$ while maintaining an apparent safety rate of 97.8\% even under defense settings. Our findings highlight a gap in existing LLM safety evaluations under humorized settings.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the overlooked safety risks of using humor as a defense mechanism in LLMs. The authors conduct a large-scale study revealing that LLM-based humorization can introduce stereotypes and toxicity. They propose HumorSafe (a framework for evaluating latent risk propagation during humorization) and HumorPIA (a prompt injection attack exploiting humor-based defenses), demonstrating that harmful content can evade detection while appearing safe and humorous.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety defenses rely on fixed-form refusal strategies, which are vulnerable to prefix injection attacks. Recent work proposes humor-based indirect refusal to mitigate over-refusal and reduce prefix injection risks, but it implicitly assumes humorous responses are inherently safe. The authors challenge this assumption, questioning whether humorization itself introduces safety risks — a gap that remains unexplored in current LLM safety evaluations.
AI.method: The authors conduct an exploratory study using over 30,000 real-world agent interaction records and 45 stand-up comedians to identify practical safety concerns in LLM-based humorization. They propose HumorSafe, a framework that enables LLMs to learn harmful humorization patterns and transform benign content into humor with latent safety risks. They further develop HumorPIA, a prompt injection attack that preserves the appearance of safe humorous refusal while covertly injecting harmful content, designed to evade existing detection mechanisms.
AI.result: Across five frontier LLMs, the study finds that humorization can introduce stereotypes and toxicity. HumorPIA increases toxicity by 3.14× while maintaining an apparent safety rate of 97.8% under defense settings, demonstrating that latent risks in humor-based defenses can effectively bypass existing safety mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a critical gap in existing LLM safety evaluations under humorized settings. Humor-based defense strategies, while promising against over-refusal and prefix injection, introduce latent safety risks (stereotypes, toxicity) that current detection mechanisms fail to capture. The work calls for more comprehensive safety evaluation frameworks that account for these humorization-induced vulnerabilities.

title: DECODEM: Data Extraction from Corporate Organizational Documents via Enhanced Methods
summary:
Much empirical legal research depends on translating unstructured text into structured variables. In corporate governance research as elsewhere, this translation has traditionally relied on human coding of documents such as charters and bylaws, a process that is costly, difficult to scale, and often opaque. This paper introduces DECODEM, a set of benchmark datasets for evaluating the automated extraction of corporate governance variables from organizational documents. The benchmarks pair randomly sampled corporate charters and bylaws with high-quality human annotations covering a range of governance provisions commonly studied in empirical work.
  Using these datasets, the paper evaluates several large-language-model extraction pipelines that vary in prompt design, task decomposition, and document handling. The underlying task consists of a set of document-level binary classification problems, one for each governance variable. The results show that automated extraction is feasible at a high level of accuracy for many provisions, with median performance near the upper bound across approaches. At the same time, performance varies systematically across variables, with a small number of provisions accounting for most of the remaining errors. More elaborate prompting strategies and cascading pipelines do not consistently improve performance for frontier models, but substantially narrow the gap between frontier and efficiency-oriented models in some settings, suggesting that pipeline design can partly substitute for model capability.
  By providing a standardized benchmark and a systematic evaluation of extraction methods, the paper demonstrates that current frontier models can extract legally meaningful information from complex corporate documents with high accuracy and suggests an important future role for automated feature extraction in constructing corporate governance datasets.

AI.tldr: DECODEM introduces benchmark datasets for evaluating automated extraction of corporate governance variables from charters and bylaws using LLMs, finding frontier models achieve high accuracy with simpler pipelines while sophisticated prompting helps close the gap for smaller models.
AI.motivation: Traditional human coding of corporate governance documents (charters, bylaws) for empirical legal research is costly, difficult to scale, and opaque. Automating this translation from unstructured text to structured variables could dramatically improve efficiency, but requires standardized benchmarks to rigorously evaluate extraction methods.
AI.method: The authors construct DECODEM, a benchmark dataset pairing randomly sampled corporate charters and bylaws with high-quality human annotations across multiple governance provisions. They then evaluate several LLM-based extraction pipelines varying in prompt design, task decomposition, and document handling. The task is framed as document-level binary classification for each governance variable. Pipelines range from simple prompting to cascading, multi-stage strategies, tested across both frontier and efficiency-oriented models.
AI.result: Automated extraction achieves high accuracy for most governance provisions, with median performance near the human-annotation upper bound. However, performance varies systematically across variables — a small number of provisions account for most errors. Elaborate prompting and cascading pipelines do not consistently improve frontier model performance but substantially narrow the gap between frontier and efficiency-oriented models, suggesting pipeline design can partly substitute for model capability.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can extract legally meaningful information from complex corporate documents with high accuracy. The DECODEM benchmark provides a foundation for future work in automated feature extraction for corporate governance datasets, with pipeline design offering a path to democratize access by enabling smaller models to approach frontier-level performance.

title: Behavioral Controllability of Agentic Models for Information Extraction: From Fixed Workflows to Reflective Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for complex information-extraction tasks, yet it remains unclear whether agentic components such as reflection and memory lead to observable and controllable improvements over fixed LLM workflows. We study this question through conference-paper dataset extraction, where a system must identify datasets mentioned in scholarly PDFs and produce structured records. We compare a fixed workflow baseline with reflective agent variants and specify an optimized agent condition (S2) that extends the same task with richer PDF tools and dynamic tool selection. Our evaluation emphasizes process-level behavior--including tool execution, retries, reflection, memory use, runtime, and failure recovery--while treating extraction coverage and field completeness as secondary outcome measures. The paper characterizes when agentic mechanisms change system behavior, whether these changes improve task completion, and how the observed failure modes motivate an optimized agent design under the same evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether agentic components (reflection, memory) in LLM-based systems yield observable and controllable improvements over fixed workflows for dataset extraction from scholarly PDFs, comparing baseline workflows with reflective agents and an optimized agent variant (S2), with emphasis on process-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed for complex information-extraction tasks, but it remains unclear whether agentic mechanisms like reflection and memory provide genuine, measurable benefits over simpler fixed workflows. There is a need for rigorous, process-level evaluation that goes beyond outcome metrics to understand when and why agentic behaviors matter.
AI.method: The authors design a conference-paper dataset extraction task where systems identify datasets in scholarly PDFs and produce structured records. They compare three conditions: (1) a fixed workflow baseline without agentic features, (2) reflective agent variants incorporating reflection and memory, and (3) an optimized agent condition (S2) with richer PDF tools and dynamic tool selection. Evaluation prioritizes process-level metrics—tool execution, retries, reflection, memory usage, runtime, and failure recovery—with extraction coverage and field completeness as secondary outcomes.
AI.result: The paper characterizes the conditions under which agentic mechanisms alter system behavior, whether these behavioral changes translate to improved task completion, and how observed failure modes inform the design of the optimized S2 agent. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Agentic mechanisms can change system behavior in observable ways, but their impact on task performance is context-dependent. Failure mode analysis drives the design of the optimized S2 agent, suggesting that process-level evaluation is critical for understanding and controlling LLM agent systems in information-extraction tasks.

title: Diffusion models recover accurate mixture weights despite score function insensitivity
summary: Score-based generative models exhibit a puzzling behavior: they often appear to cover all modes of a target multimodal distribution and yet may fail to learn the correct relative mode amplitudes, which can be interpreted as mixture weights. We resolve this apparent paradox by relating the diffusion score matching (DSM) loss to the error in estimating mixture weights from generated samples. We show that, even when the target score is insensitive to mixture weights, generated samples can recover the weights accurately if the scores at intermediate noise levels are informative about the weights. Accordingly, we define the diffusion score sensitivity index (DSSI) as the variation in the DSM loss relative to changes in a parameter. We then show that the DSSI governs the accuracy with which the parameter of the target distribution can be estimated from generated samples. For Gaussian mixtures in arbitrary dimensions, we prove that the mixture weight estimation errors are on the same order as the DSM loss under mild conditions. Empirically, we show the emergence of sensitivity during the noising process of benchmark data distributions under typical noise schedules, and that these sensitivity values predict how well a well-trained model recovers mixture weights. Furthermore, we show that the choice of noise schedule can reduce diffusion sensitivity, leading to mode amplification. Although we focus on mixture weights, the proposed sensitivity framework governs the recovery of any qualitative parameter of the target distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the paradox of why score-based generative models can cover all modes yet misestimate mixture weights. It introduces the Diffusion Score Sensitivity Index (DSSI), which quantifies how informative intermediate noise levels are about distribution parameters, and proves that parameter estimation errors are governed by this sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Score-based generative models exhibit a puzzling behavior: they visually cover all modes of a multimodal distribution but often fail to learn correct relative mode amplitudes (mixture weights). The authors aim to resolve this paradox by understanding when and why generated samples recover mixture weights accurately.
AI.method: The authors relate the diffusion score matching (DSM) loss to mixture weight estimation error. They define the Diffusion Score Sensitivity Index (DSSI) as the variation in DSM loss relative to parameter changes. For Gaussian mixtures in arbitrary dimensions, they prove that mixture weight estimation errors are on the same order as the DSM loss under mild conditions. Empirically, they demonstrate sensitivity emergence during the noising process and show DSSI predicts mixture weight recovery quality.
AI.result: The DSSI governs how accurately a target distribution parameter can be estimated from generated samples. The choice of noise schedule affects diffusion sensitivity, where reduced sensitivity leads to mode amplification. The framework generalizes beyond mixture weights to any qualitative parameter of the target distribution.
AI.conclusion: The apparent paradox of mode coverage without correct weighting is resolved by the DSSI framework: accurate weight recovery requires intermediate noise levels to be sufficiently sensitive to mixture weights. The noise schedule is a critical factor, and the sensitivity framework applies broadly to any distribution parameter recovery.

title: AI Watermark Evidence Fails Forensic Readiness: An Empirical Evaluation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. A version of this paper was submitted to the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES) 2026
summary:
Governments are increasingly mandating that LLM-generated content carry watermarks. The EU AI Act calls for markings that are "sufficiently reliable and robust." California's SB 942 requires disclosure that is "permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove." Both mandates rest on an untested assumption: that watermark detection yields evidence reliable enough for courts. This paper tests that assumption directly.
  We evaluate three representative LLM watermarking methods -- KGW, Unigram, and the MarkLLM implementation of SynthID-Text -- against the Daubert admissibility criteria and the NIST SP 800-86 digital forensic process. To structure this evaluation, we propose a Forensic Readiness Score (FRS) framework with 12 criteria, three mandatory gates, and a 60-point scoring system. We focus on meaning-preserving paraphrase as the attack vector, since it is both legally realistic and difficult to dismiss as evidence tampering.
  The results raise serious evidentiary concerns. Out of 846 valid paraphrase runs across 15 diverse prompts per method, every single initially-detected KGW and Unigram text lost its watermark after paraphrasing -- 100% conditional removal. SynthID fared only slightly better at 98.3%. Even before any attack, false-negative rates were already high: 70% for KGW, 83% for Unigram, 80% for SynthID. The SynthID configuration also flagged 5.4% of paraphrased human-written controls as AI-generated and showed an 18.6% paradox rate, with 80% of its own pristine watermarked output landing in the uncertainty deadband. None of the three methods satisfy more than two of five Daubert factors. We also find that the FRS point-based scoring system, despite working as designed, cannot fully capture forensic uselessness -- a limitation worth noting for future framework design.
  These configurations, as tested, do not meet the evidentiary bar that courts require.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates three LLM watermarking methods (KGW, Unigram, SynthID-Text) against legal evidentiary standards (Daubert criteria) and digital forensic processes. Using meaning-preserving paraphrase attacks, all methods show catastrophic failure rates: 100% watermark removal for KGW/Unigram, 98.3% for SynthID, plus high pre-attack false-negative rates (70-83%). None satisfy more than two of five Daubert factors, raising serious doubts about the forensic reliability of current watermarking for court use.
AI.motivation: Governments (EU AI Act, California SB 942) are mandating watermarking of LLM-generated content under the untested assumption that watermark detection yields court-admissible evidence. This paper directly challenges that assumption by subjecting watermarking methods to rigorous legal and forensic scrutiny.
AI.method: The authors propose a Forensic Readiness Score (FRS) framework with 12 criteria, three mandatory gates, and a 60-point scoring system. They evaluate three watermarking methods — KGW, Unigram, and MarkLLM's SynthID-Text — against the Daubert admissibility criteria and NIST SP 800-86 digital forensic process. The primary attack vector is meaning-preserving paraphrase, chosen for its legal realism. Testing involved 846 valid paraphrase runs across 15 diverse prompts per method, plus analysis of false-positive rates, paradox rates, and deadband behavior.
AI.result: All three methods failed catastrophically: KGW and Unigram suffered 100% conditional watermark removal under paraphrase; SynthID achieved 98.3% removal. Pre-attack false-negative rates were already severe: 70% (KGW), 83% (Unigram), 80% (SynthID). SynthID also flagged 5.4% of paraphrased human text as AI-generated and exhibited an 18.6% paradox rate, with 80% of its own watermarked output falling into an uncertainty deadband. None satisfied more than two of five Daubert factors. The FRS scoring system, while functional, could not fully capture forensic uselessness.
AI.conclusion: As tested, none of the three watermarking configurations meet the evidentiary bar required by courts. Current watermarking mandates rest on a flawed assumption of forensic reliability. The authors highlight the need for more robust methods and note a limitation in point-based scoring frameworks for capturing total forensic failure.

title: Induction in Both Directions: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: While the internal mechanisms of autoregressive (AR) transformers have been studied extensively, much less is known about diffusion language models (DLMs), an emerging alternative that generates text by iterative denoising. In this work, we study how DLMs implement induction, a mechanism behind in-context learning in which the model finds a repeated context and copies the token that followed it. Our analysis compares attention-only AR models and absorbing-mask DLMs with matched architectures. We find that DLMs learn a bidirectional induction circuit, where previous-token and next-token heads write local context into the residual stream and later induction heads use it to find and copy the answer from the matching source position. The circuit is direction-symmetric, working whether the source appears in the past or in the future. When only left context is visible, matching what an AR model sees, the DLM does not outperform its AR counterpart in induction capabilities. However, we observe it has stronger induction when both sides of the masked token are visible, pointing to bidirectional context access rather than a stronger one-sided mechanism. Beyond induction, we provide causal evidence that DLMs compute the global fraction of masked tokens and use it as an implicit timestep, even though they are given no explicit timestep embedding.

AI.tldr: This paper reverse-engineers how diffusion language models implement induction (a key in-context learning mechanism), finding they use a bidirectional circuit that leverages both past and future context, and that they implicitly compute masked token fractions as a timestep signal without explicit embeddings.
AI.motivation: While autoregressive transformers' internal mechanisms are well-studied, diffusion language models (DLMs) — which generate text via iterative denoising — remain poorly understood mechanistically. The authors aim to uncover how DLMs implement induction, a core operation behind in-context learning.
AI.method: The authors analyze attention-only AR models and absorbing-mask DLMs with matched architectures. They use mechanistic interpretability techniques (attention pattern analysis, causal intervention, logit attribution) to identify circuits responsible for induction and timestep representation.
AI.result: DLMs learn a bidirectional, direction-symmetric induction circuit: previous-token and next-token heads write local context into the residual stream, and induction heads use it to copy the answer from matching source positions (past or future). When only left context is visible, DLMs do not outperform AR models; their induction advantage comes from bidirectional context access, not a stronger one-sided mechanism. Additionally, DLMs implicitly compute the global fraction of masked tokens as a timestep signal, despite lacking explicit timestep embeddings.
AI.conclusion: DLMs' stronger induction capabilities stem from bidirectional context rather than fundamentally different induction computation. The implicit timestep mechanism reveals how DLMs coordinate denoising without explicit conditioning, advancing understanding of both DLM internals and the broader relationship between autoregressive and diffusion-based language generation.

title: NeurOWL: An LLM-Based Neural-symbolic Framework for Incomplete OWL Ontology Reasoning
summary: OWL ontologies provide a formal knowledge representation framework that enables semantic reasoning, and have been widely adopted across domains such as healthcare and bioinformatics. In practice, however, real-world ontologies are often incomplete, which pose challenges for reasoning. In this work, we focus on a fundamental subsumption reasoning problem: given an incomplete ontology and a candidate (non-entailed) subsumption, determine whether the subsumption is semantically plausible and, if so, providing a logically sound explanation containing potential missing axioms. This task unifies subsumption verification with ontology abduction, and generalizes the latter by removing the need for a predefined candidate set of missing axioms. To address this subsumption reasoning problem, we propose NeurOWL, an end-to-end neuro-symbolic framework that jointly performs verification and abduction, leveraging both formally defined semantics and textual semantics through Large Language Models and ontology embeddings. We evaluate NeurOWL on real-world ontologies across multiple domains, demonstrating strong and robust performance across different domains.

AI.tldr: NeurOWL is an end-to-end neuro-symbolic framework that unifies subsumption verification with ontology abduction, determining whether a non-entailed subsumption is plausible and generating logically sound explanations with missing axioms, using LLMs and ontology embeddings.
AI.motivation: Real-world OWL ontologies are often incomplete, hindering semantic reasoning. Existing approaches either verify subsumptions or perform abduction with a predefined candidate set of missing axioms. This work addresses the gap by unifying both tasks without requiring a predefined candidate set.
AI.method: NeurOWL is an end-to-end neuro-symbolic framework that jointly performs subsumption verification and ontology abduction. It leverages formally defined semantics (logical reasoning) alongside textual semantics through Large Language Models (LLMs) and ontology embeddings to determine plausibility and generate explanations containing potential missing axioms.
AI.result: NeurOWL was evaluated on real-world ontologies across multiple domains (healthcare, bioinformatics, etc.), demonstrating strong and robust performance across different domains.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach of combining formal semantics with LLMs and embeddings effectively addresses the unified subsumption reasoning problem, offering a robust solution for incomplete ontology reasoning across diverse real-world domains.

title: An Auto-Scaling Approach for Serverless Environments Based on a Multi-Expert Consensus Mechanism
comment: 26 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables, and 7 algorithms. Published in the Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments
summary: Serverless computing provides automatic resource management and pay-per-use execution, but effective autoscaling remains challenging because of dynamic workloads, cold-start latency, and dependencies among functions. We present a dependency-aware autoscaling framework that integrates graph-based bottleneck identification, short-term workload forecasting, multi-model consensus, and cost-aware scaling control. Serverless applications are represented as directed dependency graphs, and structurally important functions are identified using weighted degree centrality. Resource demand is predicted using lightweight MLP, LSTM, and CNN models. Their outputs are combined through a performance-weighted probabilistic ensemble inspired by Bayesian model averaging. The controller further incorporates cold-start awareness and cost comparison to select among scale-up, scale-down, and hold actions. Experiments using real workload traces show that supervised forecasting substantially outperforms unsupervised clustering for autoscaling decision generation. The proposed ensemble achieves 99.88 percent prediction accuracy and reduces prediction error compared with representative hybrid forecasting methods. Evaluations across multiple cloud pricing models also demonstrate consistent infrastructure cost reductions while maintaining performance targets. The results show that combining dependency analysis, multi-expert forecasting, and cost-aware control provides a robust and practical solution for serverless autoscaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dependency-aware autoscaling framework for serverless computing that combines graph-based bottleneck identification, multi-model ensemble forecasting (MLP, LSTM, CNN with Bayesian-inspired weighting), and cost-aware scaling control to achieve 99.88% prediction accuracy and consistent cost reductions across cloud pricing models.
AI.motivation: Serverless autoscaling is hindered by dynamic workloads, cold-start latency, and inter-function dependencies. Existing approaches lack integrated consideration of these factors, motivating a framework that jointly addresses dependency structure, workload prediction, and cost-efficient scaling decisions.
AI.method: Serverless applications are modeled as directed dependency graphs with weighted degree centrality identifying bottleneck functions. Resource demand is forecasted using lightweight MLP, LSTM, and CNN models, whose outputs are fused via a performance-weighted probabilistic ensemble inspired by Bayesian model averaging. A scaling controller then evaluates cold-start impact and cost trade-offs to select among scale-up, scale-down, and hold actions.
AI.result: Supervised forecasting significantly outperforms unsupervised clustering for autoscaling. The ensemble achieves 99.88% prediction accuracy and lower prediction error compared to representative hybrid forecasting methods. Evaluations on real workload traces demonstrate consistent infrastructure cost reductions across multiple cloud pricing models while maintaining performance targets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating dependency analysis, multi-expert forecasting, and cost-aware control yields a robust and practical solution for serverless autoscaling, effectively balancing prediction accuracy, cold-start mitigation, and cost efficiency.

title: Gasp: A DeFi Application Specic Rollup as a Consolidation Layer for All Assets
summary: Gasp is a decentralized exchange designed as an application-specific Layer 2 (L2) rollup with omnichain connectivity, leveraging EigenLayer's restaked ETH for computation correctness and finalization. With a goal of being a consolidation layer for all crypto assets, the Gasp platform employs optimistic rollup technology to facilitate gas-free, native cross-chain swaps without reliance on traditional bridges, ensuring tokens retain their original L1 grade security. By combining an app-chain architecture with escape hatch mechanisms, Gasp guarantees withdrawal, while MEV minimization through Themis architecture reduces value extraction risks. Gasp's proof-of-liquidity framework unlocks staked liquidity, enhancing capital efficiency and liquidity depth by integrating staking with liquidity provisioning. Additionally, the protocol introduces a time-based reward mechanism, incentivizing long-term liquidity commitment via an asymptotic reward curve. This paper examines the current challenges in cross-chain communication, delineates Gasp's architectural innovations and security guarantees, and examines novel approaches to optimizing DeFi ecosystems.

AI.tldr: Gasp is an L2 optimistic rollup DEX with omnichain connectivity that uses EigenLayer restaking for security, enabling gas-free native cross-chain swaps without bridges, while integrating MEV minimization, proof-of-liquidity, and time-based rewards.
AI.motivation: Address challenges in cross-chain communication, bridge reliance and associated security vulnerabilities, capital inefficiency in liquidity provisioning, and MEV extraction risks in existing DEX architectures.
AI.method: Gasp employs an application-specific optimistic rollup with omnichain connectivity, EigenLayer restaked ETH for computation correctness and finalization, escape hatch mechanisms for guaranteed withdrawals, Themis architecture for MEV minimization, a proof-of-liquidity framework integrating staking with liquidity provisioning, and an asymptotic time-based reward curve for long-term liquidity incentives.
AI.result: The paper delineates Gasp's architectural innovations, security guarantees, and novel approaches to DeFi optimization, though specific quantitative or empirical results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Gasp presents a consolidation layer for crypto assets that combines L2 rollup technology with EigenLayer security to deliver gas-free cross-chain swaps, enhanced capital efficiency, and reduced MEV risks, advancing the state of cross-chain DeFi infrastructure.

title: From Plausible to Actionable: A Position on LLM Self-Explanations
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate natural language explanations that rationalize their own decisions, a phenomenon commonly referred to as self-explanations.Such explanations have emerged as a promising direction for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), particularly for interpreting LLM behavior.However, while self-explanations often appear plausible, whether they faithfully reflect a model's underlying reasoning process remains an open question. In this opinion paper, we argue that self-explanations can be highly plausible, questionably faithful, and yet highly actionable. From a traditional XAI perspective, we identify the limitations of standard evaluation protocols for LLM-generated self-explanations and propose practical guidelines for assessing their plausibility and faithfulness. Moreover, we argue that evaluation should extend beyond these criteria to actionability, highlighting applications of LLM rationalization capabilities that support informed decision-making and appropriate action across diverse stakeholders.

AI.tldr: This opinion paper argues that LLM self-explanations (rationales) are often highly plausible but questionably faithful to actual reasoning. The authors critique existing XAI evaluation protocols and propose extending assessment beyond plausibility/faithfulness to include actionability — the practical utility of rationales for diverse stakeholders in decision-making contexts.
AI.motivation: Existing XAI evaluation protocols focus narrowly on plausibility and faithfulness of LLM-generated self-explanations, but these criteria are insufficient. Plausibility does not guarantee faithfulness, and even unfaithful explanations can be practically useful. The authors seek to reframe evaluation around actionability to better capture real-world value.
AI.method: This is an opinion/position paper. The authors provide a conceptual analysis: (1) they identify limitations in standard XAI evaluation protocols for LLM self-explanations, (2) propose practical guidelines for assessing plausibility and faithfulness, and (3) advocate extending evaluation to the criterion of actionability, illustrated through stakeholder-centric application scenarios.
AI.result: The paper delineates a tripartite characterization: LLM self-explanations are highly plausible (surface-level convincingness), questionably faithful (uncertain alignment with actual reasoning), and highly actionable (enabling informed decisions despite potential unfaithfulness). The authors provide concrete guidelines for operationalizing each evaluation dimension.
AI.conclusion: The XAI community should move beyond a binary plausibility-faithfulness framework and embrace actionability as a central evaluation criterion. Plausible but unfaithful rationales can still drive effective human decision-making, and evaluation protocols must reflect this pragmatic reality to fully harness LLM rationalization capabilities.

title: Cache-Aware Prompt Compression:A Two-Tier Cost Model for LLM API Caching
summary: Production LLM deployments combine two cost-reduction primitives: prompt caching (a discounted rate for re-used token prefixes) and prompt compression (fewer tokens sent). The compression literature has standardized on query-aware methods that produce a different compressed prefix per query, mechanically invalidating the prefix-strict cache on every call. We characterize this cost empirically on Anthropic's Sonnet 4.6 API and find caching is far from the rho=1.0 ideal the literature assumes: Sonnet's cache has a two-tier architecture with a sharp threshold near 3,500 tokens, below which the hit rate plateaus at rho~0.83 across 30-call sessions. Our cost model predicts, and experiments confirm, that under realistic rho, query-aware compression beats naive caching at high compression ratios (r>=6). We propose Cache-Aware Prompt Compression (CAPC), pairing query-agnostic compression with explicit cache_control plus a tier-preserving ratio bound that prevents over-compression from pushing the cached prefix into the hot tier. CAPC is the cheapest strategy in 16/16 configurations on LongBench-v2, with mean savings of 49% over cache-only, 64% over query-aware compression, and 90% over vanilla, at quality within 0.05 of the uncompressed baseline. We validate CAPC on three production workloads: an enterprise tool-using assistant with a 94k-token schema prefix (51.7% cost reduction at r=3); a graphify knowledge-graph RAG pipeline across two codebases (9.3x vs cache-all on FastAPI, 2.4x on httpx); and the public tau-bench retail benchmark (50 tasks), where CAPC is the cheapest of four strategies with reward exactly equal to vanilla (both 36/50, p=1.00) while query-aware compression is the most expensive at +40.1% over vanilla -- the first production confirmation of the crossover model's negative-ROI prediction on a public benchmark.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes Cache-Aware Prompt Compression (CAPC), which combines query-agnostic compression with explicit cache control and a tier-preserving ratio bound to exploit real-world LLM prompt caching architectures that deviate from ideal assumptions. CAPC achieves 49–90% cost savings over baselines on LongBench-v2 and validates on three production workloads, including the first public-benchmark confirmation of negative ROI from query-aware compression under realistic caching.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt compression literature assumes an ideal prompt cache (hit rate ρ=1.0), but real production APIs like Anthropic's Sonnet 4.6 exhibit two-tier caching with hit rates plateauing at ~0.83 for prefixes under ~3,500 tokens. Query-aware compression methods produce distinct prefixes per query, invalidating cache reuse, while naive caching yields suboptimal savings. The true cost crossover between these strategies under realistic ρ is unknown, motivating a new compression paradigm that accounts for real cache behavior.
AI.method: The authors (1) empirically characterize Sonnet 4.6's two-tier cache architecture, measuring hit rate decay and the 3,500-token threshold; (2) build a cost model predicting the crossover point where query-aware compression beats naive caching at high ratios (r≥6); (3) propose CAPC, which uses query-agnostic compression (one prefix for all queries), explicit `cache_control` markers, and a tier-preserving ratio bound preventing over-compression that would push the prefix into the more expensive hot tier; (4) evaluate on LongBench-v2 and three production workloads (enterprise tool-using assistant, Graphify RAG, tau-bench).
AI.result: CAPC is cheapest in 16/16 LongBench-v2 configurations with mean savings of 49% over cache-only, 64% over query-aware compression, and 90% over vanilla, maintaining quality within 0.05 of uncompressed baseline.
