Production results: 51.7% cost reduction at r=3 on the 94k-token enterprise assistant; 9.3× and 2.4× savings over cache-all on FastAPI and httpx Graphify pipelines; and on tau-bench (50 tasks), CAPC ties vanilla at 36/50 reward while being cheapest, whereas query-aware compression costs +40.1% over vanilla — the first public-benchmark confirmation of negative ROI from query-aware compression.
AI.conclusion: Real-world LLM prompt caching deviates significantly from the ρ=1.0 ideal assumed in prior compression work, creating a cost crossover that CAPC exploits through query-agnostic compression with tier-aware constraints. The negative-ROI result for query-aware compression on tau-bench demonstrates that the standard compression paradigm is economically counterproductive in production settings, validating the need for cache-aware prompt compression strategies.

title: DoSQ: A Cross-Layer Denial of Service Quality Attack by Exploiting Side Channels in 5G NR
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (CNS)
summary: The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)'s Fifth Generation New Radio (5G NR) is critical to supporting mission-critical services. However, 5G systems are vulnerable to smart jamming attacks that can propagate to applications running on top of these networks (i.e., cross-layer). The 5G gNB broadcasts resource scheduling information for the legitimate UEs over the air interface, with a prevailing assumption that this surface alone reveals nothing useful about a user device. However, we show that using the Downlink Control Information (DCI) is sufficient to degrade Application layer service quality, i.e., Denial of Service Quality (DoSQ), by inferring the Application layer Goodput (i.e., via side-channel analysis). Therefore, we present DoSQ, a protocol-aware attack that decodes per-slot DCI to inject interference onto the victim UE's Physical Resource Blocks (PRBs) within the same 1 ms slot, while a cross-layer classifier estimates the victim's Goodput state and trend from DCI features alone, without observing a single encrypted byte. Evaluated on a private 5G NR testbed against YouTube Live, DoSQ drives the target's Goodput down by up to 50% at sparse hit-rates, while a co-located non-target UE remains largely unaffected. Moreover, the classifier achieves a precision of 0.87 at the top 1% of attack-now confidence, a 4.21 times lift over the base rate. Furthermore, we propose an SSB frequency-time-hopping countermeasure that increases the attacker's resynchronization cost. The result is the first empirical measurement of a radio-to-application side channel that any protocol-aware adversary can exploit.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DoSQ, a cross-layer attack on 5G NR that infers Application-layer Goodput from unencrypted Downlink Control Information (DCI) via side-channel analysis, enabling targeted smart jamming that degrades a victim's video streaming quality by up to 50% while leaving co-located UEs largely unaffected.
AI.motivation: 5G NR is designed to support mission-critical services, yet prevailing assumptions hold that broadcast scheduling information (DCI) reveals nothing useful about individual user devices. The authors challenge this assumption by demonstrating that DCI alone — without decrypting any application data — leaks sufficient information to mount a cross-layer denial-of-service-quality attack, exposing a critical radio-to-application side channel.
AI.method: The authors design DoSQ, a protocol-aware attack with two components: (1) a per-slot DCI decoder that extracts scheduling information to inject targeted interference onto the victim's PRBs within the same 1 ms slot, and (2) a cross-layer classifier that estimates the victim's Application-layer Goodput state and trend solely from DCI features. The attack is evaluated on a private 5G NR testbed against YouTube Live streaming, with a co-located non-target UE as a control. A countermeasure using SSB frequency-time hopping is also proposed.
AI.result: DoSQ degrades the target UE's Application-layer Goodput by up to 50% using sparse hit-rates, while a co-located non-target UE remains largely unaffected. The cross-layer classifier achieves 0.87 precision at the top 1% attack-now confidence threshold, representing a 4.21× lift over the base rate. The proposed SSB frequency-time-hopping countermeasure increases the attacker's resynchronization cost.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first empirical measurement of a radio-to-application side channel in 5G NR, demonstrating that unencrypted DCI alone enables effective cross-layer DoSQ attacks. The findings challenge the security assumption that scheduling information is benign and highlight the need for countermeasures such as SSB frequency-time hopping.

title: BayesPO: Bayesian Prompt Optimization via Parallel-Tempered Gradient-Guided Discrete MCMC
summary: Prompt optimization adapts large language models (LLMs) without updating model parameters, but many automatic prompt optimizers remain heuristic search procedures over candidate instructions. This paper studies prompt optimization as Bayesian posterior sampling over discrete prompt tokens. We define a posterior distribution by combining a task likelihood term, which rewards prompts that explain input-output examples, with a language-model prior, which favors fluent instructions. This converts prompt optimization into an energy-based posterior sampling problem, for which gradients can be used to guide discrete Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) proposals over vocabulary tokens. We refer to our framework as BayesPO, short for Bayesian Prompt Optimization. In this paper, BayesPO is instantiated with Markov chain Monte Carlo: it uses a Metropolis-Hastings corrected Gibbs-with-Langevin (GwL) proposal and integrates parallel tempering for global exploration of rugged LLM-induced energy landscapes. The concrete sampler further adapts the GwL sampler to the practical constraints of non-weight-tied LLM embeddings. Experiments with Qwen2.5 models show that the sampler discovers semantically meaningful prompts on diagnostic tasks, that parallel tempering helps escape a local optimum in a poetry completion task, and that post-optimizing APE prompts on 24 instruction-induction subtasks improves average accuracy from 60.04% to 63.23%. The study also reveals two main limitations: energy minimization may overfit small optimization sets, and the current sampler remains computationally expensive. These findings position Bayesian prompt sampling as a principled post-optimization tool and point to a promising direction for probabilistic prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: BayesPO frames prompt optimization as Bayesian posterior sampling over discrete tokens, using MCMC with a Gibbs-with-Langevin proposal and parallel tempering to sample prompts that balance task performance with fluency. Experiments show improved accuracy over APE baselines but reveal overfitting and computational cost limitations.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic prompt optimizers rely on heuristic search over candidate instructions, lacking principled probabilistic foundations. The authors aim to formalize prompt optimization as Bayesian posterior sampling, providing a theoretically grounded framework that balances task likelihood with language-model fluency priors.
AI.method: The method defines a posterior distribution combining a task likelihood term (rewarding prompts that explain input-output examples) with an LLM prior (favoring fluent instructions). This yields an energy-based model over discrete tokens. Optimization uses discrete MCMC with a Metropolis-Hastings corrected Gibbs-with-Langevin (GwL) proposal, which leverages gradient information to guide proposals over vocabulary tokens. Parallel tempering is integrated for global exploration of rugged energy landscapes. A concrete sampler variant adapts GwL for non-weight-tied LLM embeddings.
AI.result: On diagnostic tasks, the sampler discovers semantically meaningful prompts. Parallel tempering successfully escapes a local optimum in a poetry completion task. Post-optimizing APE prompts on 24 instruction-induction subtasks improves average accuracy from 60.04% to 63.23%. Limitations include energy minimization overfitting small optimization sets and computationally expensive sampling.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian prompt sampling is positioned as a principled post-optimization tool. The work points toward probabilistic prompt optimization as a promising research direction, while acknowledging that scalability and overfitting remain open challenges.

title: Knowledge-Centric Agents for Workflow Generation
summary: Workflow generation in visual creation systems such as ComfyUI demands not only syntactic accuracy but also expert-level reasoning over modular compositions. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches often treat this as a direct text-to-JSON generation task, struggling with structural brittleness and lacking the experiential knowledge required for effective design. We argue that successful workflow generation requires modeling knowledge itself, including its structure, hierarchy, and reasoning dynamics. To this end, we propose a knowledge-centric framework that learns to invert, inject, and infer with knowledge across multiple abstraction levels. We first perform knowledge inversion to distill hierarchical representations, ranging from full pseudo-codes and skeletons to high-level strategies, from large collections of real-world workflows. We then conduct knowledge injection through supervised fine-tuning, teaching the model to reason from task descriptions to strategies and from strategies to executable structures. During inference, the model performs reversible reasoning to synthesize executable workflows, augmented by self-refinement for structural coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces workflows with richer node diversity, more coherent structures, and higher execution success rates than existing systems, establishing a new foundation for knowledge-driven, agentic workflow generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a knowledge-centric framework for ComfyUI workflow generation that performs knowledge inversion, injection, and inference across hierarchical abstraction levels, outperforming direct text-to-JSON LLM approaches in node diversity, structural coherence, and execution success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM approaches treat workflow generation as direct text-to-JSON generation, resulting in structural brittleness and a lack of the experiential, hierarchical reasoning knowledge required for effective modular visual composition design.
AI.method: A three-stage knowledge-centric framework: (1) Knowledge Inversion — distilling hierarchical representations (pseudo-codes, skeletons, high-level strategies) from real-world workflows; (2) Knowledge Injection — supervised fine-tuning that teaches the model to reason from task descriptions to strategies, then from strategies to executable structures; (3) Inference with reversible reasoning — synthesizing workflows augmented by self-refinement for structural coherence.
AI.result: The method achieves richer node diversity, more coherent structures, and higher execution success rates compared to existing systems.
AI.conclusion: The knowledge-driven approach establishes a new foundation for agentic workflow generation by explicitly modeling knowledge structure, hierarchy, and reasoning dynamics rather than relying on brittle end-to-end generation.

title: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
comment: This work addresses the first half of the model-harness coevolution loop
summary: Under model--harness co-evolution, harnesses are not merely inference-time scaffolds but data-generating components whose execution traces can shape future foundation models. This motivates harness-in-the-loop learning: optimizing harnesses for both immediate agent performance and the quality of traces used for future model training. However, continually updating provider-built scaffolds is costly and labor-intensive. We therefore investigate whether optimizing user-constructed harnesses in a task-specific manner can improve execution-trace quality while remaining computationally lightweight and requiring only a few update iterations. To this end, we introduce Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI), which represents the harness as a prompt-level specification of the agent loop and iteratively refines it using pairwise feedback over its own revision history. Across 30 synthetic machine-learning research tasks spanning quantitative finance, robotics, and pharmacy, a few RHI iterations suffice to substantially raise the performance ceiling of low-reasoning-effort agents, exceeding the corresponding maximum-reasoning-effort setting while reducing inference cost by up to 60%. We show that these gains arise primarily from improved task-specific context management through more effective inter-agent information flow rather than longer reasoning traces. Finally, we formalize this behavior as an information-theoretic hypothesis for RHI's implicit optimization objective, suggesting RHI as a practical algorithm for continual learning within the paradigm of model--harness co-evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI), a method that iteratively refines user-constructed, prompt-level agent harnesses using pairwise feedback to improve both agent performance and execution-trace quality. Tested on 30 synthetic ML research tasks, RHI enables low-reasoning-effort agents to outperform their maximum-reasoning-effort counterparts while cutting inference costs by up to 60%, with gains attributed to improved task-specific context management rather than longer reasoning traces.
AI.motivation: Under the model–harness co-evolution paradigm, harnesses generate execution traces that influence future foundation model training. Optimizing provider-built scaffolds is expensive and labor-intensive, motivating the need for lightweight, task-specific, user-constructed harness optimization that improves both immediate agent performance and trace quality for downstream training.
AI.method: RHI represents a harness as a prompt-level specification of the agent loop and iteratively refines it using pairwise feedback over its own revision history. The method requires only a few update iterations and operates in a computationally lightweight manner. Evaluation spans 30 synthetic ML research tasks across quantitative finance, robotics, and pharmacy.
AI.result: A few RHI iterations substantially raise the performance ceiling of low-reasoning-effort agents, exceeding the maximum-reasoning-effort setting while reducing inference cost by up to 60%. Gains stem primarily from improved task-specific context management through more effective inter-agent information flow, not longer reasoning traces.
AI.conclusion: The authors formalize RHI's behavior as an information-theoretic hypothesis for its implicit optimization objective, positioning RHI as a practical algorithm for continual learning under model–harness co-evolution.

title: Evaluating Open-Weight LLMs for Generating Structured Threat Information for Autonomous Vehicle Vulnerabilities
summary: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) rely on interconnected software and hardware components, including sensors, Electronic Control Units, in-vehicle infotainment systems, and telematics units, where vulnerabilities can compromise assets, users, and vehicle operations. These vulnerabilities are commonly documented as plain text in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database; however, security practitioners require structured information about affected assets, types of weaknesses, and attack behaviors to effectively mitigate the risks from these vulnerabilities. To this end, we evaluate open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) for generating Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX), a well-known structured format for representing threat information, for CAV-related CVEs. We construct a dataset called CAV-STIXGen that maps CAV vulnerability descriptions to STIX domain objects (SDO), STIX relationship objects (SRO), Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE), and MITRE ATT&CK techniques mappings. Using this dataset, we evaluated 11 open-weight LLMs (4B to 120B parameters) across various prompting strategies and temperatures. Single-model configurations achieve F1 scores of 0.94 for SDO, 0.63 for SRO, and 0.99 for CWE mapping, while complete MITRE ATT&CK mapping remains challenging. In a multi-agent setup, Gemma-4-31B and Codestral-22B achieve F1 scores of 0.91 for SDOs and 0.43 for SROs, respectively. Lastly, we analyze CWE and MITRE ATT&CK co-occurrences to identify recurring threat patterns in the CAV domain, demonstrating how AI-assisted vulnerability-to-STIX translation can automate threat intelligence and prioritize defense in transportation security.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates open-weight LLMs for automatically converting CAV vulnerability descriptions from the CVE database into STIX structured threat intelligence format, using a new dataset called CAV-STIXGen. Single-model setups achieve F1 scores up to 0.94 for STIX domain objects and 0.99 for CWE mapping, while multi-agent configurations show promise but lower performance on relationship objects (0.43 F1).
AI.motivation: CAV vulnerabilities are documented as unstructured plain text in CVE databases, but security practitioners need structured threat information (affected assets, weakness types, attack behaviors) to effectively mitigate risks. Manual conversion is impractical at scale, motivating automated translation using LLMs.
AI.method: The authors constructed CAV-STIXGen, a dataset mapping CAV vulnerability descriptions to STIX domain objects (SDO), STIX relationship objects (SRO), CWE, and MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They evaluated 11 open-weight LLMs (ranging from 4B to 120B parameters) under various prompting strategies and temperature settings, in both single-model and multi-agent configurations.
AI.result: Single-model: F1 of 0.94 (SDO), 0.63 (SRO), 0.99 (CWE mapping). MITRE ATT&CK mapping remains challenging overall. Multi-agent: Gemma-4-31B achieved 0.91 F1 for SDOs; Codestral-22B achieved 0.43 F1 for SROs. CWE–ATT&CK co-occurrence analysis revealed recurring threat patterns specific to the CAV domain.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs can effectively automate vulnerability-to-STIX translation for CAV-related CVEs, particularly for domain objects and weakness classification. Relationship extraction and full ATT&CK mapping remain difficult. AI-assisted structured threat intelligence generation can help prioritize defenses in transportation security.

title: Candidate Attended Dialogue State Tracking Using BERT
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Presented at the DSTC8 workshop, AAAI-20 (poster session)
summary: Dialogue state tracking (DST) is one of the core components in task-oriented dialogue systems. At each turn in a conversation, DST estimates the user belief or dialogue state, which is used as input for downstream modules to predict system actions and generate responses. The increasingly popular dialogue system applications like Google Assistant, Siri and Alexa need to support a large number of services and APIs, resulting in growing attention to the scalability of such systems. Especially for some domains with little or no training data, the capability of transferring existing knowledge of other domains is highly desired. In this paper, we present a novel scalable framework for multi-domain dialogue state tracking. The proposed system leverages the pretrained BERT model to achieve zero-shot generalization, making it easy to quickly adapt to new domains without additional training. The performance of our model is evaluated on recently released schema-based dialogue (SGD) dataset, showing significant improvement compared to previous baseline.

AI.tldr: A scalable multi-domain dialogue state tracking framework using pretrained BERT that achieves zero-shot generalization to new domains without additional training, evaluated on the SGD dataset with significant improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Task-oriented dialogue systems (e.g., Google Assistant, Siri, Alexa) must support many services/APIs, requiring scalable DST. Many domains lack training data, so transferring knowledge from data-rich domains to low-resource or unseen domains is critical. Existing methods struggle with this scalability and cross-domain transfer.
AI.method: A scalable DST framework that leverages a pretrained BERT model for zero-shot generalization. The system encodes dialogue context and schema information jointly using BERT, enabling it to track dialogue states across multiple domains and generalize to new domains without any additional fine-tuning or training data.
AI.result: Evaluated on the Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD) dataset, the proposed model achieves significant performance improvement over previous baseline methods, particularly demonstrating effective zero-shot transfer to unseen domains.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained language models like BERT can be effectively harnessed for scalable, zero-shot multi-domain DST, enabling rapid adaptation to new domains without requiring annotated training data, thereby addressing a key bottleneck in industrial dialogue systems.

title: DSWorld: A Data Science World Model for Efficient Autonomous Agents
summary: Despite strong capabilities in data understanding and decision-making, autonomous data science agents still heavily rely on trial-and-error workflows that involve expensive computation. This bottleneck motivates models that can anticipate the effects of data science operations before real execution. In this paper, we introduce the concept of Data Science World Model, which model the data science execution environment by predicting environment state transitions conditioned on current workflow states and candidate operations. We further propose DSWorld, a practical framework that combines structured state construction, cost-aware routing, lightweight real execution, and an LLM-based simulator for expensive operations. To support training, we construct an 8K-scale transition trajectory dataset and introduce Reflective World Model Optimization, an error-aware reinforcement learning strategy for improving transition prediction. Experiments show that DSWorld accelerates RL-based agent training by approximately $14\times$ and search-based inference by approximately $3$-$6\times$ while maintaining competitive performance, and outperforms the strongest LLM baseline by 35.6% on transition prediction tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DSWorld.

AI.tldr: DSWorld introduces a Data Science World Model that predicts environment state transitions for data science operations, enabling faster agent training (14× acceleration) and inference (3-6× acceleration) by simulating expensive operations with an LLM-based simulator trained via error-aware reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Autonomous data science agents rely on costly trial-and-error workflows. The authors aim to reduce expensive computation by building a world model that can anticipate the effects of data science operations before real execution.
AI.method: Proposes DSWorld, combining (1) structured state construction for representing workflow states, (2) cost-aware routing between lightweight real execution and LLM-based simulation, and (3) Reflective World Model Optimization — an error-aware RL strategy for training the transition predictor on an 8K-scale transition trajectory dataset.
AI.result: DSWorld accelerates RL-based agent training by ~14× and search-based inference by 3-6× while maintaining competitive performance. It also outperforms the strongest LLM baseline by 35.6% on transition prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: A learnable world model for data science environments is both feasible and highly beneficial, enabling dramatic speedups in agent training and inference while preserving task performance.

title: Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks for Small Language Models
summary: Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) replace fixed node activations with learned one-dimensional edge functions, offering an explicit interface for interpretation and a possible alternative to transformer feed-forward networks. We test these claims separately. In a six-layer, 10M-parameter B-spline KAN, we reconstruct all 884,736 feed-forward edges: 87.8\% exceed (NLS>0.1) and 0.4\% are inactive. Pruning the lowest-activity 20--25\% causes negligible loss increase, although structured MLP neuron pruning tolerates comparable sparsity. The audit replicates on BabyLM, but grid-size sweeps show that near-total fPCA compression and high closed-form-fit coverage are properties of the low-capacity grid-2 basis, not universal KAN behavior. For replacement, we evaluate MLP, SwiGLU, grouped Chebyshev, and rational GR-KAN networks on BabyLM. The KAN-family and gated variants improve validation loss over the GELU MLP, but this ordering does not transfer to standardized benchmarks: across ten seeds and 59,875 BLiMP pairs, accuracies span 62.4--63.1\%, EWoK remains at chance, and a (+0.7)-point GR-KAN effect on BLiMP reverses on the supplement. Larger tests are also cautionary: parameter-matched MLPEdge underperforms the MLP on Wikitext-103, and 286M-parameter GR-KAN remains below a SwiGLU ClimbMix baseline after stabilization. Thus, small-basis KANs provide a practical, corpus-transferable interface for auditing learned scalar transformations, but the tested replacements show no consistent benchmark, quality, or latency advantage over strong MLP baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper tests KANs' claims of interpretability and as transformer FFN replacements. While small-basis KANs enable auditability of learned scalar transformations, they show no consistent advantage over strong MLP baselines in benchmarks, quality, or latency.
AI.motivation: KANs have been proposed as interpretable alternatives to MLPs in transformer feed-forward networks, with claims of explicit interpretability and competitive performance. The authors systematically test both claims through rigorous empirical evaluation.
AI.method: The authors audit a 10M-parameter B-spline KAN by reconstructing all 884,736 edges, measuring NLS (>0.1 threshold), and testing pruning robustness. They benchmark KAN-family variants (GR-KAN, grouped Chebyshev), gated variants (SwiGLU), and MLP baselines on BabyLM, BLiMP (59,875 pairs across 10 seeds), EWoK, and Wikitext-103 with parameter-matched controls including a 286M-parameter GR-KAN vs. SwiGLU ClimbMix baseline.
AI.result: In the B-spline KAN, 87.8% of edges exceed NLS>0.1 and 0.4% are inactive; pruning the lowest 20-25% activity edges causes negligible loss increase, comparable to structured MLP neuron pruning. Near-total fPCA compression and high closed-form fit coverage are properties specific to the low-capacity grid-2 basis, not universal KAN behavior. KAN-family and gated variants improve validation loss over GELU MLP on BabyLM, but this does not transfer: BLiMP accuracies span 62.4-63.1% across all models, EWoK remains at chance, and a +0.7-point GR-KAN effect on BLiMP reverses on the supplement. MLPEdge underperforms MLP on Wikitext-103, and 286M-parameter GR-KAN remains below SwiGLU ClimbMix after stabilization.
AI.conclusion: Small-basis KANs provide a practical, corpus-transferable interface for auditing learned scalar transformations. However, the tested KAN replacements show no consistent benchmark, quality, or latency advantage over strong MLP baselines, tempering enthusiasm for their adoption as transformer FFN substitutes.

title: Loop the Loopies!
summary: We present Loopie, the most powerful looped Transformer to date. The Loopie series consists of two Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: a 20B-parameter model with 2B active parameters and a 6Bparameter model with 0.6B active parameters. Looped Transformers have long faced a challenge: given an N-fold increase in pre-training compute, increasing the parameter count by a factor of N usually outperforms looping a model N times. Loopie addresses this challenge. Extensive ablation studies, including comparisons with a vanilla 30B-A3B model, show that Loopie substantially outperforms vanilla Transformer baselines trained with the same compute budget. Our novel post-training pipeline equips Loopie with strong reasoning abilities. At the 2025 IMO and IPhO, Loopie achieves gold-medal performance without tools.

AI.tldr: Loopie is a series of looped Mixture-of-Experts Transformers (20B/2B active and 6B/0.6B active) that overcomes the traditional limitation where scaling parameters beats iterative looping. With a novel post-training pipeline, Loopie achieves gold-medal performance at the 2025 IMO and IPhO without external tools.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers have historically underperformed compared to simply scaling parameter count under the same compute budget — an N-fold compute increase favors N× parameters over N× looping. The authors aim to close this gap and demonstrate that looped architectures can be competitive.
AI.method: The authors develop two MoE-based looped Transformer models (20B total/2B active and 6B total/0.6B active). They conduct extensive ablation studies comparing against a vanilla 30B-A3B baseline under matched compute budgets. A novel post-training pipeline is introduced to instill strong reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: Loopie substantially outperforms vanilla Transformer baselines trained with equivalent compute. At the 2025 International Mathematics Olympiad (IMO) and International Physics Olympiad (IPhO), Loopie achieves gold-medal-level performance without relying on external tools.
AI.conclusion: Looped Transformer architectures, when properly designed with MoE and a dedicated post-training pipeline, can overcome their historical compute-efficiency disadvantage and achieve state-of-the-art reasoning performance on elite competition benchmarks.

title: A Formally Grounded ODRL Evaluator: Implementation and Comparison
summary: The ODRL policy language is emerging as the de-facto standard for policy modelling data access and usage preferences, AI governance policies and data workflows in European dataspaces. The current standard has no mathematical formal semantics to describe how a system should implement policy evaluation. This has resulted in a variety of systems and tools that implement their own interpretation of the language, which limits interoperability and cannot guarantee consistent results. Based on an existing semantic model of ODRL, we formalise the problems of ODRL evaluation for the access control and monitoring scenarios, in both static and streaming settings, and we provide a novel, efficient algorithm and implementation. We present the first ODRL Evaluator with transparent formal semantics and supporting all rule types. We experimentally measure its performance, analysing different scalability dimensions related to policy complexity and size of the data on which a policy is evaluated. We compare our system with the state-of-the-art by providing a comparative review of existing ODRL evaluators, which highlights the differences in supported ODRL features and evaluation modes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first formally-specified ODRL evaluator with complete rule-type support, providing rigorous mathematical semantics for both static and streaming policy evaluation scenarios (access control and monitoring), along with an efficient implementation and comprehensive performance benchmarks comparing against existing ODRL tools.
AI.motivation: ODRL is becoming the de-facto standard for policy modelling in European dataspaces, AI governance, and data workflows, yet it lacks formal mathematical semantics for policy evaluation. This semantic gap has led to divergent, non-interoperable implementations with inconsistent evaluation results across systems.
AI.method: Building on a prior semantic model of ODRL, the authors formalize ODRL evaluation problems for both access control and monitoring scenarios in static and streaming settings. They design a novel, efficient evaluation algorithm and implement it in a system that provides transparent formal semantics supporting all ODRL rule types. Performance is experimentally measured across policy complexity and data-size scalability dimensions, complemented by a comparative review of existing ODRL evaluators.
AI.result: The paper delivers the first ODRL Evaluator with transparent formal semantics covering all rule types. Experimental results characterize its performance along scalability dimensions of policy complexity and data volume. A comparative review of state-of-the-art evaluators highlights significant differences in feature coverage and evaluation modes across existing tools.
AI.conclusion: A formally-grounded ODRL evaluator closes the semantic gap in the ODRL ecosystem, enabling interoperable, consistent policy evaluation. The work establishes a foundation for reliable ODRL-based governance in dataspaces and AI systems, with the comparative analysis serving as a benchmark for future ODRL tool development.

title: Publicly-Verifiable Certificates for Statistical Algorithms
summary:
Following Goldwasser, Rothblum, Shafer, and Yehudayoff, who defined a framework for interactive proofs of learning [ITCS'21], we initiate the study of non-interactive proofs of learning. We define and study a new notion: Publicly-Verifiable Certificates of Statistical Validity (pvCSVs), which allow for public, distributionally-robust certification that the result of a learning algorithm is valid. In a pvCSV, a learner publishes a hypothesis $h$ and corresponding certificate $π$; then, any user, who holds a user-specific distribution, can read the pair $(h,π)$ and determine efficiently whether the hypothesis is valid according to the user-specific distribution.
  We construct pvCSVs in the context of Adaptive Statistical Query (SQ) Algorithms. To certify SQ algorithms that makes $k$ adaptive queries, we construct pvCSVs where the sample complexity scales with $O(\log k)$, whereas the sample complexity of the best learning algorithms scale with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{k})$. More generally, we study proof systems for learning in the SQ model, demonstrating the model's strengths as well as its limitations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Publicly-Verifiable Certificates of Statistical Validity (pvCSVs), a non-interactive proof system for learning where a learner publishes a hypothesis with a certificate that any user can verify against their own distribution. The authors construct pvCSVs for Adaptive Statistical Query algorithms, achieving sample complexity of O(log k) for certification versus Õ(√k) for learning, and explore broader proof systems in the SQ model.
AI.motivation: Prior work by Goldwasser et al. established interactive proofs of learning, but interactive protocols are cumbersome in practice — they require back-and-forth communication between prover and verifier. The authors seek to eliminate interactivity, enabling a learner to publish a single certificate that any user can verify independently against their own distribution. This addresses a practical need for publicly verifiable, distributionally-robust certification of learning outcomes.
AI.method: The paper formally defines pvCSVs and then constructs them specifically for Adaptive Statistical Query (SQ) algorithms. The construction leverages the structure of SQ queries — which ask for expectations of bounded functions over the data distribution — to build certificates whose verification requires only O(log k) samples, exploiting the fact that SQ queries have inherent stability properties. The authors also conduct a broader investigation into the power and limitations of proof systems within the SQ framework.
AI.result: For adaptive SQ algorithms making k queries, the constructed pvCSVs require sample complexity scaling as O(log k), which is an exponential improvement over the Õ(√k) sample complexity required by the best learning algorithms in this model. The paper also delineates strengths and limitations of SQ-based proof systems more generally.
AI.conclusion: Non-interactive, publicly-verifiable certification of learning is feasible in the SQ model with significantly better sample complexity than interactive counterparts. The O(log k) vs. Õ(√k) separation demonstrates that verification can be substantially cheaper than learning in this setting, and the SQ model proves to be a fruitful framework for studying the foundations of certifiable learning.

title: Frontier AI performance across the business disciplines: a case-grounded benchmark of knowledge work and analytical reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are improving rapidly as reflected in benchmark scores, yet these AI benchmarks largely test capabilities such as factual recall, narrow question answering, mathematical problem-solving, and coding and agentic tool-use. What remains poorly measured is AI progress on the analytical knowledge work white-collar professionals perform daily, including synthesizing complex information, exercising judgment under uncertainty and incomplete information, applying strategic and adversarial thinking in multi-stakeholder settings, weighing trade-offs, and producing defensible, structured analyses. This gap is even more pronounced for subjective components of such work, where success can be challenging to define. The "case method" form of education practiced by top business schools provides a natural foundation for addressing this measurement gap, and we construct BusinessCaseBench, a benchmark spanning hundreds of questions drawn from business cases across eighteen disciplines, each paired with a grading rubric derived from the expert-written instructor case solution. On BusinessCaseBench, frontier AI models already score highly against instructor rubrics, and capability within one model family improves substantially over two years. These results provide strong evidence that AI performance on this class of work is already high and rapidly improving, with implications for business schools, where case pedagogy trains undergraduates and MBAs in this kind of analytical reasoning, and for entry-level professional roles, where such skills have historically anchored early-career work.

AI.tldr: BusinessCaseBench introduces a benchmark using business case method pedagogy to measure LLM capabilities on white-collar analytical reasoning—synthesis, judgment under uncertainty, strategic thinking, and trade-off analysis. Frontier models already score highly, with rapid improvement over two years, signaling AI's growing competence in knowledge work historically performed by entry-level professionals and MBA graduates.
AI.motivation: Existing AI benchmarks focus on factual recall, math, coding, and agentic tasks, but fail to capture the complex, subjective analytical reasoning that defines daily white-collar knowledge work—particularly synthesizing ambiguous information, exercising judgment, and producing structured, defensible analyses. The gap is especially acute for subjective tasks where success is hard to define. The case method from business education offers a principled framework to fill this measurement void.
AI.method: The authors construct BusinessCaseBench, a benchmark comprising hundreds of questions derived from business cases across eighteen disciplines. Each question is paired with a grading rubric based on the expert-written instructor case solution. Models are evaluated against these rubrics to assess performance on analytical knowledge work tasks mirroring professional practice.
AI.result: Frontier AI models already achieve high scores against instructor-developed rubrics on BusinessCaseBench. Within a single model family, capability on this class of analytical work improves substantially over a two-year period, demonstrating both current strength and rapid trajectory of progress.
AI.conclusion: AI performance on complex analytical knowledge work is already high and improving rapidly. This has direct implications for business schools, where case-based pedagogy trains analytical reasoning, and for entry-level professional roles where such skills have traditionally anchored early-career work.

title: Closing the AI Trust Gap: The Case for Independent Certification for Trustworthy AI
summary: Over the past decade, responsible AI (RAI) has produced a substantial body of practice for identifying and mitigating the risks AI poses in high-stakes settings. Yet this work has not produced a market that rewards trustworthiness. Firms that invest seriously in safety, fairness, and oversight cannot consistently prove to consumers, regulators, and shareholders that their systems go beyond the bare minimum of compliance. What is missing is a way for society to recognize or compare the difference. The result is a trust gap: a structural condition in which responsible development efforts happen inside organizations but produce no external, independently recognized and verifiable signal of trustworthy outcomes. We argue this gap is sustained in part because of a focus on responsible AI (a matter of internal process) as opposed to trustworthy AI (a matter of independently verifiable real-world outcomes), and that it persists because of three compounding failures: (1) the market cannot distinguish trustworthy systems from their imitations; (2) evaluation targets models and outputs rather than deployed sociotechnical systems and their outcomes; (3) the measurement ecosystem is oriented toward avoiding harm rather than demonstrating benefit. Reviewing existing AI governance instruments and comparing them to certification regimes in healthcare, sustainability, and security, we show that none integrate a governance baseline, independently verified positive-outcome evidence, and market signaling in a single framework. We propose independent, outcome-oriented certification as the connective layer that can close the trust gap, complementing regulation and internal governance by making trustworthiness measurable, comparable, and commercially rewarded.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a "trust gap" exists in AI markets where responsible internal development practices fail to produce externally verifiable signals of trustworthiness. It attributes this to three failures—market inability to distinguish trustworthy systems, evaluation focusing on models rather than sociotechnical outcomes, and measurement oriented toward harm avoidance rather than benefit demonstration. The authors propose independent, outcome-oriented certification as the solution to bridge this gap.
AI.motivation: Despite a decade of responsible AI (RAI) practices, there is no functioning market that rewards trustworthiness. Firms cannot credibly signal their investments in safety, fairness, and oversight to consumers, regulators, or shareholders. This "trust gap" represents a structural market failure where internal responsible development efforts generate no externally verifiable, independently recognized signal of trustworthy outcomes.
AI.method: The paper takes a diagnostic-analytic approach: it first defines and characterizes the trust gap as a structural condition, identifies three compounding failures sustaining it, then conducts a comparative review of existing AI governance instruments against certification regimes in healthcare, sustainability, and security domains. This cross-domain analysis reveals that no existing AI governance framework integrates all three necessary components: a governance baseline, independently verified positive-outcome evidence, and market signaling.
AI.result: The analysis finds that existing AI governance approaches are fragmented and incomplete. Current frameworks focus on responsible AI (internal process) rather than trustworthy AI (verifiable outcomes). Evaluation targets models/outputs rather than deployed sociotechnical systems. The measurement ecosystem emphasizes harm avoidance over benefit demonstration. No single framework combines governance baselines, independent outcome verification, and market signaling—a gap that certification regimes in healthcare, sustainability, and security successfully fill.
AI.conclusion: Independent, outcome-oriented certification can serve as the connective layer to close the trust gap, complementing both regulation and internal governance. By making trustworthiness measurable, comparable, and commercially rewarded, such certification would enable markets to distinguish genuinely trustworthy AI systems from their imitations and incentivize firms to invest seriously in safety and fairness.

title: From Feasibility to Desirability: Plan, Learn, Adapt (PLA) Framework for Personalized On-Device Itinerary Generation
summary: Generating personalized trip itineraries is a complex planning task and involves a tension between hard combinatorial feasibility and soft latent desirability. Classical optimization enforces constraints but fails to capture subjective traveler preferences. While learning-based approaches model preferences, they cannot guarantee feasibility. Mobile deployment imposes additional resource constraints on both. To address this, we propose Plan, Learn, Adapt (PLA), a three-stage framework for personalized on-device itinerary generation. The Plan stage builds a heterogeneous ensemble of lightweight planners that produces structurally diverse feasible candidates. From pairwise itinerary comparisons, Learn fits a compact Bradley-Terry reward model that captures emergent schedule properties such as pacing, geographic coherence, and day balance, which per-POI signals miss. Finally, Adapt applies feasibility-preserving local refinement within a device-aware compute budget; every intermediate state is feasible by construction. On 2,519 pairwise human comparisons across more than 100 U.S. cities, the reward-guided ensemble achieves a 67.8% win rate, 11.2 percentage points above the best single planner, with 100% feasibility. Three frontier LLMs, GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro, achieve 0% feasibility under the same constraints. The reward model generalizes across held-out cities, with a 67.6% mean leave-one-city-out accuracy. In production deployment within FlyEnJoy, PLA increased itinerary completion rates by 91%, with 109.9 ms average on-device latency.

AI.tldr: PLA is a three-stage framework (Plan, Learn, Adapt) for generating personalized trip itineraries on-device that guarantees 100% combinatorial feasibility while achieving a 67.8% win rate in human comparisons, outperforming both classical planners and frontier LLMs (which scored 0% feasibility).
AI.motivation: Generating personalized trip itineraries involves a fundamental tension between hard combinatorial feasibility constraints (e.g., opening hours, travel time) and soft latent desirability (subjective preferences like pacing and balance). Classical optimization enforces constraints but misses preferences; learned models capture preferences but fail feasibility. Mobile deployment compounds these challenges with limited compute. No existing approach simultaneously satisfies all three requirements.
AI.method: PLA: (1) Plan — a heterogeneous ensemble of lightweight planners generates structurally diverse, feasible candidate itineraries; (2) Learn — a compact Bradley-Terry reward model is fit from pairwise itinerary comparisons, capturing emergent schedule-level properties (pacing, geographic coherence, day balance) that per-POI signals cannot; (3) Adapt — feasibility-preserving local refinement within a device-aware compute budget, where every intermediate state remains feasible by construction.
AI.result: On 2,519 pairwise human comparisons across 100+ U.S. cities, the reward-guided ensemble achieved a 67.8% win rate (11.2 pp above the best single planner) with 100% feasibility. Frontier LLMs (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro) achieved 0% feasibility under identical constraints. The reward model generalized to held-out cities with 67.6% mean leave-one-city-out accuracy. In FlyEnJoy production deployment, itinerary completion rates increased by 91%, with 109.9 ms average on-device latency.
AI.conclusion: PLA demonstrates that a structured hybrid approach — combining an ensemble of constraint-aware planners with a learned pairwise preference model and budgeted local refinement — can simultaneously deliver hard feasibility guarantees and soft preference alignment on resource-constrained mobile devices, outperforming both single planners and LLMs in real-world deployment.

title: Frontier Language Models Struggle to Copy: Text Can Be Better Viewed in 2D
summary: While large language models (LLMs) can solve advanced reasoning problems in seconds, we show that even frontier models fail to perform a much simpler operation: exactly copying an input string that lies well within their context windows. We attribute this failure to positional encodings in Transformer architectures, whose inductive bias favors copying through a shortcut based on matching local contexts rather than carefully locating the corresponding input positions. To address this issue, we introduce 2D-RoPE, which organizes text into a 2D grid rather than a 1D sequence and assigns each token a row ID and a column ID. Under this view, copying becomes simply retrieving input tokens at a fixed column offset, which makes the task easy to learn. In synthetic copy experiments, shallow Transformers with 2D-RoPE achieve perfect copying at input lengths hundreds of times longer than those seen during training, whereas standard positional encodings fall far behind. We further show that the advantage of 2D-RoPE language models on copy tasks consistently holds in large-scale pretraining on DCLM with model sizes up to 1.4B parameters. Overall, our results suggest that viewing text in 2D can benefit language modeling, and we hope this encourages future work to further explore the potential of 2D positional encodings.

AI.tldr: LLMs surprisingly fail at exact string copying due to Transformer positional encodings favoring local-context shortcuts. The authors propose 2D-RoPE, which arranges text in a 2D grid with row/column IDs, making copying a simple fixed-column-offset retrieval task. This achieves perfect copying at lengths far exceeding training lengths and scales to 1.4B-parameter models.
AI.motivation: Despite advanced reasoning capabilities, even frontier LLMs struggle with exact string copying within their context windows. The authors attribute this to an inductive bias in standard Transformer positional encodings: models learn a "shortcut" based on matching local contexts rather than precisely locating the corresponding input positions, leading to copy failures.
AI.method: 2D-RoPE reorganizes text from a 1D sequence into a 2D grid, assigning each token a (row, column) coordinate. Copying then reduces to retrieving input tokens at a fixed column offset, which is structurally trivial. The authors test this on synthetic copy experiments with shallow Transformers and on large-scale DCLM pretraining up to 1.4B parameters.
AI.result: In synthetic experiments, shallow Transformers with 2D-RoPE achieve perfect copying at input lengths hundreds of times longer than training lengths, far surpassing standard positional encodings. This advantage persists in large-scale pretraining on DCLM with models up to 1.4B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Organizing text in 2D can benefit language modeling by structurally simplifying copy-like operations. The authors encourage future exploration of 2D positional encodings for broader language tasks.

title: SciForge: An AI-Native, Multimodal Workbench for Scientific Discovery
summary: Scientific work increasingly spans heterogeneous artifacts -- papers, code, datasets, scientific file formats, model outputs, figures, manuscripts, and team decisions -- yet general-purpose AI assistants rarely preserve these objects as a coherent, auditable research state. We present SciForge, a multimodal research-native AI workbench that reserves the graphical interface for human judgment while search, parsing, model routing, workflow execution, plotting, writing, and presentation generation run as modular agent-accessible services. SciForge is built around five pillars: (i) \emph{goal-scoped scientific decision governance} for \textbf{goal-oriented} research, with review gates and shared review surfaces; (ii) \emph{translate-then-reason} for \textbf{multimodal} input, routing scientific objects through domain translators before the agent reasons; (iii) \emph{evidence governance} for \textbf{auditable} traceability, linking claims to provenance chains and audit findings; (iv) \emph{collaborative team science} for \textbf{collaborative} research, enabling multi-role decision governance, with shared team workspaces planned for future releases; and (v) \emph{real-world application scenarios} for \textbf{practical} impact, demonstrated through eight end-to-end user cases, with flagship demonstrations including multi-day agentic research sprints for gene discovery, AI-guided de novo protein design, molecular optimization, and genome-to-BGC discovery. The system combines a thin interaction layer, contextual research capability patterns, an Agent Runtime and Workflow Engine, an Evidence-DAG audit sidecar and a Scientific Model Router. SciForge currently runs as a desktop application, with mobile supervision support; future releases will deepen team collaboration. The system is open-source and available at https://github.com/AGI4Sci/SciForge

AI.tldr: SciForge is an open-source, multimodal AI workbench for scientific research that integrates papers, code, datasets, and workflows into a coherent, auditable system. It combines agent-accessible modular services with a human-judgment-oriented GUI, built around goal-scoped governance, translate-then-reason multimodal routing, evidence provenance chains, collaborative team science, and demonstrated through eight real-world use cases including gene discovery and protein design.
AI.motivation: General-purpose AI assistants fail to preserve heterogeneous scientific artifacts (papers, code, datasets, figures, models, etc.) as a coherent, auditable research state. There is a need for a research-native AI system that maintains traceability and governance across the full lifecycle of scientific work while reserving the graphical interface for human judgment.
AI.method: SciForge is architected around five pillars: (1) goal-scoped scientific decision governance with review gates; (2) translate-then-reason for multimodal input, routing objects through domain translators before agent reasoning; (3) evidence governance linking claims to provenance chains via an Evidence-DAG audit sidecar; (4) collaborative team science with multi-role decision governance; (5) real-world validation through eight end-to-end use cases. The system integrates a thin interaction layer, contextual research capability patterns, an Agent Runtime and Workflow Engine, and a Scientific Model Router.
AI.result: SciForge was demonstrated through eight end-to-end user cases, with flagship demonstrations including multi-day agentic research sprints for gene discovery, AI-guided de novo protein design, molecular optimization, and genome-to-BGC discovery. The system currently runs as a desktop application with mobile supervision support.
AI.conclusion: SciForge provides a practical, open-source workbench that bridges the gap between general-purpose AI and scientific research needs by preserving auditable research state, enforcing evidence governance, and supporting multimodal scientific workflows. Future releases will deepen team collaboration capabilities.

title: Hard Rules, Soft Preferences: Bridging Reasoning, Learning, and Optimization for Personalized Packing Checklist Generation
summary: Packing for air travel is recurring and error-prone: the checklist must be personal and context-aware, yet feasible under safety rules, item dependencies, and luggage limits. Existing packing assistants are template-driven and generic, or recommendation-driven but unconstrained, leaving users to manually patch regulatory and capacity violations. We propose a reasoning-guided learning framework with three stages: (1) a symbolic engine that generates a regulation-aware seed checklist with explicit dependency structure, (2) a two-stage preference learner that estimates inclusion and priority utilities from user add and remove actions while mitigating survivorship bias, and (3) a CP-SAT optimizer that selects a compact, compliant subset. The architecture instantiates a general pattern for constrained personalization, applicable wherever hard feasibility coexists with sparse preference signals. On 604 labeled trip scenarios, comprising 29K inclusion labels and 343K pairwise comparisons, the symbolic engine attains 99.7% recall and 0.96 rubric validity, compared with 0.78 to 0.81 for frontier LLMs. Gradient-boosted trees and LambdaMART reach an AUC-ROC of 0.943 and an NDCG@5 of 0.923. CP-SAT attains 100% constraint satisfaction, compared with 28% for greedy selection and 10% for random selection. Deployment in FlyEnJoy, a production iOS travel app, doubled checklist completions and reduced editing and completion time.

AI.tldr: A three-stage reasoning-guided learning framework for personalized air travel packing that combines symbolic regulation encoding, preference learning from user edits, and CP-SAT optimization, achieving near-perfect constraint satisfaction and doubling checklist completions in production.
AI.motivation: Existing packing assistants are either rigid template-based tools that lack personalization or unconstrained recommender systems that ignore hard regulatory and capacity constraints. Users must manually resolve safety violations and luggage limits, making the process error-prone and inefficient.
AI.method: A three-stage framework: (1) a symbolic engine generates regulation-aware seed checklists with explicit dependency structures; (2) a two-stage preference learner (gradient-boosted trees + LambdaMART) estimates inclusion and priority utilities from user add/remove actions while correcting for survivorship bias; (3) a CP-SAT optimizer selects a compact, compliant item subset.
AI.result: On 604 labeled trip scenarios (29K inclusion labels, 343K pairwise comparisons), the symbolic engine achieved 99.7% recall and 0.96 rubric validity (vs. 0.78–0.81 for frontier LLMs). Preference models reached AUC-ROC of 0.943 and NDCG@5 of 0.923. CP-SAT achieved 100% constraint satisfaction vs. 28% (greedy) and 10% (random). Deployed in FlyEnJoy iOS app, checklist completions doubled and editing/completion time decreased.
AI.conclusion: The architecture instantiates a general pattern for constrained personalization — combining symbolic reasoning for hard feasibility with learned preferences from sparse signals — applicable wherever regulatory or physical constraints coexist with personalized recommendations.

title: Controlling Implicit Shortcut Reliance in L2 Spoken English Auto-markers
summary: Increasingly, speech and language processing tasks take either audio or text directly rather than extracting features from these as the input to the classifier or regressor. Often these systems make use of complex, for example transformer-based, processes that have the ability to derive highly non-linear mappings between the input and the output. Unfortunately these systems can also learn ''shortcuts'' where the classifier is overly reliant on particular aspects of the input to yield the output. For the task of language proficiency assessment, this over-reliance can enable learners to increase their score by exploiting the shortcut rather than improving their ability. This paper introduces a novel training criterion that is able to reduce the classifier's reliance on shortcuts, thus for example limiting this option for malpractice in language assessment. This process is illustrated on two forms of assessment system, one based on the audio the other on the speech recognition text. The results show that, for both systems, there is higher correlations with features that could be exploited for malpractice than expected from the human reference, indicating an over-reliance on these features. By introducing the modified training criterion, this correlation can be reduced to be closer to the reference correlation.

AI.tldr: A novel training criterion is proposed to reduce classifier reliance on "shortcuts" in automated language proficiency assessment systems, preventing learners from exploiting spurious correlations (e.g., in audio or ASR text input) to inflate scores. The method brings feature correlations closer to human reference levels in both audio-based and text-based assessment systems.
AI.motivation: Modern speech/language processing systems using complex architectures (e.g., transformers) can learn "shortcuts" — spurious correlations between specific input features and output scores — rather than genuinely assessing language proficiency. This creates a vulnerability where test-takers can game the system (malpractice) by exploiting these shortcuts instead of improving actual language ability.
AI.method: The authors introduce a modified training criterion designed to explicitly penalize the classifier's reliance on identified shortcut features. The method is demonstrated on two assessment system types: an audio-based system and one operating on automatic speech recognition (ASR) text. The training criterion reduces the correlation between model predictions and shortcut-exploitable features.
AI.result: Both audio-based and text-based assessment systems exhibited higher correlations with shortcut-exploitable features than what is observed in human reference scores, confirming over-reliance. The proposed training criterion successfully reduced these correlations, bringing them closer to human reference levels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training criterion effectively mitigates shortcut learning in automated language proficiency assessment, reducing the potential for score manipulation and making the systems more robust and aligned with genuine proficiency measurement.

title: Harmonizing AI Safety Thresholds
summary: Frontier AI companies have published capability thresholds that differ substantially, making it difficult for third parties to verify whether a threshold has been crossed or to compare requirements across companies. Moreover, without common minimum thresholds, risk mitigation may be inconsistent, creating a potential race to the bottom in safety standards. We develop a methodology for deriving harmonized thresholds across three risk domains. For misuse risks (cyber and biological), we take expected harm as the key primitive and use an explicit risk-modeling approach that accounts for risk channels and model release conditions. For automated AI R&D, we base our proposed threshold on the observed rate of AI progress rather than expected harm. Our analysis expands upon prior work and highlights existing empirical gaps and limitations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a methodology for harmonizing AI capability thresholds across companies by deriving common benchmarks in three risk domains: misuse (cyber/biological) using expected-harm modeling, and automated AI R&D using observed AI progress rates, aiming to prevent a race to the bottom in safety standards.
AI.motivation: Frontier AI companies publish divergent capability thresholds, making third-party verification and cross-company comparison difficult. Without common minimum thresholds, inconsistent risk mitigation may trigger a race to the bottom in safety standards.
AI.method: For misuse risks (cyber and biological), the authors use expected harm as the core primitive with an explicit risk-modeling approach that incorporates risk channels and model release conditions. For automated AI R&D risk, thresholds are derived from the observed rate of AI progress rather than expected harm. The methodology aims to harmonize thresholds across all three domains.
AI.result: The analysis expands upon prior work on capability thresholds and identifies key empirical gaps and limitations in current threshold-setting practices, providing a structured framework for deriving harmonized, cross-company benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Harmonized, risk-domain-specific thresholds are feasible and necessary to enable third-party verification, facilitate cross-company comparison, and prevent inconsistent risk mitigation that could undermine safety standards industry-wide.

title: Information-Directed Sampling for Causal Bandits
summary: Causal bandits exploit structural relationships among variables to share information across interventions and accelerate the identification of high-reward decisions. In many applications, however, some variables cannot be directly manipulated, even though they influence the reward and provide useful information about the underlying causal system. We study contextual causal bandits with non-manipulable variables, where context variables are observed before action selection and additional variables are observed after each intervention. Assuming a known causal graph without latent confounding, we adopt a Bayesian formulation in which the conditional probability tables of the observational distribution constitute the unknown parameter. This representation allows observations collected under one intervention to update reward estimates for other interventions through their shared causal mechanisms. We develop causal variants of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling (IDS) for this setting. For Thompson Sampling, we establish an entropy-dependent sublinear Bayesian regret bound. For IDS, we derive an entropy-dependent regret bound that explicitly quantifies the additional error introduced by Monte Carlo approximation of the expected regret and information gain; when these quantities are available exactly, the bound recovers the standard sublinear IDS rate. We further provide high-probability confidence bounds for the Monte Carlo estimates used by the algorithm. Experiments on several synthetic causal bandit tasks show that the proposed methods outperform causal and non-causal baselines by more effectively exploiting information shared across interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper extends causal bandits to settings with non-manipulable variables (contexts observed pre-action and post-action variables), proposing Bayesian Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling variants that exploit the known causal graph to share information across interventions, with theoretical regret bounds and empirical validation.
AI.motivation: In many real-world applications, certain variables that influence rewards cannot be directly manipulated, yet they carry valuable information about the underlying causal system. Existing causal bandit frameworks typically assume all relevant variables are intervenable, limiting their applicability. The authors aim to bridge this gap by studying contextual causal bandits where some variables are non-manipulable but still informative for cross-intervention inference.
AI.method: The authors adopt a Bayesian formulation where the unknown parameter consists of the conditional probability tables (CPTs) of the observational distribution, assuming a known causal graph without latent confounding. Two algorithm variants are developed: (1) Causal Thompson Sampling, which samples CPTs from the posterior and selects interventions that maximize expected reward; (2) Causal Information-Directed Sampling (IDS), which balances expected regret and information gain using Monte Carlo approximation. Regret bounds are derived for both: an entropy-dependent sublinear Bayesian regret bound for Thompson Sampling, and an entropy-dependent bound for IDS that accounts for Monte Carlo approximation error.
AI.result: For Thompson Sampling, the authors prove an entropy-dependent sublinear Bayesian regret bound. For IDS, they derive a regret bound that explicitly quantifies the error introduced by Monte Carlo approximation of expected regret and information gain; when exact computation is available, the bound recovers the standard sublinear IDS rate. High-probability confidence bounds for the Monte Carlo estimates are also provided. Experiments on synthetic causal bandit tasks demonstrate that both proposed methods outperform causal and non-causal baselines by more effectively leveraging shared information across interventions.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating non-manipulable variables into the causal bandit framework—via a Bayesian CPT-based representation and adapted Thompson Sampling and IDS algorithms—enables more efficient information sharing across interventions, yielding improved empirical performance and theoretically grounded sublinear regret guarantees.

title: Rate-Utility Frontiers for Language Encodings: Comparing Tokens, Bytes, and Pixels Under Controlled Linguistic Content
summary: Language models encode text as subword tokens, raw bytes, or rendered pixels, but these encodings are usually compared under modeling constraints that expose different amounts of linguistic content to models across different languages. We instead ask what each encoding preserves when both the content and the downstream capacity are controlled. Using verified parallel sentences across thirteen languages and five scripts, we compare tokens, bytes, and pixels through a shared bottleneck whose width is swept to trace rate-utility frontiers. This separates three quantities that are often conflated: the number of input positions an encoding creates, the latent capacity available after encoding, and the task-relevant information that survives compression. We evaluate three utilities: surface form preservation, cross-lingual sentence alignment, and topic classification. No encoding dominates across tasks or capacity regimes. Pixels preserve surface form best, bytes preserve cross-lingual alignment best, especially in same-script multilingual settings, and tokens support topic prediction best. These performances are not explained by sequence length alone. Short inputs can discard useful meaning, while long inputs can preserve information that compresses well. Choosing an encoding is therefore not a fixed preference for tokens, bytes, or pixels, but a rate-utility tradeoff that depends on the task, language mix, capacity regime, and compute budget.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares token, byte, and pixel encodings for language models across 13 languages and 5 scripts using a controlled bottleneck framework. It reveals that no single encoding dominates — performance depends on the task, capacity regime, and language mix — and that sequence length alone does not explain encoding performance.
AI.motivation: Prior comparisons of tokenization, byte-level, and pixel-based encodings confound encoding choice with model capacity and linguistic content exposure. The authors aim to isolate what each encoding inherently preserves when content and downstream capacity are strictly controlled, disentangling input positions, latent capacity, and task-relevant information.
AI.method: The authors use verified parallel sentences across 13 languages and 5 scripts. They pass tokens, bytes, and pixels through a shared information bottleneck whose width is systematically swept to trace rate-utility frontiers. Three downstream utilities are evaluated: surface form preservation (character-level reconstruction), cross-lingual sentence alignment, and topic classification.
AI.result: No encoding is universally best. Pixels excel at surface form preservation. Bytes excel at cross-lingual alignment, particularly in same-script multilingual settings. Tokens excel at topic prediction. Crucially, sequence length does not explain these differences: short inputs may discard useful meaning, while long inputs can preserve compressible information.
AI.conclusion: Encoding choice should be viewed as a rate-utility tradeoff rather than a fixed preference. Optimal selection depends on the task, language mix, capacity regime, and compute budget, with each encoding offering distinct advantages in different operating regions.

title: CRAFT: Clustering Rubrics to Diagnose Weak LLM Capabilities and Generate Targeted Fine-Tuning Data
summary: Evaluations should do more than measure a models current performance. They should tell us what to fix for the next model iteration and provide a way to generate targeted post training data. Most evaluation pipelines identify weak examples, topics, or categories, but they leave the underlying capability failure implicit: they say where a model fails, not why. We introduce CRAFT, a method that converts any rubric based evaluation dataset into a model specific diagnosis of weak capabilities. CRAFT treats each grading criterion as a capability probe: it extracts a capability description from every prompt rubric pair, clusters these descriptions into a hierarchical capability tree, scores the target model at every node, and selects low performing nodes dynamically across tree levels, at the granularity where each failure is clearest. The selected weak capabilities then direct the generation of targeted supervised finetuning data. Holding the data generation, finetuning, and evaluation setup fixed, we compare CRAFT against prompt level EvalTree clustering and untargeted random generation on four open source models, two professional domains (finance and legal), and 13 held out benchmarks disjoint from the diagnostic data. CRAFT achieves the strongest finance domain average for all four models under repeated temperature decoding; on legal domain, it is strongest for three of four models and remains within the decoding variance bands of the best baseline on the fourth. Diagnosing weaknesses at the level of rubric criteria, rather than prompts or categories, thus yields both a sharper picture of what a model cannot do and measurably better models after finetuning on that diagnosis.

AI.tldr: CRAFT converts rubric-based evaluation datasets into model-specific diagnoses of weak capabilities by extracting capability descriptions from prompt-rubric pairs, clustering them into a hierarchical tree, and using low-performing nodes to generate targeted SFT data. It outperforms prompt-level clustering and random generation baselines on finance and legal domain benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation pipelines identify *where* a model fails (specific examples, topics, or categories) but not *why* — the underlying capability failure remains implicit. There is a need for evaluation methods that directly inform model improvement by diagnosing specific weak capabilities and generating targeted post-training data.
AI.method: CRAFT operates in four stages: (1) treats each rubric criterion as a capability probe, extracting a capability description from every prompt-rubric pair; (2) clusters these descriptions into a hierarchical capability tree; (3) scores the target model at every node and selects low-performing nodes dynamically across tree levels at the granularity where failure is clearest; (4) uses selected weak capabilities to direct generation of targeted supervised finetuning (SFT) data.
AI.result: On four open-source models across 13 held-out benchmarks in finance and legal domains, CRAFT achieves the strongest finance domain average for all four models under repeated temperature decoding. In the legal domain, it is strongest for three of four models and remains within decoding variance bands of the best baseline on the fourth.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing weaknesses at the level of rubric criteria — rather than prompts or categories — yields both a sharper picture of model capabilities and measurably better models after targeted finetuning based on that diagnosis.

title: Rethinking Transfer in Continual Learning: A Replay-Based Realisation
summary: Continual learning studies how deployed language models can continually acquire new tasks without expensive retraining from scratch. Existing methods, whether rehearsal-based (replaying stored past data) or rehearsal-free (regularising or isolating parameters), overwhelmingly target one objective: preventing catastrophic forgetting. Forward transfer, the past helping the future, has meanwhile been pursued almost exclusively through parameter reuse, with no explicit account of when transfer should be expected at all. We begin one step earlier: before designing a transfer mechanism, we ask when transfer should exist at all. We answer with a framework of three measurable conditions: the target task must leave room for improvement beyond its own limited supervision, transferable information must survive continued optimisation, and replay must come from compatible previous tasks. We instantiate this view as Transfer-Selective Replay (TSR), which selects replay data predicted to benefit the incoming task rather than replaying past examples indiscriminately. Selection is guided by a zero-training task signature, while distillation preserves stability on previous tasks. Under the standard continual learning protocol in the low-budget regime, TSR consistently improves forward transfer while maintaining stability, outperforming existing replay baselines across heterogeneous and homogeneous task streams. More broadly, the results argue for treating transfer as a first-class objective of continual learning, to be understood before it is engineered.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework that asks *when* forward transfer should exist in continual learning before engineering it, defining three measurable conditions, and instantiates this as Transfer-Selective Replay (TSR), which selectively replays past data predicted to benefit the incoming task, outperforming existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods overwhelmingly focus on preventing catastrophic forgetting, while forward transfer (past knowledge helping future learning) is pursued almost exclusively through parameter reuse without explicitly accounting for *when* transfer should be expected. The authors argue transfer should be treated as a first-class objective, understood before being engineered.
AI.method: The authors establish a framework of three measurable conditions for when transfer should exist: (1) the target task must have room for improvement beyond limited supervision, (2) transferable information must survive continued optimization, and (3) replay must come from compatible previous tasks. They instantiate this as Transfer-Selective Replay (TSR), which uses a zero-training task signature to select replay data predicted to benefit the incoming task, combined with distillation for stability on previous tasks.
AI.result: Under the standard continual learning protocol in the low-budget regime, TSR consistently improves forward transfer while maintaining stability, outperforming existing replay baselines across both heterogeneous and homogeneous task streams.
AI.conclusion: Forward transfer should be treated as a first-class objective in continual learning, pursued through principled conditions rather than ad-hoc mechanisms. TSR demonstrates that selective replay guided by compatibility can simultaneously improve transfer and maintain stability.

title: ToolSciVer: Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification with Visual Tool Augmented Reinforcement Learning
