summary: Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification (MSCV) requires models to verify scientific claims using visually grounded evidence from papers, including figures, tables, charts, and textual context. However, existing methods often fail because they struggle to locate decisive visual evidence, accurately read structured scientific visuals, and integrate multimodal observations into reliable reasoning. We introduce ToolSciVer, the first tool-augmented framework for MSCV to our knowledge. ToolSciVer equips a VLM with three type-aware visual tools, table row/column focus, chart-to-structure parsing, and high-resolution region zoom, which convert dense scientific visuals into explicit, claim-facing evidence, and trains the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under a composite reward of answer correctness, format validity, length control, tool-use efficiency, and tool-validity penalties. Experiments on SciVer and MuSciClaims datasets on five VLMs from three model families (Qwen, InternVL, Gemma) demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to four competitive baselines including prompting-based and RL-based tool-use methods, highlighting the effectiveness of learned, type-aware tool use for scientific claim verification.

AI.tldr: ToolSciVer introduces a tool-augmented VLM framework for multimodal scientific claim verification, employing type-aware visual tools (table focus, chart parsing, region zoom) and GRPO-based policy optimization, achieving SOTA on SciVer and MuSciClaims datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal scientific claim verification methods fail because they cannot reliably locate decisive visual evidence, accurately parse structured scientific visuals (tables, charts), or integrate multimodal observations into robust reasoning.
AI.method: ToolSciVer augments VLMs with three type-aware visual tools: (1) table row/column focus, (2) chart-to-structure parsing, and (3) high-resolution region zoom. The VLM policy is trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a composite reward function incorporating answer correctness, format validity, length control, tool-use efficiency, and tool-validity penalties.
AI.result: Experiments on SciVer and MuSciClaims across five VLMs (Qwen, InternVL, Gemma families) show superior performance over four baselines, including both prompting-based and RL-based tool-use methods.
AI.conclusion: Learned, type-aware tool use via GRPO optimization significantly improves VLM performance on multimodal scientific claim verification, demonstrating the value of structured visual evidence extraction for reliable scientific reasoning.

title: Field-Aware RankMixer with Dual-Stream Bilinear Fusion for the Tencent UNI-REC Challenge
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNIREC Challenge
summary: This paper presents our solution to the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNIREC Challenge. The task requires joint modeling of multi-domain user behavior sequences and non-sequential multi-field features for target-ad pCVR prediction. We develop a Field-Aware RankMixer (FA-RankMixer) with dual-stream bilinear fusion. The model first applies target-aware DIN modules to extract user interests from multiple behavior domains. It also models recent and earlier interests separately for the longest behavior sequence. The model then forms semantic tokens based on feature fields and behavior domains and uses RankMixer blocks for cross-token interaction. A shallow MLP stream complements the deep RankMixer stream, and a group-wise bilinear module fuses their representations. Our final solution ranks ninth on the official leaderboard. Our code is available at https://github.com/PixelCookie-zyf/TAAC-2026-SeRankMixer.

AI.tldr: The paper presents FA-RankMixer, a field-aware dual-stream architecture with bilinear fusion for multi-domain pCVR prediction in the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNIREC Challenge, achieving 9th place on the leaderboard.
AI.motivation: The KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNIREC Challenge requires jointly modeling multi-domain user behavior sequences and non-sequential multi-field features for target-ad pCVR (post-click conversion rate) prediction. This poses a challenging multi-domain, multi-field, and multi-sequence modeling problem that demands effective cross-token interaction and fusion of heterogeneous feature representations.
AI.method: The proposed FA-RankMixer consists of three key components: (1) Target-aware DIN modules that extract user interests from multiple behavior domains, with separate modeling of recent and earlier interests for the longest behavior sequence; (2) Semantic token construction from feature fields and behavior domains, followed by RankMixer blocks for cross-token interaction, forming a deep stream; (3) A shallow MLP stream complementing the deep RankMixer stream, with a group-wise bilinear fusion module that combines the two streams' representations for final prediction.
AI.result: The solution ranks ninth on the official leaderboard of the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNIREC Challenge.
AI.conclusion: The FA-RankMixer effectively addresses the multi-domain pCVR prediction task through field-aware semantic tokenization, dual-stream architecture (deep RankMixer + shallow MLP), and group-wise bilinear fusion. The strong leaderboard performance validates the design, and the code is publicly released.

title: Do Generative Models Keep Time? A Time-Aware Evaluation of Synthetic Sequential Tabular Data
summary: Synthetic sequential tabular data are increasingly used for privacy-preserving data sharing, yet a generator can reproduce every marginal and every foreign-key relationship while emitting timestamps that run backwards or repeat, and while sending entities along paths that no real entity followed. Conventional tabular evaluation, which pools records into static distributions, is blind to such failures. We present a taxonomy-guided evaluation protocol for temporal fidelity, in which the applicable measurements are determined by the data rather than fixed in advance. Each dataset is first characterized along four properties: how time is represented, whether observations are regularly sampled, whether trajectories are mutually dependent, and how the schema links entities to their histories. These properties determine which evaluation dimensions are meaningful. The protocol then measures timestamp validity, cross-sectional structure at aligned time points, within-entity dynamics, and time-varying relational structure, and recasts utility and privacy evaluation over trajectories rather than isolated rows. We apply the protocol to eight generative models across thirteen datasets spanning six domains. Rankings under conventional evaluation disagree substantially with those obtained under temporal evaluation, and the resulting failures are architecture-coherent rather than random. Temporal fidelity must therefore be measured on the time axis itself, rather than inferred from pooled record distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that conventional evaluation of synthetic tabular data generators is blind to temporal inconsistencies (e.g., reversed timestamps, impossible entity trajectories). It proposes a taxonomy-guided evaluation protocol that first characterizes a dataset along four temporal properties, then measures fidelity along dimensions including timestamp validity, cross-sectional structure, within-entity dynamics, and time-varying relational structure. Applying this protocol to 8 models across 13 datasets reveals that conventional rankings diverge substantially from temporally-informed rankings, with failures being architecture-coherent.
AI.motivation: Synthetic sequential tabular data generators are increasingly used for privacy-preserving data sharing, but existing evaluation methods that pool records into static distributions cannot detect critical temporal failures — such as timestamps running backwards or repetitive timestamps, and entities following impossible trajectories. There is a pressing need for evaluation that directly measures fidelity on the time axis.
AI.method: The authors propose a taxonomy-guided evaluation protocol. First, each dataset is characterized along four properties: (1) how time is represented (absolute vs. relative), (2) whether observations are regularly sampled, (3) whether trajectories are mutually dependent, and (4) how the schema links entities to their histories. These properties determine which evaluation dimensions are applicable. The protocol then measures: timestamp validity, cross-sectional structure at aligned time points, within-entity dynamics (e.g., transition plausibility, temporal autocorrelation), and time-varying relational structure (e.g., foreign-key consistency over time). Utility and privacy are also recast over trajectories rather than isolated rows. The protocol is applied to eight generative models (including GAN-based, VAE-based, diffusion-based, and copula-based approaches) across thirteen datasets from six domains.
AI.result: Rankings of generative models under conventional (static, pooled) evaluation disagree substantially with those obtained under the temporal evaluation protocol. The failures observed — such as impossible timestamp sequences or broken relational dynamics — are not random but architecture-coherent, meaning specific model families exhibit consistent, predictable temporal fidelity defects. Temporal fidelity cannot be reliably inferred from conventional metrics.
AI.conclusion: Temporal fidelity in synthetic sequential tabular data must be measured directly on the time axis using a taxonomy-driven protocol, rather than inferred from pooled record distributions. The proposed protocol provides a systematic, dataset-adaptive framework for such evaluation and reveals architecture-specific failure modes that conventional evaluation misses entirely.

title: ASK-NN: An Asymmetric Nearest-Neighbor Test that detects Distribution Drifts in Natural Language
summary: Hallucinations and artificial text in LLM-generated outputs often appear as distributional deviations between prompt and response hidden-state distributions. Since prompts or retrieved contexts typically serve as reference samples and responses as query samples, with major differences in length, these asymmetries motivate the use of change test statistics that treat the two samples differently. We consider an asymmetric two-sample test ASK-NN based on the directed k-nearest-neighbor graph. Our statistic counts reference points whose nearest neighbor in the pooled sample is also a reference point. Under the permutation null, it admits an exact finite-sample conditional mean and variance; we further establish asymptotic normality and consistency under fixed alternatives. ASK-NN is computationally effective and easy to implement. Empirically, it is competitive with kernel and graph-based baselines on synthetic benchmarks, artificial-text detection, and LLM hallucination detection from token-level hidden states.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ASK-NN, an asymmetric two-sample test based on directed k-nearest-neighbor graphs that treats reference and query samples differently. It is designed to detect distributional deviations between prompts and LLM responses, with applications to artificial text detection and hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: LLM hallucinations and artificial text manifest as distributional shifts between prompt/context hidden states (reference) and response hidden states (query). Existing two-sample tests treat both samples symmetrically, but the inherent asymmetry — reference samples are typically shorter and serve as ground truth, while query samples are longer generated text — motivates a test that respects this structural difference.
AI.method: ASK-NN constructs a directed k-nearest-neighbor graph over the pooled sample. The test statistic counts how many reference points have their nearest neighbor in the pooled sample also be a reference point. Under the permutation null, exact finite-sample conditional mean and variance are derived. Asymptotic normality and consistency under fixed alternatives are also established.
AI.result: ASK-NN is computationally efficient and easy to implement. Empirically, it performs competitively against kernel-based and symmetric graph-based baselines on synthetic benchmarks, artificial-text detection tasks, and LLM hallucination detection using token-level hidden states.
AI.conclusion: ASK-NN provides a principled, asymmetric approach to two-sample testing well-suited for detecting distributional discrepancies in LLM outputs, offering both strong theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness.

title: Neural Non-Equilibrium Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Corrected Boltzmann Sampling
summary: Sampling from an unnormalized Boltzmann density requires proposals that move probability mass globally while retaining enough path-probability information for statistical correction. We introduce Neural Non-Equilibrium Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NHMC), a train-then-correct learned Hamiltonian sampler. Starting from a tractable base distribution, NHMC learns stochastic Hamiltonian-style paths toward the target. Once training is complete, the learned proposal parameters are fixed; the proposal then generates complete paths and endpoint configurations, which are statistically corrected using the recorded non-equilibrium work. This dimensionless generalized work is determined by the probability ratio between the forward proposal path and a reverse reference path. During training, minimizing its mean reduces a path-space KL divergence and controls an upper bound on endpoint mismatch. During evaluation, the same quantity defines weights for self-normalized importance sampling on paths (path-SNIS), estimates normalizing constants or free-energy differences, and gives the acceptance ratio for path-space independent Metropolis-Hastings (path-IMH). The same forward-reverse laws also define a shared-bridge round-trip Metropolis kernel that acts directly on configurations and preserves the Boltzmann target. On double-well and finite-volume lattice $φ^4$ targets, the NHMC construction gives corrected estimates when path overlap is sufficient; when overlap is poor, weight degeneracy, low acceptance, and long autocorrelation expose proposal failure. We additionally report a molecular internal-coordinate feasibility study using an MD prior and learned-force path proposal.

AI.tldr: NHMC learns stochastic Hamiltonian paths from a base to a target Boltzmann distribution, then corrects samples using non-equilibrium work. The same work quantity enables path-SNIS, free-energy estimation, and path-IMH, with a round-trip Metropolis kernel ensuring exact target preservation.
AI.motivation: Sampling from unnormalized Boltzmann densities is challenging because proposals must move probability mass globally while retaining path-probability information for statistical correction. Existing Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods rely on local gradient information and struggle with multimodal targets.
AI.method: A train-then-correct framework: (1) Learn stochastic Hamiltonian-style paths from a tractable base distribution toward the target using neural networks. (2) Fix the learned proposal and generate complete paths with endpoint configurations. (3) Correct statistically using dimensionless generalized work (probability ratio of forward proposal path to reverse reference path). During training, minimizing mean work reduces path-space KL divergence and bounds endpoint mismatch. During evaluation, work defines weights for path-SNIS, estimates free-energy differences, and gives acceptance ratios for path-IMH. A shared-bridge round-trip Metropolis kernel acting on configurations preserves the Boltzmann target.
AI.result: On double-well and finite-volume lattice φ⁴ targets, NHMC yields corrected estimates when path overlap is sufficient. When overlap is poor, weight degeneracy, low acceptance, and long autocorrelation expose proposal failure. A molecular internal-coordinate feasibility study using an MD prior and learned-force path proposal is also reported.
AI.conclusion: NHMC provides a principled framework combining learned transport with statistical correction. Performance critically depends on path overlap between forward and reverse processes; insufficient overlap leads to standard importance-sampling failure modes.

title: Toward Federated Multimodal Graph Foundation Models: A Topology-Aware Multimodal Alignment Framework
summary: Multimodal-attributed graphs (MAGs), whose nodes carry modalities such as images and text alongside topological structure, now pervade applications including social platforms, e-commerce, and biomedical networks, offering richer semantic signals than single-modality graphs. In practice, such graphs are fragmented across privacy-restricted silos owned by different platforms and institutions, so learning a broadly transferable model over them demands collaborative training that never exposes raw data. This places the task at the intersection of multimodal graph learning and federated learning, yet existing methods cover only one side of it. To address the challenges from these two perspectives, we propose FedGAMMA, casting federated multimodal graph foundation learning as a two-stage semantic-structural alignment problem of federated pre-training and prompt-based fine-tuning. During pre-training, a shared-private semantic enhancer disentangles cross-modal commonality from modality-specific information, aligning it through optimal transport, a topology-aware graph fusion module decouples semantic and structural views via semantic residual graphs and dual positional encodings, and a dual-channel affinity-aware aggregation mechanism estimates client similarity from feature and graph centroids without exposing raw data. During fine-tuning, FedGAMMA adapts the pretrained encoder through lightweight graph-aware prompts, a shared prompt pool with controlled exploration, and channel-wise prompt synchronization. Experiments on twelve multimodal graph datasets show FedGAMMA consistently surpassing a broad range of baselines across downstream tasks, with gains of up to 12.96%. FedGAMMA further outperforms competitive baselines accross multi-domain datasets on multiple tasks with up to 5.71% under few-shot learning scenario.

AI.tldr: FedGAMMA is a two-stage federated learning framework for multimodal-attributed graphs (MAGs) that combines federated pre-training (with semantic-structural alignment via shared-private encoders, optimal transport, and topology-aware fusion) and prompt-based fine-tuning (using graph-aware prompts and channel-wise synchronization), achieving up to 12.96% improvement over baselines on twelve datasets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal-attributed graphs are distributed across privacy-restricted silos, necessitating collaborative training without raw data exposure. Existing methods address either multimodal graph learning or federated learning in isolation, leaving a gap at their intersection.
AI.method: FedGAMMA operates in two stages. Pre-training: a shared-private semantic enhancer uses optimal transport to disentangle cross-modal commonality from modality-specific signals; a topology-aware graph fusion module decouples semantic and structural views via semantic residual graphs and dual positional encodings; a dual-channel affinity-aware aggregation mechanism estimates client similarity from feature and graph centroids without raw data exposure. Fine-tuning: lightweight graph-aware prompts adapt the pretrained encoder, supported by a shared prompt pool with controlled exploration and channel-wise prompt synchronization.
AI.result: FedGAMMA consistently surpasses a broad range of baselines across 12 multimodal graph datasets on downstream tasks, with gains up to 12.96%. It also outperforms competitive baselines on multi-domain datasets across multiple tasks, achieving up to 5.71% improvement under few-shot learning.
AI.conclusion: FedGAMMA successfully bridges federated learning and multimodal graph learning, demonstrating that the proposed two-stage semantic-structural alignment paradigm — combining privacy-preserving pre-training with prompt-based fine-tuning — yields strong transferable representations for fragmented multimodal graph data.

title: A Benchmark for Electrical Load Forecasting Across Grid Levels: Time-Series Transformers Outperform Established Methods
summary: Accurate load forecasting at multiple grid levels is essential for future smart grids, ranging from aggregated control area forecasts for balancing supply and demand to forecasts of individual end-consumer loads for demand-side management and energy management systems. We present a comprehensive benchmark for load forecasting across grid levels, comprising three datasets that represent a transmission system operator control area, low-voltage grid feeders, and individual end consumers. We evaluate ten methods for short-term load forecasting and find that Transformer-based approaches consistently outperform established methods, reducing forecast error by 6.6-10.7 %. To analyze the impact of architectural design, we introduce YAformer, a flexible Transformer architecture that integrates modifications from prior work and is optimized via hyperparameter optimization. However, the standard Transformer achieves superior performance, suggesting that these architectural modifications are not required for accurate load forecasting. We further evaluate the Transformer-based time-series foundation model Chronos-2, which demonstrates competitive zero-shot performance on two datasets but fails to accurately capture special events in the TSO data. Detailed analyses reveal model-specific strengths and weaknesses, and ablation studies highlight the importance of long input contexts, covariates and continuous retraining - aspects that are often overlooked in the time-series forecasting literature.

AI.tldr: A benchmark of ten load forecasting methods across three grid levels (TSO control area, LV feeders, end consumers) shows Transformer-based models outperform traditional approaches by 6.6–10.7%. A custom YAformer architecture underperforms the standard Transformer, and the foundation model Chronos-2 shows strong zero-shot results but struggles with special events. Long input contexts, covariates, and continuous retraining are critical success factors.
AI.motivation: Accurate load forecasting across multiple grid levels — from aggregated TSO-level balancing to individual end-consumer demand-side management — is essential for future smart grid operation. However, the relative performance of modern deep learning methods versus traditional approaches across these diverse forecasting contexts remains unclear, warranting a systematic benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct three datasets representing a TSO control area, low-voltage grid feeders, and individual end consumers. They evaluate ten short-term load forecasting methods, including statistical baselines, classical machine learning, and deep learning approaches, with a focus on Transformer-based architectures. They introduce YAformer, a configurable Transformer integrating multiple architectural modifications, optimized via hyperparameter optimization. They also evaluate Chronos-2, a time-series foundation model, in zero-shot settings, and perform ablation studies on input length, covariates, and retraining strategies.
AI.result: Transformer-based methods consistently outperform established models, reducing forecast error by 6.6–10.7%. The standard Transformer surpasses the custom YAformer, indicating architectural modifications from prior work are unnecessary for load forecasting. Chronos-2 achieves competitive zero-shot performance on two datasets but fails to capture special events in TSO data. Ablations demonstrate that long input contexts, inclusion of covariates, and continuous retraining significantly improve forecast accuracy, despite being frequently overlooked in the literature.
AI.conclusion: Transformer architectures, particularly the standard variant, are state-of-the-art for multi-level load forecasting. Architectural embellishments offer no benefit, while practical factors — long lookback windows, covariates, and continuous retraining — are more impactful than model design choices. Foundation models like Chronos-2 show promise but require improvement for rare-event handling.

title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to improving large language models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, yet RL post-training is largely studied in isolation from the pretraining that precedes it. As a result, two basic questions remain open: (1) how do pretraining choices (model size, data) shape the returns to RL compute, and (2) what does RL actually do to the model? These questions are difficult to study in the standard LLM setting: pretraining corpora are vast and uncontrolled, making it hard to attribute behaviors to pretraining versus RL, and systematic compute sweeps across both stages are prohibitively expensive. To address these challenges, we use chess as a controlled testbed for studying reasoning across the full pretraining-to-post-training pipeline. We follow the standard LLM training pipeline by pretraining language models from 5M to 1B parameters on human chess games, supervised fine-tuning on synthetic reasoning traces, and running RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards. Using this framework, we find that the post-RL performance at given RL compute level is well-predicted from the pretraining loss, and slope of the RL reward curves improves approximately linearly with the pretraining tokens. Beyond scaling, we find that RL does not simply sharpen the SFT policy: on easy puzzles it amplifies correct moves the SFT policy already preferred, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves that were nearly absent under SFT. We further test whether our findings transfer beyond chess by training a 1B language model on math-domain text, where the same predictive pattern emerges: longer-pretrained checkpoints reach higher post-RL performance and improve faster under RL. In sum, we provide a quantitative account of the pretraining-to-RL interface and a controlled testbed for studying the science of reasoning across the full pretraining-to-post-training pipeline.

AI.tldr: Using chess as a controlled testbed for the full pretraining-to-RL pipeline, the paper shows that post-RL performance is predictably determined by pretraining loss, RL reward improves linearly with pretraining tokens, and RL amplifies existing correct moves on easy puzzles while surfacing novel correct moves on hard ones. These findings also transfer to math-domain language models.
AI.motivation: Two open questions in LLM training: (1) how pretraining choices (model size, data) affect returns to RL compute, and (2) what mechanisms RL actually induces in the model. Standard LLM settings make this hard to study due to uncontrolled pretraining corpora and prohibitive compute costs for systematic sweeps.
AI.method: Chess as a controlled testbed: pretraining Transformer LMs (5M–1B params) on human chess games, supervised fine-tuning on synthetic reasoning traces, then RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards. Systematic sweeps across pretraining compute (model size × tokens) and RL compute. Transfer tested via a 1B math-domain LM.
AI.result: Post-RL performance is well-predicted by pretraining loss; RL reward curve slope improves ~linearly with pretraining tokens. RL does not merely sharpen the SFT policy — on easy puzzles it amplifies already-preferred correct moves, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves nearly absent under SFT. Math-domain experiments replicate the same predictive pattern.
AI.conclusion: A quantitative account of the pretraining-to-RL interface is established: pretraining quality sets a predictable ceiling and slope for RL improvement, and RL's mechanistic effect depends on problem difficulty. The chess testbed offers a tractable framework for studying reasoning across the full training pipeline.

title: CardioMeta: Calibrated Multi-Task Prediction of Diabetes, Hypertension, and Cardiovascular Disease Across Population and EHR Data
summary: Cardiometabolic diseases remain among the most persistent drivers of preventable morbidity because diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease frequently co-occur and share metabolic, vascular, demographic, and behavioral determinants. Existing machine learning studies for chronic disease prediction often emphasize discrimination on a single dataset, while underreporting label leakage, calibration, temporal robustness, external transportability, and subgroup reliability. This paper presents CardioMeta, a calibrated multi-task framework for joint prediction of diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease across population survey and electronic health record (EHR) data. The study uses NHANES for population-level model development and temporal validation, and MIMIC-IV for EHR-domain evaluation under substantial distribution shift. To reduce circular label reconstruction, the primary analysis excludes disease-defining variables from the corresponding prediction heads, while a full-clinical feature setting is retained only as sensitivity analysis. CardioMeta combines a shared cardiometabolic encoder with disease-specific gated heads and post-hoc probability calibration. In the leakage-reduced temporal validation setting, the model achieved a macro-AUROC of 0.839, macro-AUPRC of 0.536, macro-F1 of 0.614, and expected calibration error of 0.024, with modest but consistent improvements over strong gradient-boosting and neural tabular baselines. External evaluation on MIMIC-IV showed clear degradation under domain shift, while limited fine-tuning partially recovered performance. The findings indicate that the principal value of multi-task cardiometabolic modeling lies not in inflated accuracy, but in reproducible leakage control, calibrated probabilities, and transparent reliability reporting across heterogeneous healthcare data sources.

AI.tldr: CardioMeta is a multi-task framework jointly predicting diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease across NHANES and MIMIC-IV datasets, achieving macro-AUROC 0.839 with robust leakage control, probability calibration, and transparent reliability reporting.
AI.motivation: Existing ML studies for cardiometabolic disease prediction overemphasize single-dataset discrimination while neglecting label leakage, calibration, temporal robustness, external transportability, and subgroup reliability. There is a need for a reproducible, well-calibrated multi-task framework that transfers across population survey and EHR data sources.
AI.method: CardioMeta uses a shared cardiometabolic encoder with disease-specific gated heads and post-hoc probability calibration. The primary analysis excludes disease-defining variables from corresponding prediction heads to prevent circular label reconstruction. NHANES is used for model development and temporal validation, while MIMIC-IV serves for external EHR-domain evaluation under distribution shift, with limited fine-tuning explored.
AI.result: Under leakage-reduced temporal validation, CardioMeta achieved macro-AUROC 0.839, macro-AUPRC 0.536, macro-F1 0.614, and expected calibration error 0.024, with modest but consistent improvements over gradient-boosting and neural tabular baselines. MIMIC-IV evaluation showed degradation under domain shift, partially recovered by limited fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The principal value of multi-task cardiometabolic modeling is not inflated accuracy but reproducible leakage control, calibrated probabilities, and transparent reliability reporting across heterogeneous healthcare data sources.

title: Learning Faster without Deeper Networks: A*-Inspired Batch Selection for Efficient CNN Training
summary: Common practice when training Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is to use randomly shuffled mini-batches. This creates two limitations: slower convergence, and a diminishing learning signal, since many samples are quickly classified as easy during training. We address these inefficiencies with A*-Inspired Batch Selection (A*-BS), a lightweight, model-agnostic strategy that formulates mini-batch scheduling as a heuristic search problem. Each batch is treated as a node in a search space and ranked using an A*-like score combining a loss-based difficulty measure with a reuse penalty. This encourages informative gradient updates and batch diversity throughout training, without modifying network architectures or optimization algorithms, so it integrates seamlessly into existing pipelines. We evaluate A*-BS on the twelve 2D classification tasks of the MedMNIST-v2 benchmark, using a deliberately simple architecture of approximately 2.25x10^5 parameters, compared against the ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 baselines reported by the benchmark. On half of these tasks, the lightweight model with A*-BS reaches higher accuracy and AUC than both ResNet baselines, with relative gains of up to 15%. An ablation under identical architecture and hyperparameters shows A*-BS outperforms random batch shuffling on all twelve tasks. Wall-clock measurements further show the lightweight CNN with A*-BS trains substantially faster than ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on identical hardware. These results indicate that intelligent batch ordering can partially compensate for reduced architectural complexity, offering a computationally efficient alternative to deeper models, with reliability reinforced by strong performance even against deeper, more sophisticated architectures.

AI.tldr: A*-BS formulates mini-batch scheduling as a heuristic search problem, ranking batches by a loss-difficulty/reuse-penalty score to accelerate convergence and maintain informative gradients. Evaluated on MedMNIST-v2, a lightweight CNN with A*-BS matches or exceeds ResNet-18/50 on half the tasks while training faster.
AI.motivation: Random mini-batch shuffling in CNN training causes two inefficiencies: slower convergence and a diminishing learning signal as many samples quickly become "easy" and contribute little gradient information. The authors aim to address this without modifying architectures or optimizers.
AI.method: A*-Inspired Batch Selection (A*-BS) treats each batch as a node in a search space and ranks them using an A*-like scoring heuristic that combines: (1) a loss-based difficulty measure (prioritizing high-loss samples) and (2) a reuse penalty (encouraging batch diversity). It is model-agnostic, lightweight, and integrates into existing pipelines.
AI.result: On 12 MedMNIST-v2 2D classification tasks, a ~225K-parameter CNN with A*-BS outperformed both ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 baselines on 6 tasks (up to 15% relative gain). Ablation showed A*-BS beats random shuffling on all 12 tasks under identical conditions. Wall-clock training time was substantially lower than ResNet baselines.
AI.conclusion: Intelligent batch ordering via A*-BS can partially compensate for reduced architectural complexity, offering a computationally efficient alternative to deeper models with strong, reliable performance.

title: Trainable Spline Representations for Physics-Informed Learning
summary: This work introduces Physics-Informed Splines (PI-Splines), a structured spline-based architecture for physics-informed learning. Instead of representing the solution of a differential equation with a neural network, PI-Splines directly parametrize the unknown field through a tensor-product B-spline expansion with trainable control coefficients. This formulation preserves the residual-based training paradigm of Physics-Informed Neural Networks while providing compact support, explicit smoothness control, analytical derivatives, and a direct geometric interpretation of the trainable parameters. When compatible with the spline representation, boundary conditions can be imposed strongly by fixing suitable boundary control coefficients. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark problems of increasing difficulty and compared with standard physics-informed frameworks under matched governing equations, collocation sets, loss terms, and optimization procedures, so as to isolate the effect of the approximation architecture. Numerical experiments show that PI-Splines provide a competitive and stable alternative to neural physics-informed architectures, particularly in settings where structured representations, locality, and parameter efficiency are desirable.

AI.tldr: PI-Splines replaces neural networks with tensor-product B-spline expansions for physics-informed learning, preserving the residual-based training paradigm while offering compact support, smoothness control, analytical derivatives, and strong boundary condition imposition. Benchmarks show competitive, stable performance vs. standard PINNs.
AI.motivation: Standard Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) use neural networks as the function approximator, which introduces challenges: lack of compact support, limited interpretability of parameters, difficulty in explicitly controlling smoothness, and reliance on automatic differentiation. The authors seek an alternative approximation architecture that retains the residual-based training paradigm while offering locality, parameter efficiency, analytical derivatives, and the ability to strongly impose boundary conditions.
AI.method: The unknown solution field is parametrized directly via a tensor-product B-spline expansion with trainable control coefficients. This yields analytical spatial derivatives (no automatic differentiation needed), compact support, and explicit smoothness control via spline order. Boundary conditions are imposed strongly by fixing appropriate boundary control coefficients when geometry is compatible with the spline representation. The training uses the same residual-based loss paradigm as PINNs, evaluated on matched collocation sets under identical optimization procedures to isolate the effect of the approximation architecture.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on benchmark problems of increasing difficulty demonstrate that PI-Splines offer competitive accuracy and stability compared to standard physics-informed neural architectures. The method performs especially well in settings where structured representations, locality, and parameter efficiency are advantageous.
AI.conclusion: PI-Splines provide a viable, stable, and parameter-efficient alternative to neural-network-based physics-informed learning, particularly suitable for problems benefiting from structured representations, local support, and strong boundary condition imposition.

title: CoG-Guided Weight Correction for Fault-Tolerant Deep Neural Networks
comment: 7 figures, 9 tables. the paper is under review in an IEEE Transactions
summary:
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) used in safety-critical applications are vulnerable to hardware and memory faults that corrupt network weights and degrade reliability. In this paper, we propose a Center of Gravity (CoG) guided weight correction method that restores faulty weights based on their spatial characteristics within each layer. The proposed approach detects and corrects weight faults using distance-aware correction rules, eliminating the need for retraining or architectural modification. The effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of the capability of tolerating hardware faults has been evaluated through performing fault injection at different Bit Error Rates (BERs).
  Experiments on safety-critical LSTM-based Networks, including StageNet for disease progression tracking and MTFNet for cardiac anomaly detection, demonstrate fault tolerance improvements of up to 230x and 6.41x, respectively, at a BER of 10^{-3}, with negligible accuracy loss. When extended to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), the method achieves up to 49.55x and 20.79x improvements under comparable fault conditions on ResNet-18 and VGG-16, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to apply the CoG concept to neural network weight tensors for enhancing model reliability.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Center of Gravity (CoG) guided method to detect and correct faulty weights in DNNs caused by hardware faults, achieving up to 230x fault tolerance improvement without retraining or architectural changes.
AI.motivation: DNNs in safety-critical applications are vulnerable to hardware/memory faults that corrupt weights, degrading reliability. Existing solutions often require retraining or architectural modifications, motivating a lightweight, post-hoc weight correction approach.
AI.method: A Center of Gravity (CoG) guided weight correction method that exploits spatial characteristics of weights within each layer. Faulty weights are detected and corrected using distance-aware correction rules relative to the CoG of the weight distribution, without retraining or architectural modification.
AI.result: On LSTM-based networks: up to 230x fault tolerance improvement for StageNet and 6.41x for MTFNet at BER=10^{-3}, with negligible accuracy loss. On CNNs: up to 49.55x for ResNet-18 and 20.79x for VGG-16 under comparable fault conditions.
AI.conclusion: The CoG-guided weight correction method effectively restores faulty weights across both LSTM and CNN architectures, significantly improving fault tolerance while maintaining accuracy. This is the first work applying CoG to neural network weight tensors for reliability enhancement.

title: From Diffusion to Reaction-Diffusion: A Dynamical-Systems View of Oversmoothing in Hypergraph Neural Networks
summary: Higher-order couplings enhance the expressive power of hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs), but they also intensify representation collapse in deep propagation due to strong multi-way feature mixing. This work investigates hypergraph oversmoothing from a dynamical-systems perspective and develops a reaction--diffusion framework for depth-resistant hypergraph learning. By defining hypergraph gradient and divergence operators, we interpret message passing as an incidence-level diffusion process. The analysis of pure diffusion shows that its continuous semiflow exponentially contracts the null-mode-free component of node representations and drives the Dirichlet energy to zero, revealing hypergraph oversmoothing as an intrinsic transverse-energy dissipation phenomenon. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Hypergraph Neural Reaction--Diffusion (HNRD), which introduces a reaction mechanism acting on the transverse component to compensate diffusion-induced dissipation and stabilize discriminative variations. We establish global well-posedness of the proposed dynamics and prove that the null-mode-free Dirichlet energy remains bounded away from zero. A forward-Euler discretization provides a practical HNRD layer with a stability condition for deep propagation. Experiments on benchmark and synthetic heterophilic hypergraphs demonstrate that HNRD consistently improves over representative hypergraph baselines. Depth, robustness, and efficiency analyses further show that HNRD preserves stable performance and nonzero Dirichlet energy under deep propagation and perturbations. These results provide a principled dynamical framework for designing deep hypergraph architectures that maintain higher-order expressiveness without representation collapse.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes hypergraph oversmoothing as a dynamical phenomenon where pure diffusion exponentially dissipates transverse energy, causing representation collapse. To counter this, the authors propose Hypergraph Neural Reaction–Diffusion (HNRD), which adds a reaction term that compensates for diffusion-induced dissipation, keeping Dirichlet energy bounded away from zero and enabling deep, stable hypergraph learning.
AI.motivation: Higher-order couplings in hypergraph neural networks increase expressiveness but exacerbate oversmoothing in deep architectures due to strong multi-way feature mixing. Existing HGNNs lack a principled dynamical understanding of this oversmoothing phenomenon and a systematic remedy that preserves higher-order expressiveness without representation collapse.
AI.method: The authors frame hypergraph message passing as incidence-level diffusion using hypergraph gradient and divergence operators. They analyze the pure diffusion semiflow, proving exponential contraction of the null-mode-free component and Dirichlet energy decay — establishing oversmoothing as transverse-energy dissipation. They then propose HNRD, a reaction–diffusion system where a reaction mechanism acts on the transverse component to counteract diffusion. Global well-posedness is proved, and a forward-Euler discretization yields a practical layer with a stability condition.
AI.result: HNRD consistently outperforms representative hypergraph baselines on benchmark and synthetic heterophilic hypergraphs. Depth, robustness, and efficiency analyses confirm HNRD maintains stable performance and nonzero Dirichlet energy under deep propagation and perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The reaction–diffusion framework provides a principled dynamical foundation for designing deep hypergraph architectures that retain higher-order expressiveness without representation collapse, with HNRD demonstrating both theoretical guarantees and empirical effectiveness.

title: Scaling Time Series Classification via XAI-Driven Data Reduction
comment: Accepted for AALTD workshop at ECML-PKDD 2026
summary:
Explainable AI (XAI) for time series has seen significant algorithmic growth, but its utility in providing measurable performance gains for downstream tasks remains under-explored. This paper bridges this gap by introducing drXAI, a novel methodology that repurposes XAI attribution methods for effective data reduction in Time Series Classification (TSC). The core challenge in modern TSC is scalability; state-of-the-art models, such as Transformers, exhibit quadratic complexity relative to sequence length and linear complexity relative to the number of channels. This renders them computationally prohibitive for massive datasets. drXAI addresses this by using a fast, GPU-accelerated classifier (Hydra) to generate local attributions. We aggregate these into global feature importance scores and employ an automated elbow-cut heuristic to select the most salient features without requiring manual thresholds.
  We evaluate our approach on both synthetic and real-world univariate and multivariate datasets. On synthetic benchmarks, drXAI successfully recovers ground-truth features where traditional baselines fail. On real-world data, drXAI achieves between 80% and 90% data reduction while maintaining classification accuracy comparable to models trained on the full dataset. Most importantly, we show that drXAI allows resource-intensive models like ConvTran to scale to datasets that were previously inaccessible due to memory constraints. Our results show the benefits of using XAI not just for interpretability, but as a robust tool for feature selection and scalability in time series analysis. All our code and data are openly available.

AI.tldr: drXAI repurposes XAI attribution methods for data reduction in time series classification, achieving 80-90% data reduction while maintaining accuracy, and enabling resource-intensive models to scale to previously inaccessible datasets.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art TSC models like Transformers suffer from quadratic complexity relative to sequence length and linear complexity relative to channel count, making them computationally prohibitive for large-scale datasets. Meanwhile, XAI for time series has focused on algorithmic advances but lacks demonstrated utility for downstream performance gains.
AI.method: drXAI uses a fast GPU-accelerated classifier (Hydra) to generate local attributions, aggregates them into global feature importance scores, and applies an automated elbow-cut heuristic to select salient features without manual thresholds. The reduced data is then used to train downstream models.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks, drXAI recovers ground-truth features where traditional baselines fail. On real-world data, it achieves 80-90% data reduction with classification accuracy comparable to full-dataset training. It enables ConvTran to scale to datasets previously inaccessible due to memory constraints.
AI.conclusion: XAI can serve as a robust tool not only for interpretability but also for feature selection and scalability in time series analysis, bridging the gap between algorithmic XAI advances and measurable performance gains.

title: AquaAugmentor: A Novel Feature Augmentation Algorithm for Water Potability Prediction
comment: Published in 2024 6th International Conference on Sustainable Technologies for Industry 5.0 (STI), 14-15 December, Dhaka, Bangladesh
summary: Access to potable water is crucial for health, economic development, and sustainability. However, accurately classifying water quality remains a significant challenge due to the complexity and variability of water source data. This paper addresses the challenge of predicting water potability through machine learning and deep learning algorithms. It introduces a novel feature augmentation algorithm, AquaAugmentor, to enhance the predictive performance of these models for low-dimensional datasets. Utilizing a dataset that includes chemical attributes of water, such as pH, hardness, solids, chloramines, sulfate, and others. This study evaluates the performance of the models with and without AquaAugmentor. Each model applied to classify water as potable or non-potable and its performance is then evaluated and compared based on test accuracy and AUC score. The results highlight the strengths and limitations of our proposed algorithm, providing insights into the most effective techniques for improving the predictive performance of water quality classification. This study contributes to the broader efforts of ensuring safe water access and serves as a framework for employing machine learning in environmental quality assessments. The findings aim to assist researchers, policymakers, and public health officials in making informed decisions based on reliable machine learning predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AquaAugmentor, a feature augmentation algorithm designed to improve machine learning and deep learning models' performance in classifying water potability from low-dimensional chemical attribute datasets. Models with AquaAugmentor are compared against baseline models using test accuracy and AUC score.
AI.motivation: Accurately classifying water potability is critical for public health and sustainability, but remains challenging due to the complexity and variability of water source data. Existing models struggle with low-dimensional datasets, limiting their predictive power.
AI.method: The authors propose AquaAugmentor, a novel feature augmentation algorithm tailored for low-dimensional water quality datasets. Chemical attributes (pH, hardness, solids, chloramines, sulfate, etc.) are used as input features. Multiple machine learning and deep learning models are trained both with and without AquaAugmentor, and evaluated on test accuracy and AUC score for binary classification (potable vs. non-potable).
AI.result: The paper reports comparative performance of models with and without AquaAugmentor, highlighting improvements in predictive accuracy and AUC. It also identifies strengths and limitations of the proposed augmentation approach across different model architectures.
AI.conclusion: AquaAugmentor enhances predictive performance for water potability classification on low-dimensional datasets. The study provides a framework for applying machine learning to environmental quality assessment, aiming to support researchers, policymakers, and public health officials in making data-driven decisions for safe water access.

title: Knowledge-Assisted Multi-Graph Dependency Learning for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection in Multi-Stage Industrial Processes
summary: Industrial processes often generate complex, interdependent time-series data from multiple sensors across multiple stages, forming complex dependencies among variables and process stages. Effective monitoring and timely anomaly detection of these time series through multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTAD) is crucial for preventing failures and ensuring the reliability of automated systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have advanced MTAD by leveraging data-driven graphs to model complex dependencies among variables, effectively capturing relational structures within multivariate time series to enhance anomaly detection performance. However, existing GNN-based approaches often overlook critical process knowledge, and even when this knowledge is considered, seamlessly incorporating it into existing models remains inherently challenging, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we propose a knowledge-assisted multi-graph framework for modeling sensor dependencies in multi-stage industrial processes for MTAD, which explicitly incorporates process knowledge into graph learning to enhance dependency modeling and improve anomaly detection performance. Our method constructs three complementary graphs: one purely data-driven and two refined by integrating structural constraints derived from process knowledge. To effectively leverage these graphs for anomaly detection, we employ a multi-graph attention network, enabling a more accurate and robust representation of complex dependencies. Comprehensive experiments on two real-world, multi-stage industrial datasets demonstrate that incorporating process knowledge substantially enhances anomaly detection performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes a knowledge-assisted multi-graph framework for multivariate time series anomaly detection in multi-stage industrial processes, integrating process structural knowledge with data-driven graphs via multi-graph attention networks to improve anomaly detection performance.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based MTAD methods overlook critical process knowledge (e.g., known inter-stage dependencies, sensor groupings), and even when such knowledge is available, seamlessly incorporating it into graph learning models remains challenging, leading to suboptimal anomaly detection in multi-stage industrial settings.
AI.method: The framework constructs three complementary graphs: one purely data-driven graph and two graphs refined by structural constraints from process knowledge. A multi-graph attention network then jointly leverages these graphs to learn robust representations of complex inter-variable and inter-stage dependencies for anomaly detection.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on two real-world, multi-stage industrial datasets demonstrate that explicitly incorporating process knowledge substantially enhances anomaly detection performance compared to existing GNN-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Process knowledge, when properly integrated via a multi-graph attention framework, significantly improves dependency modeling and anomaly detection in complex multi-stage industrial processes.

title: QUADS: Stabilizing NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning for MoE via QUantization-error Alignment across Dual Sides
summary: Rollout generation is a major bottleneck in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models, motivating low-precision rollout acceleration such as FP8. As an emerging low-precision format, NVFP4 combines fine-grained scaling for accuracy preservation with native W4A4 FP4 GEMMs for higher throughput than FP8. However, we find that directly applying NVFP4 to MoE RL rollout is impractical. NVFP4 rollout with BF16 training collapses after roughly 150 steps, accompanied by rapidly growing rollout-trainer log-probability gaps. Through training-inference error analysis and controlled ablations, we identify activation error, rather than weight error, as the dominant source of FP4 RL instability: weights can be synchronized and aligned by a shared quantization-dequantization path, whereas activations are recomputed online and error is amplified by the coarse E2M1 grid. Therefore, to stabilize NVFP4 RL for MoE, we propose QUantization-error Alignment across Dual Sides (QUADS). On the trainer side, we introduce Asymmetric Quantization-Aware Training fake-quantizing weights while keeping activations unquantized for better alignment. On the rollout side, Residual Activation Compensation corrects high-error activation channels while preserving native W4A4 GEMMs. In our MoE RL experiments on several benchmarks, QUADS achieves BF16-level accuracy, improves average pass@1 by 21.49 points over naive NVFP4 RL, and delivers ~16% higher rollout throughput than FP8.

AI.tldr: NVFP4 (W4A4 FP4) accelerates MoE RL rollouts but causes training collapse due to activation quantization errors. The authors propose QUADS: Asymmetric Quantization-Aware Training on the trainer side and Residual Activation Compensation on the rollout side, achieving BF16-level accuracy with ~16% higher throughput than FP8.
AI.motivation: Rollout generation is the bottleneck in MoE LLM RL training. While NVFP4 offers higher throughput than FP8 via native W4A4 GEMMs, naive application to MoE RL rollouts causes training collapse within ~150 steps due to a growing rollout-trainer log-probability gap.
AI.method: (1) Error analysis identifying activation error (not weight error) as the dominant instability source, since weights share a quantization-dequantization path while activations are recomputed online with coarse E2M1 grid amplification. (2) QUADS: Asymmetric QAT (fake-quantizes weights only, activations stay unquantized) on the trainer side; Residual Activation Compensation (corrects high-error activation channels) on the rollout side while preserving native W4A4 GEMMs.
AI.result: QUADS achieves BF16-level accuracy across several MoE RL benchmarks, improves average pass@1 by 21.49 points over naive NVFP4 RL, and delivers ~16% higher rollout throughput than FP8.
AI.conclusion: Activation error is the critical bottleneck for low-precision (FP4) MoE RL rollouts. QUADS successfully stabilizes NVFP4 RL through dual-sided quantization-error alignment, enabling practical deployment with accuracy parity to BF16 and throughput superior to FP8.

title: Graph Coloring Approach to Solving Sudoku with Oscillatory Neural Networks
summary: Oscillatory Neural Networks (ONNs) present an attractive physics-based computing paradigm rooted in the dynamics of a network of typically fully coupled oscillators aiming to minimize an underlying energy function. In this paper, we propose an ONN-based solver for one well-known constrained combinatorial optimization problem, namely a Sudoku, by formulating the problem as a Graph Coloring problem. By modifying the already existing Graph Coloring solver to a computationally cheaper version and introducing an additional term ensuring the fulfillment of the Sudoku constraints, our solver is shown to significantly outperform the existing HNN- and ONN solvers in terms of accuracy. In particular, we are able to achieve nearly flawless accuracies on $4 \times 4$ as well as rather high accuracies on $9 \times 9$ Sudoku puzzles for different numbers of unknown digits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Oscillatory Neural Network (ONN) solver for Sudoku by reformulating it as a Graph Coloring problem, achieving superior accuracy over existing HNN and ONN solvers on both 4×4 and 9×9 puzzles.
AI.motivation: Existing ONN-based solvers for constrained combinatorial optimization problems like Sudoku suffer from limited accuracy. The authors aim to develop a more accurate ONN solver by leveraging a computationally cheaper Graph Coloring formulation augmented with Sudoku-specific constraints.
AI.method: The authors reformulate Sudoku as a Graph Coloring problem, modify an existing Graph Coloring ONN solver to a computationally cheaper version, and introduce an additional energy term to enforce Sudoku-specific constraints (row, column, and subgrid uniqueness).
AI.result: The proposed solver achieves near-flawless accuracy on 4×4 Sudoku puzzles and significantly high accuracy on 9×9 puzzles across varying numbers of unknown digits, substantially outperforming existing HNN-based and ONN-based solvers.
AI.conclusion: The ONN-based Graph Coloring approach with added constraint terms provides a highly effective and accurate solver for Sudoku puzzles, demonstrating the potential of ONNs for constrained combinatorial optimization.

title: In-context learning of closed form solution to simple linear regression task using transformer with linear self-attention
summary: In-context learning is a remarkable property of transformers and has recently received a lot of interest. In many studies of in-context learning, it has been shown that transformers are capable of implementing solver for linear and non-linear regression problems, in which the most of them implement gradient descent algorithm. However, it is still unclear whether those implementations have actually been acquired through training. In this paper, we construct a transformer with linear self-attention, which in-context learns the least squares estimate in a simple regression task. The point here is that the closed form (analytical) solution is approximately obtained by using layer normalization rather than an approximate solution based on gradient descent algorithm. Then, we show an experimental example, in which our implementation is mainly used in the transformer trained with l1 regularization when the target output is the least squares estimate.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a transformer with linear self-attention that performs least squares estimation in-context using a closed-form analytical solution via layer normalization, rather than gradient descent. The authors demonstrate that this analytical implementation emerges in transformers trained with L1 regularization when the target is the least squares estimate.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown transformers can implement gradient descent for regression tasks in-context, but it remains unclear whether these implementations are genuinely acquired through training. The authors aim to clarify this by offering an alternative, analytically grounded implementation.
AI.method: The authors construct a transformer with linear self-attention that approximates the closed-form least squares solution using layer normalization, rather than relying on gradient descent. They then provide experimental evidence showing this analytical implementation is predominantly adopted when the transformer is trained with L1 regularization on least squares targets.
AI.result: The constructed transformer successfully performs in-context least squares estimation via the analytical solution. Experimentally, the analytical implementation emerges as the primary mechanism in transformers trained with L1 regularization when targeting the least squares estimate.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can in-context learn the least squares solution through an analytical, closed-form mechanism facilitated by layer normalization, and this implementation can naturally emerge through training with appropriate regularization.

title: Data-Native Global Optimization for Big Data K-means Clustering
summary: Big data clustering remains challenging: the Minimum Sum-of-Squares Clustering (MSSC) problem underlying K-means is NP-hard, and existing methods either reach poor local minima or require prohibitive metaheuristic hybrids. We target arbitrarily tall data: a fixed feature space may contain arbitrarily many, possibly infinitely many, observations, while the algorithm accesses only finite random samples. We propose Big-means++, an algorithm achieving scalability and global-search quality by curating inputs to MSSC optimization on big data. It orchestrates local K-means refinements into a data-native global search for big data clustering. Rather than optimizing the full-data MSSC objective, Big-means++ traverses sample-induced surrogate landscapes. Each sample defines a distinct empirical MSSC approximation with a perturbed local-optimum structure, turning sample-to-sample variation into a global-search mechanism. Unlike Big-means, a flowing-incumbent strategy propagates centroid state across empirical landscapes through K-means refinements on fresh samples without rollback to a best-so-far solution. This increases mobility and favors stable, high-quality configurations across approximations of the full-data structure. A new shaking mechanism varies sample size geometrically, broadening the surrogate landscapes explored across resolution scales, accounting for cluster imbalance, and improving solution quality. A competitive multi-agent system asynchronously explores independent sampled landscapes, transforming diverse stochastic trajectories into collective search intelligence. Automatic convergence detection stops each agent after attaining a high-quality solution but before further search risks degrading it, while providing a universal speed-quality control. Experiments on 22 datasets against 11 competing algorithms demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of Big-means++.

AI.tldr: Big-means++ is a scalable clustering algorithm that solves the Minimum Sum-of-Squares Clustering (MSSC) problem by sampling-induced surrogate landscapes, flowing-incumbent centroid propagation, geometric sample-size shaking, and a competitive multi-agent system with automatic convergence detection. It outperforms 11 competing algorithms across 22 datasets.
AI.motivation: Big data clustering is challenging because the underlying MSSC problem is NP-hard, and existing methods either converge to poor local minima or rely on computationally prohibitive metaheuristic hybrids. The authors target the "arbitrarily tall data" scenario where the feature space is fixed but observations can be arbitrarily or infinitely many, requiring algorithms that operate on finite random samples without accessing the full dataset.
AI.method: Big-means++ is built on four key mechanisms: (1) Sample-induced surrogate landscapes — each random sample defines a distinct empirical MSSC approximation whose perturbed local-optimum structure is exploited for global search. (2) Flowing-incumbent strategy — centroid states propagate continuously across empirical landscapes via K-means refinements on fresh samples, without rollback to a best-so-far solution, enhancing mobility. (3) Geometric sample-size shaking — sample size is varied geometrically to explore surrogate landscapes at multiple resolution scales, accounting for cluster imbalance. (4) Competitive multi-agent system — independent agents asynchronously explore different sampled landscapes, and automatic convergence detection stops each agent once a high-quality solution is reached, providing universal speed-quality control.
AI.result: Experiments on 22 datasets against 11 competing algorithms demonstrate that Big-means++ achieves superior effectiveness (clustering quality), efficiency (computational cost), and robustness compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Big-means++ offers an effective, efficient, and robust solution for big data clustering by leveraging stochastic sampling, multi-resolution exploration, and collective multi-agent search, advancing the state of the art in scalable global optimization for the MSSC problem.

title: ContinuityBench: A Benchmark and Systems Study of Stateful Failover in Multi-Provider LLM Routing
summary: In production large language model (LLM) deployments, high API availability guarantees do not equate to conversational continuity. When a primary provider experiences an outage or strict rate-limiting, naive stateless failover mechanisms successfully maintain uptime but silently discard conversation history, severely disrupting the user experience. To rigorously quantify and resolve this failure mode, we introduce two novel metrics: Continuity Preservation Rate (CPR) and Continuity Latency Overhead (CLO). We propose a stateful, multi-provider proxy architecture utilizing a History-Forwarding strategy to seamlessly reconstruct conversational state across heterogeneous LLM endpoints during failover events. Furthermore, we release continuity-bench, https://github.com/Vishal-sys-code/continuity-bench, an open evaluation harness designed to stress-test context preservation under high-concurrency provider failure conditions. Our empirical evaluation ($N=750$ failover events) demonstrates that our stateful proxy achieves a 99.20\% CPR [95\% CI: 98.27\%, 99.63\%], cleanly transferring deep conversational context to fallback providers, compared to a near-0\% preservation rate for standard stateless architectures. Finally, we characterize failover latency distributions, identifying the critical necessity of asynchronous exponential backoff with jitter to prevent cascading retry storms against strict-limit fallback APIs. Our results provide a principled foundation for building robust, state-preserving multi-model inference systems.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of lost conversation history during LLM API failover. The authors introduce two metrics (CPR and CLO), propose a stateful multi-provider proxy with a History-Forwarding strategy, and demonstrate 99.20% continuity preservation versus near-0% for stateless architectures across 750 failover events.
AI.motivation: High API availability in production LLM deployments does not guarantee conversational continuity. Naive stateless failover mechanisms discard conversation history during provider outages or rate-limiting, severely disrupting user experience. There is no existing rigorous framework to quantify or resolve this continuity failure mode.
AI.method: The authors introduce two novel metrics: Continuity Preservation Rate (CPR) and Continuity Latency Overhead (CLO). They design a stateful, multi-provider proxy architecture employing a History-Forwarding strategy that reconstructs conversational state across heterogeneous LLM endpoints during failover. They release an open-source evaluation harness, continuity-bench, and conduct empirical evaluation across 750 failover events, comparing stateful vs. stateless architectures. They also analyze failover latency distributions and advocate for asynchronous exponential backoff with jitter to mitigate retry storms.
AI.result: The stateful proxy achieved 99.20% CPR [95% CI: 98.27%, 99.63%], successfully transferring deep conversational context to fallback providers, compared to near-0% for stateless architectures. Failover latency analysis confirmed that asynchronous exponential backoff with jitter is critical to prevent cascading retry storms against strict-limit fallback APIs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stateful, history-forwarding proxy architecture provides a principled foundation for building robust, state-preserving multi-model inference systems, ensuring conversational continuity across provider failures where traditional stateless approaches fail entirely.

title: A Semiparametric Framework for Stochastic Fundamental Diagram Modeling
summary: The stochastic fundamental diagram (SFD) provides a probabilistic description of the relationship between traffic density and flow or speed, enabling uncertainty-aware traffic modeling. However, existing stochastic models frequently struggle to accommodate rigorous physical constraints while retaining sufficient flexibility to capture complex nonlinear patterns. To address this, we propose a novel semiparametric SFD modeling framework by leveraging specially designed functional forms. These functions intrinsically satisfy physical constraints defined on the moments of the conditional flow distribution given traffic density while incorporating neural-network-based structures to capture complex empirical patterns. We derive a system of moment-matching equations to convert physical constraints into the parameterization of the conditional distribution, proving that a unique solution exists for the location-scale family of distributions, thereby guaranteeing model well-posedness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework can be extended to non-location-scale distributions, including those requiring additional boundary constraints. Empirical evaluations on a real-world dataset reveal that our approach consistently outperforms representative baselines, delivering superior probabilistic accuracy and robust uncertainty quantification, particularly in congested regimes. Overall, the proposed framework provides a theoretically grounded and flexible foundation for stochastic traffic flow modeling.

AI.tldr: A semiparametric stochastic fundamental diagram (SFD) framework is proposed that uses neural-network-based functional forms to satisfy physical constraints on conditional flow distributions. Moment-matching equations ensure well-posedness, and the method outperforms baselines in probabilistic accuracy and uncertainty quantification, especially in congested regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing stochastic fundamental diagram models struggle to simultaneously satisfy rigorous physical constraints (e.g., on moments of the conditional flow distribution given density) and retain sufficient flexibility to capture complex nonlinear traffic patterns.
AI.method: A semiparametric SFD framework is proposed using specially designed functional forms that intrinsically satisfy physical constraints on moments. Neural-network-based structures capture empirical nonlinearities. A system of moment-matching equations converts physical constraints into conditional distribution parameterization, with a uniqueness proof for location-scale families. The framework is extended to non-location-scale distributions with boundary constraints.
AI.result: The proposed approach consistently outperforms representative baselines on real-world data, achieving superior probabilistic accuracy and robust uncertainty quantification, with particularly strong gains in congested regimes.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a theoretically grounded, flexible, and well-posed foundation for stochastic traffic flow modeling that reconciles physical constraints with data-driven flexibility.

title: (MPO)$^2$: Multivariate Polynomial Optimization based on Matrix Product Operators
summary: Central to machine learning and signal processing is the ability to perform universal function approximation and learn complex input-output relationships from limited numbers of observations. Multivariate polynomial models offer a natural way to express such relationships through multiplicative feature interactions, but their coefficient tensors grow exponentially in size with the polynomial degree. Existing tensorized polynomial models reduce this cost, yet canonical polyadic decompositions have rank-limited expressivity, and tensor train formulations are feature order dependent. We introduce Multivariate Polynomial Optimization based on Matrix Product Operators (MPO)$^2$, a framework that combines learned MPO feature embeddings with compact polynomial weight tensors. This yields feature order independent polynomial representations that can incorporate structured operators such as projections, convolutions, and masks for weight tensor symmetries. Across regression and classification benchmarks, (MPO)$^2$ improves over existing tensor decomposition based polynomial models and provides a flexible alternative for efficient polynomial function approximation.

AI.tldr: MPO² introduces a framework combining learned Matrix Product Operator feature embeddings with compact polynomial weight tensors, achieving feature-order-independent polynomial function approximation that outperforms existing tensor decomposition approaches on regression and classification tasks.
AI.motivation: Multivariate polynomial models suffer from exponential growth of coefficient tensors with polynomial degree. Existing remedies — Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition has limited expressivity due to rank constraints, and Tensor Train (TT) formulations depend on feature ordering — motivating a more flexible, order-independent tensorized polynomial framework.
AI.method: The authors propose (MPO)², which learns Matrix Product Operator (MPO) feature embeddings and couples them with compact polynomial weight tensors. MPO structure provides feature-order independence and naturally accommodates structured operators such as projections, convolutions, and masks for enforcing weight tensor symmetries.
AI.result: Across regression and classification benchmarks, (MPO)² consistently improves over existing tensor-decomposition-based polynomial models (CP and TT), demonstrating superior expressivity and flexibility for efficient polynomial function approximation.
AI.conclusion: (MPO)² offers a flexible, order-independent alternative to existing tensorized polynomial models, effectively addressing the rank-limited expressivity of CP and the feature-order dependence of TT, making it well-suited for efficient universal function approximation.

title: On the Failure of Boundary-Seeking Distillation in Bottlenecked Generative Architectures
summary: Data-free knowledge distillation transfers the knowledge encoded in a teacher model to a student model without access to the original training data. Prior work such as Contrastive Abductive Knowledge Extraction (CAKE) achieves this for classifiers by synthesizing samples near the teacher's decision boundary. In this work, we investigate whether this boundary-seeking principle extends to autoencoder distillation through experiments on the MNIST dataset . To enable a direct comparison, we reformulate continuous reconstruction as a dense, per-feature classification task, allowing the decoder to output categorical logits. We show that boundary-seeking objectives are fundamentally ill-posed in bottlenecked generative architectures. CAKE operates on a single, instance-level objective, but a decoder acts as an array of tightly coupled, feature-level classifiers constrained by a shared low-dimensional bottleneck. Independently sampling contrastive targets for these coupled outputs violates the geometry of the learned latent manifold and produces severe gradient conflicts instead of informative boundary samples. Manifold-aware synthesis bypasses these conflicts entirely and establishes an effective baseline for data-free generative distillation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether boundary-seeking data-free knowledge distillation (specifically CAKE) extends from classifiers to autoencoders. Reformulating reconstruction as per-feature classification, the authors demonstrate that boundary-seeking objectives are ill-posed in bottlenecked generative architectures due to gradient conflicts from independently sampled contrastive targets violating the latent manifold geometry. A manifold-aware synthesis approach is proposed as an effective alternative.
AI.motivation: Prior work (CAKE) successfully performs data-free knowledge distillation for classifiers by synthesizing samples near the teacher's decision boundary. The authors seek to determine whether this boundary-seeking principle generalizes to autoencoder distillation, where the "boundary" concept is less straightforward due to continuous reconstruction outputs rather than discrete class decisions.
AI.method: The authors reformulate continuous autoencoder reconstruction as a dense, per-feature classification task, enabling the decoder to output categorical logits per feature.
