This allows direct application of CAKE-style boundary-seeking objectives to autoencoders. Experiments are conducted on MNIST. The core analysis examines how independently sampling contrastive targets for each coupled feature output interacts with the shared low-dimensional bottleneck, revealing gradient conflicts. A manifold-aware synthesis baseline is introduced that respects latent manifold geometry.
AI.result: Boundary-seeking objectives fundamentally fail in bottlenecked generative architectures. A decoder comprises tightly coupled, feature-level classifiers sharing a low-dimensional bottleneck; independently sampling contrastive targets for these coupled outputs violates the learned latent manifold geometry, producing severe gradient conflicts rather than informative boundary samples. Manifold-aware synthesis avoids these conflicts and serves as an effective baseline.
AI.conclusion: The boundary-seeking principle underlying CAKE does not directly transfer to autoencoder distillation. The architectural constraint of a shared bottleneck in decoders renders independent per-feature boundary-seeking ill-posed. Manifold-aware synthesis is a more appropriate strategy for data-free generative distillation.

title: Knowledge-Guided Cross-Modal Fusion for Adult-to-Pediatric ECG Transfer via Label-Conditioned Contrastive Alignment
summary: Adult and pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation relies on age-sensitive criteria, and models pretrained mainly on adult ECGs often transfer poorly to pediatric populations when pediatric labels are scarce. Existing multimodal ECG--text methods typically align waveforms and text at the global sample level, entangling evidence from co-occurring diagnoses and limiting transfer under this gap. We propose Pediatric-Adult ECG Alignment via Cross-modal Enhancement (PEACE), a knowledge-guided framework pretrained on the largely adult MIMIC-IV ECG corpus. PEACE describes each diagnosis along rhythm, morphology, and ST--T axes and, per recording, composes only positive-label descriptors into three axis tokens and a fused embedding. A label query network (LQN) uses diagnostic labels as queries to cross-attend over ECG tokens and axis tokens, while label set aware bidirectional contrastive learning (LSBC) aligns pooled ECG features with the fused embedding when recordings share diagnoses. Curriculum adaptive fusion (CAF) gates alignment strength according to smoothed classification loss and training progress, limiting disruption during early optimization. The knowledge branch is used only for training supervision; inference uses ECG signals alone. On ZZU-pECG, PEACE reaches macro average AUCs of 59.39%, 81.74%, and 91.56% under zero-shot, 50-shot, and full fine-tuning, with the clearest gains over foundation and knowledge-pretraining baselines under limited supervision; versus domain adaptation initializations, zero-shot improves substantially while 50-shot AUC is comparable to DANN. After fine-tuning on PTB-XL, PEACE reaches 96.90% macro average AUC over nine harmonized labels. Ablations confirm that label-conditioned knowledge alignment, rather than global text fusion, is the key driver of pediatric transfer gains.

AI.tldr: PEACE is a knowledge-guided ECG pretraining framework that uses diagnostic label-conditioned axis tokens (rhythm, morphology, ST–T) and label-aware contrastive learning to bridge the adult-to-pediatric transfer gap, achieving strong zero-shot and few-shot performance on pediatric ECG benchmarks without needing pediatric labels during pretraining.
AI.motivation: Adult-pretrained ECG models transfer poorly to pediatric populations due to age-sensitive diagnostic criteria and scarce pediatric labels. Existing multimodal approaches align waveforms with global text, entangling evidence from co-occurring diagnoses, which limits fine-grained transfer.
AI.method: PEACE introduces three components: (1) diagnostic descriptions decomposed along rhythm, morphology, and ST–T axes, composed into three axis tokens and a fused embedding per recording using only positive labels; (2) a Label Query Network (LQN) where diagnostic labels cross-attend over ECG tokens and axis tokens; (3) Label Set Aware Bidirectional Contrastive learning (LSBC) aligning pooled ECG features with fused embeddings for shared-diagnosis recordings, gated by Curriculum Adaptive Fusion (CAF) using smoothed classification loss and training progress. The knowledge branch is used only during training.
AI.result: On ZZU-pECG, PEACE achieves macro average AUCs of 59.39% (zero-shot), 81.74% (50-shot), and 91.56% (full fine-tuning). Gains are largest under limited supervision versus foundation and knowledge-pretraining baselines. Zero-shot substantially improves over domain adaptation initializations; 50-shot AUC is comparable to DANN. On PTB-XL fine-tuning, PEACE reaches 96.90% macro AUC over nine harmonized labels.
AI.conclusion: Label-conditioned knowledge alignment, rather than global text fusion, is the key driver of pediatric transfer gains. PEACE demonstrates that structured, axis-level diagnostic knowledge injected during pretraining enables effective cross-domain ECG transfer even when target-domain labels are extremely scarce.

title: An Exploratory Study of Single Channel Surface Electromyography for Hand Gesture Classification
summary: Accurate hand gesture recognition using surface electromyography (sEMG) typically relies on multichannel sensor arrays and computationally intensive models. This limits practical deployment in low-power and embedded systems. This study investigates the feasibility of classifying ten hand gestures using a single sEMG channel combined with lightweight machine learning architectures. Raw sEMG signals were transformed into a comprehensive feature-based representation, including time-domain, frequency-domain, higher-order-crossing, and relative-intensity features. Feature redundancy was reduced using Pearson correlation filtering and the removal of highly correlated features, while dimensionality-reduction techniques (LDA and PCA) were applied selectively. Three classifiers, a feed-forward neural network (NN), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and a support vector machine (SVM), were systematically evaluated across four experiments. Results demonstrate that combining time and frequency features with Pearson filtering and a compact NN can achieve up to 90 percent accuracy, even with limited temporal and spatial information. These findings highlight the potential of single-channel sEMG systems for cost-effective, low-power gesture-recognition applications.

AI.tldr: A single sEMG channel combined with lightweight classifiers (NN, KNN, SVM) and filtered time/frequency features achieves up to 90% accuracy for classifying 10 hand gestures, enabling low-power embedded deployment.
AI.motivation: Traditional sEMG-based hand gesture recognition requires multichannel sensor arrays and computationally intensive models, which are impractical for low-power, embedded, and cost-constrained systems. The authors aim to reduce hardware complexity to a single channel while maintaining acceptable classification accuracy.
AI.method: Raw sEMG from a single channel is transformed into time-domain, frequency-domain, higher-order-crossing, and relative-intensity features. Pearson correlation filtering removes redundant features; LDA and PCA are selectively applied for dimensionality reduction. Three classifiers — feed-forward NN, KNN, and SVM — are evaluated across four experimental configurations.
AI.result: Combining time and frequency features with Pearson filtering and a compact feed-forward neural network yields up to 90% classification accuracy across 10 gestures, despite reduced spatial and temporal information.
AI.conclusion: Single-channel sEMG systems with lightweight machine learning are viable for cost-effective, low-power gesture recognition, broadening applicability in embedded and wearable devices.

title: DebrisTracer: Reliable Tracking in Hypervelocity Impact Fast Imaging
comment: 14 pages (12 + appendix), 16 figures. Accepted at IEEE VIS 2026. To appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)
summary: This application paper presents DebrisTracer, a framework for the reliable tracking of debris in hypervelocity impact fast imaging. These noisy and highly specific datasets capture the ejection of a large number of debris fragments after the impact of a projectile launched at hypervelocity into a target material. The reliable estimation of debris mass and speed distributions is of major importance in aerospace applications. We document how to extend an off-the-shelf topology tracking framework based on critical point extraction and matching, in order to incorporate domain knowledge and physical assumptions. Our approach automatically produces an accurate and reliable debris tracking, enabling an interpretable visual analysis of this complex space-time phenomenon. Extensive experiments demonstrate the accuracy improvements provided by our approach over established tools used by domain experts in terms of physical validation, specifically via the prediction of the experimental ejected mass and crater depth profiles. We illustrate the utility of our approach across several use cases (with varying impact angles and physics). We show that our statistical summaries enable the visual identification of distinct regimes within the debris population, corroborating and refining prior expectations of domain experts. Our database and our C++ implementation are available at this address: https://github.com/tloloum/DebrisTracer.

AI.tldr: DebrisTracer is a framework that extends a topology-based critical point tracking method with domain-specific physical constraints to reliably track debris fragments in hypervelocity impact fast-imaging data, enabling accurate estimation of mass and speed distributions.
AI.motivation: Hypervelocity impact experiments produce noisy, complex fast-imaging datasets with large numbers of ejected debris fragments. Reliably estimating debris mass and speed distributions is critical for aerospace applications (e.g., spacecraft shielding design), but existing tools used by domain experts lack accuracy and physical consistency. Prior off-the-shelf tracking methods fail to incorporate the specific physical assumptions of this domain.
AI.method: The authors extend an existing topology tracking framework based on critical point extraction and matching. They incorporate domain knowledge and physical assumptions (e.g., constraints on fragment trajectories, mass conservation) into the tracking pipeline. The approach automatically produces debris tracks from high-speed image sequences, generating interpretable statistical summaries of the space-time phenomenon.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate significant accuracy improvements over established tools, validated physically through improved prediction of ejected mass and crater depth profiles. The statistical summaries enable visual identification of distinct regimes within the debris population, corroborating and refining domain expert expectations across multiple use cases with varying impact angles and physics.
AI.conclusion: DebrisTracer provides a reliable, automated solution for debris tracking in hypervelocity impact imaging, outperforming existing tools and offering interpretable visual analysis. The code and database are publicly available.

title: Presentation, Not Mechanism: A Render Confound in Deprecation-Aware Memory Evaluation
summary: AI systems increasingly retrieve from records that revise themselves: issue threads, encyclopedic histories, policy logs, and long conversations. The challenge is not only finding relevant evidence, but deciding which claims remain in force, which were superseded, and when to abstain. Structured memories promise to solve this with typed edges, temporal updates, and conflict status, yet evaluations often change mechanism and prompt presentation together. We study this as Evidence-State Revision, comparing flat retrieval, coarse edge invalidation, and fine-grained RevisionLedger on 2,907 high-agreement questions from GitHub, multi-repo issue histories, Wikipedia, and DyKnow-style temporal streams. A render-matched control (same layout, deprecation disabled) reveals the central confound: when a value is changed and later restored, RevisionLedger appears to beat a flat baseline by +0.182, but almost all the gain comes from easier presentation; the fine-grained mechanism residual is indistinguishable from zero (+0.021 to +0.025 across two judge families). After presentation is controlled, coarse invalidation is the only mechanism that pays for current-state queries, beating the fine ledger by 0.084; the same query-sufficiency principle says provenance mainly needs retained invalidated evidence, not richer typing. Memory evaluations should hold render fixed, and deprecation-aware systems should deploy the coarsest retained state that covers their queries.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how AI systems should handle evidence that changes over time (revising records). Through controlled experiments, it reveals that apparent gains from fine-grained revision tracking are largely attributable to presentation format rather than the mechanism itself. When presentation is controlled, coarse-grained invalidation outperforms fine-grained ledgers, suggesting that systems should use the simplest retained state sufficient for their queries.
AI.motivation: AI systems increasingly retrieve from self-revising records (issue threads, wiki histories, policy logs), creating a dual challenge: finding relevant evidence AND determining which claims are current versus superseded. Structured memory approaches with typed edges and temporal updates have been proposed, but prior evaluations confound mechanism changes with presentation changes, making it unclear whether proposed mechanisms actually improve reasoning or merely present information more clearly.
AI.method: The authors frame the problem as Evidence-State Revision and conduct a controlled comparison of three approaches: flat retrieval, coarse edge invalidation, and fine-grained RevisionLedger. Their key methodological innovation is a render-matched control condition where the same layout is used but deprecation functionality is disabled. They evaluate on 2,907 high-agreement questions across four domains (GitHub issues, multi-repo histories, Wikipedia, DyKnow temporal streams). Two judge families are used to measure performance, isolating the contribution of mechanism from presentation.
AI.result: When presentation is uncontrolled, RevisionLedger appears to outperform flat baseline by +0.182. However, the render-matched control reveals this gain is almost entirely attributable to easier presentation; the fine-grained mechanism residual is negligible (+0.021 to +0.025). Coarse invalidation is the only mechanism that provides genuine benefit for current-state queries, outperforming the fine-grained ledger by 0.084. The authors find that provenance primarily needs retained invalidated evidence, not richer typing.
AI.conclusion: Memory evaluations must hold render fixed to avoid conflating presentation with mechanism. For deprecation-aware systems, deploying the coarsest retained state that covers query needs is the optimal strategy — a "query-sufficiency principle." Richer typing and fine-grained revision tracking provide no additional benefit once presentation is controlled.

title: Constrained Hebbian Learning Supports Efficient Representational Allocation under Structural Constraints
summary:
Introduction: Biological systems face anatomical and metabolic constraints, including costly synaptic maintenance and limited connectivity. These constraints favor neural codes that compress behaviorally relevant information into low-redundancy patterns. We test whether an excitatory competitive Hebbian rule can support synaptic resource allocation under such constraints and whether the resulting representations occupy a more favorable cost-performance regime than reference learning rules.
  Methods: Representational cost is quantified using mutual-information-based measures derived from the Variational Information Bottleneck. Experiments use fixed audiovisual embeddings from three audiovisual benchmarks (AVE, Kinetics-Sounds, VGGSound100) to isolate downstream associative plasticity. Hebbian learning is compared with Dense Difference Target Propagation (DDTP) and backpropagation (BP) under matched sparsity and architectural constraints.
  Results: Hebbian learning achieves lower task-information cost (CTI) than sparse BP and DDTP in the main compressed comparisons, while reaching CTI values comparable to shallow BP with nonnegative weights. Rather than uniformly improving classification performance, Hebbian learning shifts the trade-off between task-relevant information and representational cost, yielding lower CTI at comparable functional performance in several settings.
  Discussion: The results indicate a cost-performance trade-off rather than uniform accuracy gains. For a given level of task-relevant information, Hebbian representations retain less input information while preserving functional performance, although accuracy is slightly reduced on some datasets. These findings support interpreting Hebbian learning as a mechanism for synaptic resource allocation rather than as a general strategy for maximizing audiovisual classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: Excitatory competitive Hebbian learning achieves lower task-information cost than sparse backpropagation and DDTP under matched constraints, shifting the cost-performance trade-off rather than uniformly improving classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Biological systems operate under metabolic and connectivity constraints that favor compressed, low-redundancy neural codes. The study investigates whether Hebbian plasticity can serve as an efficient synaptic resource allocation mechanism under such constraints, yielding representations with a more favorable cost-performance profile than gradient-based learning rules.
AI.method: Representational cost is quantified via mutual-information-based measures from the Variational Information Bottleneck framework. Fixed audiovisual embeddings from three benchmarks (AVE, Kinetics-Sounds, VGGSound100) isolate downstream plasticity. Hebbian learning is benchmarked against Dense Difference Target Propagation (DDTP) and backpropagation (BP) under matched sparsity and architectural constraints, using a task-information cost metric (CTI).
AI.result: Hebbian learning attained lower CTI than sparse BP and DDTP in compressed comparisons and matched shallow BP with nonnegative weights. Rather than uniformly improving accuracy, Hebbian learning shifted the trade-off: for comparable task-relevant information, Hebbian representations retained less input information while preserving functional performance, with slight accuracy reductions on some datasets.
AI.conclusion: Hebbian learning is best interpreted as a mechanism for cost-efficient synaptic resource allocation under biological constraints, not as a general strategy for maximizing audiovisual classification accuracy. It occupies a distinct, more favorable region of the cost-performance trade-off space.

title: CLaC@FinMMEval 2026 Task 3: Sentiment-Augmented Deep Reinforcement Learning for Active Trading -- An Alpha-Reward Approach
comment: Accepted to the FinMMEval Lab at CLEF 2026. Recipient of a Merit Award recognizing promising approaches and well-documented submissions
summary: This paper presents our system for Task 3 of the CLEF 2026 FinMMEval Lab, which requires daily long, flat, or short trading decisions for Bitcoin (BTC) and Tesla (TSLA) using news and historical market data. We formulate the problem as a discrete-action Markov Decision Process and compare four deep reinforcement learning algorithms: Policy Gradient (PG), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Deep Q-Learning (DQL), and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG). The agents use technical indicators, cyclical calendar encodings, and daily news sentiment scores produced by LLaMA 3.2 1B. To reduce overfitting and align training with the objective of outperforming buy-and-hold, we introduce an alpha reward based on excess market return and randomize episode start dates. Hyperparameters are optimized with Ray Tune over 180 trials per algorithm-asset pair, with early stopping and model selection based on validation Sharpe ratio. On the CLEF Task 3 test set, DDPG achieves the strongest overall performance. DQL was selected a priori for the live endpoint because it obtained the highest validation Sharpe ratio, with selection performed without access to the test period. For TSLA, DDPG and DQL achieve cumulative returns of 54.96% and 52.62%, respectively, compared with 16.45% for buy-and-hold. For BTC, DDPG achieves a positive return of 1.58% while buy-and-hold declines by -34.27%. The results also reveal a substantial validation-to-test generalization gap, highlighting the difficulty of transferring policies selected in bull-market conditions to a bear-market regime.

AI.tldr: A deep reinforcement learning system for daily trading of Bitcoin and Tesla using news sentiment and market data. DDPG and DQL significantly outperform buy-and-hold baselines, though a validation-to-test generalization gap highlights regime-shift challenges from bull to bear markets.
AI.motivation: Participate in CLEF 2026 FinMMEval Lab Task 3, which requires generating daily trading decisions (long, flat, short) for BTC and TSLA by leveraging both news text and historical market data, with the goal of maximizing risk-adjusted returns.
AI.method: The problem is cast as a discrete-action Markov Decision Process. Four DRL algorithms (PG, PPO, DQL, DDPG) are compared. State representations combine technical indicators, cyclical calendar encodings, and news sentiment scores from LLaMA 3.2 1B. An alpha reward based on excess market return and randomized episode start dates are used to mitigate overfitting. Hyperparameters are tuned via Ray Tune (180 trials per algorithm-asset pair) with early stopping and validation Sharpe ratio for model selection. DQL was chosen a priori for the live endpoint based solely on validation performance.
AI.result: DDPG achieves the strongest overall test performance. For TSLA, DDPG and DQL yield cumulative returns of 54.96% and 52.62% vs. 16.45% for buy-and-hold. For BTC, DDPG achieves +1.58% while buy-and-hold declines by -34.27%. A substantial validation-to-test generalization gap is observed, attributed to training/validation during bull markets and testing in a bear regime.
AI.conclusion: DRL-based trading agents using LLM-derived sentiment can substantially outperform passive baselines. DDPG and DQL are particularly effective for this task, but robust model selection remains challenging due to regime shifts between training and deployment periods.

title: Revisiting data-driven dynamic security assessment with a tabular foundation model
comment: Paper is in the review process
summary: Data-driven pre-fault dynamic security assessment (DSA) rapidly evaluates the dynamic risk of credible contingencies on a power system using machine learning. Existing approaches face two limitations. First, they require a large labelled database for training, with a separate model trained, tuned, and maintained for each contingency in a potentially long list of credible contingencies. Second, the trained models generalize poorly to unseen contingencies. This work addresses the limitations by using a tabular foundation model (TFM) that assesses stability through in-context learning, requiring no retraining or hyperparameter optimization. A single TFM can assess many contingencies at once, removing the need for one model per classifier. We also characterize when the use of electrical distance coordinates (EDC) as continuous features enables generalization of TFM to unseen contingencies and when they do not, demonstrating how a few labelled samples can reliably improve generalization. Through comprehensive case studies on the IEEE 68-bus system, we show that a single TFM attains an average Macro F1 score of about 90% with only 120 labelled samples per contingency, roughly two orders of magnitude fewer than conventionally assumed, without any model retraining or hyperparameter tuning. For new/unseen contingencies, we show that using just 10 labelled samples of the new contingency with EDC encoding matches the best achievable transfer learning oracle model, which requires fully labelled data and is not deployable in practice. Overall, this initial study paves the way towards developing and deploying foundation models for power system operations, with possible applications across multiple operational tasks.

AI.tldr: A single tabular foundation model (TFM) with in-context learning performs dynamic security assessment across multiple contingencies using only ~120 labelled samples per contingency, eliminating per-contingency model training. Electrical distance coordinates (EDC) enable generalization to unseen contingencies with as few as 10 labelled samples, matching oracle transfer learning performance.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning approaches for pre-fault DSA require large labelled databases and a separate model for each contingency, with poor generalization to unseen contingencies. This creates significant training, tuning, and maintenance overhead that limits practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors employ a tabular foundation model (TFM) that uses in-context learning — a single model assesses stability across many contingencies without retraining or hyperparameter optimization. They introduce electrical distance coordinates (EDC) as continuous features and analyze when EDC encoding enables generalization to unseen contingencies. Case studies are conducted on the IEEE 68-bus system.
AI.result: The TFM achieves ~90% average Macro F1 score with only 120 labelled samples per contingency (~100× fewer than conventional methods). For unseen contingencies, 10 labelled samples with EDC encoding match a transfer learning oracle that requires fully labelled data. No model retraining or hyperparameter tuning is needed.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models are a promising direction for power system DSA, offering sample efficiency, multi-contingency assessment from a single model, and strong generalization. This initial study suggests broader applicability to other operational tasks in power systems.

title: DELUGE: Towards Continental-Scale Daily Pluvial Flood Damage Prediction via Interpretable Conditioning on Foundation Model Embeddings
summary: Pluvial (rainfall-driven) flooding accounts for 45% of National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) claims in the United States and is harder to predict than its riverine and coastal counterparts, with existing approaches limited to coarse resolution, regional domains, or computationally intensive process-based models unsuitable for daily continental-scale use. We present DELUGE, a multimodal deep learning framework for daily pluvial flood damage prediction at ~1 km resolution and national scale, trained on spatially and temporally corrected NFIP claims (2017-2022) and structured around the hazard, exposure, and vulnerability components of disaster risk. Rather than blanket coverage of the Conterminous United States (CONUS), we model the top 100 highest-claim 75 km cells, distributed nationwide and accounting for ~81% of total pluvial flood claims. Our architectural novelty is a pair of parametric modules in the hydrometeorology branch, a Value Modulator and a Temporal Modulator, conditioned on terrain descriptors and AlphaEarth foundation-model embeddings, that expose directly inspectable hydrological response parameters and provide architecture-level interpretability-by-design. Under a spatial block holdout, DELUGE outperforms tuned Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM baselines by 9% to 30% on a dollar-weighted area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), a metric that emphasizes the rare, high-cost claims of greatest operational interest. Beyond DELUGE, we argue this interpretable conditioning scheme is a transferable pattern for integrating foundation-model embeddings into other geospatial prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: DELUGE is a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts daily pluvial flood damage at ~1 km resolution across the US. It uses two novel parametric modules (Value Modulator and Temporal Modulator) conditioned on terrain and foundation-model embeddings to provide interpretable hydrological parameters, outperforming tree-based baselines by 9–30% on dollar-weighted PR-AUC.
AI.motivation: Pluvial flooding accounts for 45% of NFIP claims but is poorly predicted due to limited resolution, regional scope, or prohibitive computational costs of process-based models. There is a need for a national-scale, operationally feasible daily prediction system that emphasizes rare high-cost claims.
AI.method: DELUGE frames the problem around hazard, exposure, and vulnerability components. It models the top 100 highest-claim 75 km cells (covering ~81% of total claims) rather than full CONUS. The architecture introduces two novel parametric modules — a Value Modulator and a Temporal Modulator — in the hydrometeorology branch, conditioned on terrain descriptors and AlphaEarth foundation-model embeddings, yielding inspectable hydrological response parameters. Evaluation uses spatial block holdout and dollar-weighted PR-AUC metric.
AI.result: Under spatial block holdout, DELUGE outperforms tuned Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM baselines by 9% to 30% on dollar-weighted PR-AUC, excelling at identifying rare, high-cost claims of operational interest.
AI.conclusion: DELUGE demonstrates that interpretable conditioning of parametric modules with foundation-model embeddings is effective for pluvial flood damage prediction and represents a transferable architectural pattern for other geospatial prediction tasks.

title: When Model Merging Rivals Joint Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning: A Task-Vector Geometry Analysis
summary: Model merging is promoted as a substitute for joint multi-task training, yet in the reinforcement-learning setting this substitution is essentially never tested against the baseline it claims to replace: methods merge independently released agents precisely because a joint model is unavailable. We build the missing comparison. Training difficulty-1 and difficulty-2 Qwen3-8B specialists on the AppWorld agent benchmark with LOOP, we merge them (TIES, RAM+) and pit the result against a jointly trained model on the same data. On task-goal completion, merging matches joint RL -- and every merge variant is statistically indistinguishable. To explain why merge method does not matter here, we measure the geometry of the specialists' task vectors, which carries no task-sampling noise: they are near-orthogonal (cosine 0.06 - 0.10) despite ~65% support overlap, a small, shared direction that grows over training and that we calibrate against a random-init floor and a same-run ceiling to confirm it reflects learning, not the low-rank parameterization. Because direction and support are decoupled, support and sign-based merging (RAM, TIES) collapse to near-uniform averaging. We release all code and statistics.

AI.tldr: Model merging matches joint multi-task RL training on AppWorld agents, but the success stems from near-orthogonal task vectors — not from merge algorithms. Since direction and support are decoupled, sign/support-based methods collapse to simple averaging.
AI.motivation: Model merging is widely promoted as a substitute for joint multi-task training in RL, yet no prior work has actually tested this claim against a proper joint-training baseline. The authors aim to build the missing comparison and understand when and why merging works.
AI.method: Train difficulty-1 and difficulty-2 Qwen3-8B specialist RL agents on AppWorld using LOOP. Merge specialists via TIES and RAM+, then compare against a jointly trained model on identical data. Measure task vector geometry (cosine similarity, support overlap, growth dynamics) and calibrate against random-init and same-run baselines to distinguish learning signal from parameterization artifacts.
AI.result: Merging matches joint RL on task-goal completion; all merge variants are statistically indistinguishable. Task vectors are near-orthogonal (cosine 0.06–0.10) despite ~65% support overlap. A small shared direction grows over training. Decoupling of direction and support causes sign/support-based merging (RAM, TIES) to collapse to near-uniform averaging.
AI.conclusion: Merge method choice is irrelevant when task vectors are near-orthogonal with high support overlap — the geometry itself collapses sophisticated merging to simple averaging. This explains why merging works here and provides a diagnostic framework for future merge evaluations.

title: Physics-Based Deep Spatiotemporal Hyperlocal Radar Nowcasting with a Multi-Variable U-Net for High-Resolution Precipitation Forecasting
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Precipitation nowcasting over the immediate 10-90 min period is important for flood management and real-time decision-making in urban regions. Conventional short-range forecasting with high-resolution numerical weather prediction requires frequent data assimilation, model initialization, and spin-up, introducing computational latency. Machine learning provides an alternative by learning storm evolution directly from high-frequency observations and producing forecasts quickly after training. This is particularly relevant for Mumbai, India, where monsoon convection, land-sea interactions, and localized intense rainfall make short-term prediction difficult. Here, we develop a compact radar-only nowcasting framework that combines multi-elevation reflectivity, Doppler radial velocity, and radial-velocity-gradient proxy features within an encoder-decoder U-Net. Using the most recent radar volume scan, the model predicts 12 future composite reflectivity fields at 7.5-min intervals up to 90 min lead time. The derived velocity magnitude, divergence-like, directional-shear, and vorticity-like channels represent kinematic signatures associated with convergence and boundary interactions without requiring full wind-field retrieval. A high-reflectivity attention module improves sensitivity to convective cores, and physics-guided attribution examines whether the learned sensitivities are meteorologically meaningful. The model is trained using Mumbai Doppler radar observations from May to August 2023 and evaluated on temporally independent events. At 90 min lead time, Critical Success Index values are 0.437, 0.332, and 0.193 for $\geq$10, $\geq$20, and $\geq$30 dBZ thresholds, respectively. Compared with persistence, the model gives lower RMSE and higher spatial correlation at longer lead times. Once trained, it runs on a standard computer, generating nowcasts within seconds for real-time use.

AI.tldr: A radar-only precipitation nowcasting framework using U-Net with multi-elevation radar data, kinematic proxy features, and a high-reflectivity attention module achieves skillful 90-minute forecasts for Mumbai's challenging monsoon conditions, running in seconds on standard hardware.
AI.motivation: Conventional high-resolution NWP for short-range (10–90 min) precipitation forecasting suffers from computational latency due to data assimilation and spin-up. Machine learning offers a faster alternative, and Mumbai's complex monsoon convection, land-sea interactions, and localized intense rainfall present a particularly challenging testbed for such approaches.
AI.method: A compact radar-only encoder-decoder U-Net that ingests the most recent radar volume scan — including multi-elevation reflectivity, Doppler radial velocity, and radial-velocity-gradient proxy features (velocity magnitude, divergence-like, directional-shear, and vorticity-like channels) — to predict 12 future composite reflectivity fields at 7.5-min intervals up to 90 min. A high-reflectivity attention module enhances sensitivity to convective cores, and physics-guided attribution assesses the meteorological meaningfulness of learned sensitivities. Trained on Mumbai Doppler radar data (May–August 2023).
AI.result: At 90-min lead time, Critical Success Index values reach 0.437 (≥10 dBZ), 0.332 (≥20 dBZ), and 0.193 (≥30 dBZ). The model outperforms persistence with lower RMSE and higher spatial correlation at longer lead times.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides skillful, physically interpretable precipitation nowcasts up to 90 minutes for complex urban monsoonal environments, operates within seconds on a standard computer, and demonstrates that kinematic proxy features and attention mechanisms can improve deep-learning-based nowcasting without full wind-field retrieval.

title: Neural spectroscopy of AlphaFold2 reveals encoded protein conformational landscapes
summary: AlphaFold2's 93 million parameters, shaped by the evolutionary record of protein structure encoded in the Protein Data Bank and in sequence alignments, are conventionally treated only as machinery for converting sequence to structure. We propose they are also a scientific object that can be analyzed directly: a learned encoding of protein conformational organization that can be probed and characterized. By smoothing the Evoformer's weight tensors with a Gaussian convolution and scaling the result, we show that the trained model produces physically structured conformational landscapes. Under perturbation, ubiquitin's native contacts break in the order established by decades of folding experiments. For KaiB, five independently trained models agree that the alternative fold is not recovered under perturbation. For alpha-synuclein, five models produce five different but coherent landscapes, mapping where the training signal has determined the representation and where it has not. Matched-power noise controls confirm that random corruption of equal magnitude produces debris, not conformations. The model learned to predict static structures; the conformational organization visible under perturbation was not an explicit training target, suggesting it emerged as a byproduct of that objective. AlphaFold2's weights appear to encode structural constraints, shaped by evolutionary and structural training data, that extend beyond what unperturbed inference reveals. We call the approach of reading them neural spectroscopy, and Scaled Gaussian Convolution one such protocol.

AI.tldr: AlphaFold2's trained weights, when perturbed via Scaled Gaussian Convolution, reveal physically meaningful conformational landscapes that were not explicitly trained for, suggesting structural constraints are implicitly encoded as a byproduct of structure prediction training.
AI.motivation: AlphaFold2's 93M parameters are typically treated as a black-box tool for sequence-to-structure prediction. The authors propose that these weights themselves constitute a scientific object worth analyzing directly — a learned encoding of protein conformational organization that can be probed to reveal emergent structural knowledge beyond what standard inference provides.
AI.method: The authors introduce "neural spectroscopy," specifically a protocol called Scaled Gaussian Convolution: smoothing the Evoformer's weight tensors with a Gaussian convolution and scaling the result. This perturbation is applied to trained AlphaFold2 models, and the resulting structural outputs are analyzed. Matched-power noise controls (random corruption of equal magnitude) are used to confirm that observed conformational effects are not artifacts of arbitrary perturbation.
AI.result: Three proteins validate the approach: (1) Ubiquitin — native contacts break under perturbation in the order established by decades of folding experiments. (2) KaiB — five independently trained models agree that the alternative fold is not recovered, indicating a consistent learned representation. (3) Alpha-synuclein — five models produce five different but internally coherent landscapes, delineating where the training signal has determined representation. Noise controls produce only debris.
AI.conclusion: AlphaFold2's weights encode structural constraints shaped by evolutionary and structural training data that extend beyond unperturbed inference. These conformational features emerged as a byproduct of structure-prediction training, not as an explicit objective. The neural spectroscopy framework, with Scaled Gaussian Convolution as one protocol, opens a path for directly reading learned representations in protein structure prediction models.

title: DADiff: Diffusion-Driven Cross-Domain Policy Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Transferring policies across domains poses a vital challenge in reinforcement learning, due to the dynamics mismatch between the source and target domains. In this paper, we consider the setting of online dynamics adaptation, where policies are trained in the source domain with sufficient data, while only limited interactions with the target domain are allowed. There are a few existing works that address the dynamics mismatch by employing domain classifiers, value-guided data filtering, or representation learning. Instead, we study the domain adaptation problem from a generative modeling perspective. Specifically, we introduce DADiff, a diffusion-based framework that leverages the discrepancy between source and target domain generative trajectories in the generation process of the next state to estimate the dynamics mismatch. Both reward modification and data selection variants are developed to adapt the policy to the target domain. We also provide a theoretical analysis to show that the performance difference of a given policy between the two domains is bounded by the generative trajectory deviation. More discussions on the applicability of the variants and the connection between our theoretical analysis and the prior work are further provided. We conduct extensive experiments in environments with various shifts to validate the effectiveness of our method. The results demonstrate that our method provides superior performance compared to existing approaches, effectively addressing the dynamics mismatch. We provide the code of our method at https://github.com/hanyang-chen/DADiff-release

AI.tldr: DADiff is a diffusion-based framework for online dynamics adaptation in RL that estimates domain mismatch by comparing generative trajectories from source and target domains, offering both reward modification and data selection variants with theoretical performance bounds.
AI.motivation: Transferring RL policies across domains is challenging due to dynamics mismatch. Existing methods relying on domain classifiers, value-guided filtering, or representation learning have limitations. The paper proposes tackling this from a generative modeling perspective to better capture and compensate for domain discrepancies.
AI.method: DADiff uses a diffusion model to compare generative trajectories between source and target domains. The discrepancy in next-state generation is used to estimate dynamics mismatch. Two adaptation variants are developed: reward modification (adjusting rewards based on mismatch estimates) and data selection (filtering source-domain transitions). A theoretical bound links policy performance difference between domains to generative trajectory deviation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across environments with various domain shifts show DADiff achieves superior performance compared to existing dynamics adaptation approaches, effectively mitigating the dynamics mismatch problem.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion-based generative modeling perspective provides an effective framework for online dynamics adaptation, with both theoretical grounding and empirical validation supporting its advantages over prior methods. Code is publicly released.

title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
summary: LLM powered multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex tasks. However, their advantages over single-agent systems (SAS) remain unclear, with performance varying inconsistently across settings. Here, we provide an information bottleneck perspective on elucidating the differences between MAS and SAS. Specifically, our key observation is that a SAS accumulates its full reasoning trace in one shared context, while a MAS uses isolated local contexts connected by bounded relay messages. We show that, under infinite relay bandwidth, any SAS can be simulated by a MAS that transmits the full upstream context. Thus, the nontrivial advantage of MAS arises under bounded relays, where compression introduces a fundamental trade-off: reducing redundant context can improve efficiency, but may also incur loss of task-relevant information. We formalize this trade-off as an information bottleneck controlled by an effective parameter $β$, which captures how the balance shifts with model capability, and shows that MAS gains arise when context reduction outweighs relay information loss. We conduct 18 controlled experiments across five benchmarks and three model scales to validate our theoretical studies. We observe that MAS consistently helps when relays are near-sufficient, especially for weaker models. In contrast, MAS gains shrink or reverse when relays incur information loss, especially for stronger models that can already extract useful information from redundant context and thus gain little from compression. Our study shows that multi-agent design is fundamentally an information-bottleneck optimization problem. This perspective explains when bounded inter-agent communication helps or hurts.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes multi-agent systems (MAS) vs. single-agent systems (SAS) through an information bottleneck lens, showing that MAS advantages arise under bounded inter-agent communication where context compression trades off redundancy reduction against task-relevant information loss.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems show inconsistent performance gains over single-agent systems across different settings, and the underlying reasons for when MAS helps or hurts remain theoretically unclear.
AI.method: The authors propose an information-theoretic framework: SAS accumulates full reasoning in one shared context, while MAS uses isolated local contexts with bounded relay messages. Under infinite relay bandwidth, SAS can be trivially simulated by MAS. The nontrivial MAS advantage emerges under bounded relays, formalized as an information bottleneck controlled by parameter β that captures the context-reduction benefit vs. relay information loss trade-off, modulated by model capability. Validation via 18 controlled experiments across 5 benchmarks and 3 model scales.
AI.result: MAS consistently helps when relay messages are near-sufficient, particularly for weaker models. MAS gains shrink or reverse when relays incur information loss, especially for stronger models that already exploit redundant context effectively and thus benefit little from compression.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent design is fundamentally an information-bottleneck optimization problem. The framework explains when bounded inter-agent communication helps or hurts, unifying previously inconsistent empirical findings.

title: Improving Improved Kernel PLS
summary: Improved Kernel Partial Least Squares (IKPLS) algorithms 1 and 2 are among the fastest PLS calibration algorithms. This article focuses on two shared steps, the computation of the $\mathbf{X}$ rotations, $\mathbf{R}$, and the $\mathbf{Y}$ loadings, $\mathbf{Q}$, and accelerates both. For $\mathbf{R}$, term-by-term accumulation is replaced by a direct evaluation strategy that requires the same number of multiplications but parallelizes better on modern hardware. For $\mathbf{Q}$, I identify - to the best of my knowledge, for the first time - equivalences showing that each $\mathbf{Y}$ loading is obtainable, up to explicitly derived constants, from quantities already computed earlier in the same iteration, and I exploit them in IKPLS to reduce the cost of each loading from $Θ\left(KM\right)$ to $Θ\left(M\right)$ operations whenever $M = 1$ or $2 \leq M < K$, with $K$ predictor variables (number of columns in $\mathbf{X}$) and $M$ response variables (number of columns in $\mathbf{Y}$). Both improvements provably yield exactly the same $\mathbf{W}$, $\mathbf{P}$, $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$ as the original algorithms. Benchmarks with NumPy (CPU) and JAX (GPU) show speedups of up to two orders of magnitude for the isolated steps and of approximately $2\times$ (CPU) and $6\times$ (GPU) for entire fits. Both improvements are implemented in the free, open-source Python package \texttt{ikpls}.

AI.tldr: Two algorithmic improvements to IKPLS are presented: (1) a direct evaluation strategy for computing X rotations (R) that parallelizes better, and (2) a novel equivalence that reduces Y loading (Q) computation cost from Θ(KM) to Θ(M) when M < K. These yield speedups up to ~2× (CPU) and ~6× (GPU) for full fits, with identical outputs to the original algorithms.
AI.motivation: IKPLS algorithms 1 and 2 are among the fastest PLS calibration methods, but two shared steps — computing the X rotations matrix R and the Y loadings matrix Q — present computational bottlenecks. The authors aim to accelerate these steps without altering the mathematical results.
AI.method: For R: term-by-term accumulation is replaced with a direct evaluation strategy that retains the same multiplication count but improves parallelism on modern hardware. For Q: newly identified equivalences show that each Y loading can be derived from quantities already computed earlier in the same iteration, using explicitly derived constants. This reduces per-loading cost from Θ(KM) to Θ(M) when M=1 or 2≤M<K, where K is the number of predictor variables and M the number of response variables.
AI.result: Benchmarks using NumPy (CPU) and JAX (GPU) demonstrate speedups of up to two orders of magnitude for the isolated steps. Full-fit speedups reach approximately 2× on CPU and 6× on GPU. Both improvements provably yield exactly identical W, P, Q, R, and T matrices as the original algorithms. Implemented in the open-source Python package `ikpls`.
AI.conclusion: The proposed optimizations significantly accelerate IKPLS without sacrificing numerical fidelity, making PLS calibration more efficient particularly in settings where M<K. The improvements are production-ready via the `ikpls` package.

title: PRISA: Proactive Infrastructure LiDAR Framework for Intersection Safety Assessment
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE 29th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026). 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: Urban intersections are among the most hazardous locations in road networks, posing significant risks to vehicles and vulnerable road users (VRUs) such as pedestrians and cyclists. The complexity of multi-agent interactions demands continuous, real-time monitoring systems capable of anticipating conflicts before they escalate into crashes. We present PRISA, a modular infrastructure LiDAR framework leveraging privacy-preserving, low-light-robust roadside sensors for long-term traffic observation and real-time risk detection at the edge. The framework comprises two core components: a sensing and perception layer and a plug-and-play risk assessment module. The latter automatically curates site-specific training data from accumulated perception outputs to train a trajectory prediction model without manual annotation. It then deploys the trained model for continuous motion forecasting and dual surrogate safety evaluation, using Time-to-Collision (TTC) for longitudinal conflicts and Predicted Post-Encroachment Time (PPET) for crossing and VRU-involved interactions. PRISA is evaluated on the public R-LiViT dataset and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor at a live signalized intersection in Chattanooga, Tennessee. PPET-based assessment operates at 194~ms end-to-end latency over a 2.4-second predictive horizon, with TTC-based detection and perception remaining within real-time constraints, demonstrating practical feasibility for proactive multi-agent intersection safety monitoring.

AI.tldr: PRISA is a modular infrastructure LiDAR framework for real-time intersection safety monitoring. It uses roadside LiDAR for privacy-preserving perception, auto-curates training data from accumulated observations to train trajectory prediction models, and evaluates risk using TTC and a novel PPET metric. Deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson at a live intersection, it achieves sub-200ms end-to-end latency for proactive conflict detection.
AI.motivation: Urban intersections are high-risk locations for both vehicles and vulnerable road users (VRUs). The complexity of multi-agent interactions demands continuous, real-time monitoring systems that can anticipate conflicts before collisions occur, while also preserving privacy and operating robustly in low-light conditions.
AI.method: PRISA consists of two layers: (1) a sensing and perception layer using roadside LiDAR for privacy-preserving, low-light-robust detection and tracking; (2) a plug-and-play risk assessment module that auto-curates site-specific training data from accumulated perception outputs (no manual annotation), trains a trajectory prediction model, then performs continuous motion forecasting. Risk is assessed via dual surrogate safety metrics: Time-to-Collision (TTC) for longitudinal conflicts and a novel Predicted Post-Encroachment Time (PPET) for crossing and VRU-involved interactions.
AI.result: Evaluated on the public R-LiViT dataset and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor at a live signalized intersection in Chattanooga, TN. PPET-based assessment achieves 194 ms end-to-end latency over a 2.4-second predictive horizon. TTC-based detection and perception remain within real-time constraints, demonstrating practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: PRISA demonstrates practical feasibility for proactive multi-agent intersection safety monitoring using infrastructure LiDAR, with real-time latency and automated, annotation-free site-specific model adaptation. The dual-metric approach (TTC + PPET) provides comprehensive coverage of both longitudinal and crossing/VRU conflict types.

title: Behaviour-Conditioned Neural Processes for Adaptive Residential Short-Term Load Forecasting
summary: Residential short-term load forecasting (STLF) is challenging because household demand is heterogeneous, temporally variable, and shaped by diverse behavioural routines. This work investigates whether inferred behavioural structure can be embedded within the forecasting mechanism of a Neural Process-based probabilistic model, rather than used only as an external grouping signal, for context-conditioned residential STLF. We propose a behaviour-conditioned Attentive Neural Process framework that treats each load profile as a forecasting task. Behavioural structure is represented by a discrete latent variable inferred from the available context and used for behaviour-conditioned decoder conditioning, while a continuous latent variable captures shared functional uncertainty across heterogeneous profiles. To enable conditioning without ground-truth behavioural labels, clustering-derived information provides weak supervision during training, whereas test-time conditioning relies only on context-inferred class distributions. Experiments on the Smart Grid, Smart City (SGSC) dataset use user-disjoint train/validation/test splits, variable context lengths, and multi-step forecast horizons, with comparisons against a label-agnostic ANP baseline and fixed-window deterministic STLF baselines. The proposed variants improve MAE and CRPS over ANP across horizons and context settings, with the largest gains under limited context. The best-performing variant achieves average reductions of 7.9% in MAE and 6.9% in CRPS relative to ANP. Compared with fixed-window baselines, this variant achieves lower RMSE across all evaluated horizons while maintaining competitive MAE, suggesting fewer large prediction deviations under heterogeneous consumption patterns. These results support single-model, uncertainty-aware forecasting across heterogeneous households, contexts, and horizons.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a behaviour-conditioned Attentive Neural Process framework for residential short-term load forecasting that embeds inferred behavioural structure via discrete latent variables into the forecasting mechanism, using clustering-derived weak supervision during training and context-inferred class distributions at test time, achieving notable MAE and CRPS improvements over label-agnostic baselines on the SGSC dataset.
AI.motivation: Residential STLF is difficult due to heterogeneous, temporally variable household demand shaped by diverse behavioural routines. Existing approaches use behavioural groupings only as external signals; the authors investigate whether inferred behavioural structure can be directly embedded within a Neural Process-based probabilistic forecasting mechanism for more effective context-conditioned predictions.
AI.method: A behaviour-conditioned Attentive Neural Process framework is proposed, treating each load profile as a forecasting task. A discrete latent variable captures behavioural structure inferred from context and conditions the decoder, while a continuous latent variable models shared functional uncertainty. Training uses clustering-derived weak supervision; test-time conditioning relies solely on context-inferred class distributions. Evaluated on the SGSC dataset with user-disjoint splits, variable context lengths, and multi-step horizons.
AI.result: The proposed variants improve MAE and CRPS over the ANP baseline across all horizons and context settings, with largest gains under limited context. The best variant achieves average reductions of 7.9% in MAE and 6.9% in CRPS relative to ANP. Against fixed-window baselines, it yields lower RMSE across all horizons while maintaining competitive MAE, indicating fewer large prediction deviations.
AI.conclusion: Embedding inferred behavioural structure into Neural Process-based models enables effective single-model, uncertainty-aware forecasting across heterogeneous households, contexts, and horizons, with behavioural conditioning proving particularly beneficial when context data is limited.

title: When Does Muon Help Agentic Reinforcement Learning?
summary: Muon is competitive with AdamW in large-scale pre-training, but its value for reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training remains unclear. We study vanilla Muon in sparse-reward agentic RL through matched single-seed comparisons with AdamW on ALFWorld using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Under Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO), applying Muon only to hidden weight matrices raises final-window validation success from 0.290 to 0.546 (+88%); high-rate AdamW controls retain no post-update success. The effect depends on the advantage estimator and learning rate. At 3e-5, Muon improves GRPO from 0.161 to 0.268, whereas GraphGPO's late-window gap narrows near saturation. At 1e-5, GraphGPO Muon reaches 0.901, raises normalized validation AUC from 0.399 to 0.556, and reaches 0.5 and 0.75 success 30 and 60 updates earlier, respectively. These exploratory results show that Muon can benefit agentic RL and motivate studying the policy optimizer, advantage estimator, and learning rate jointly. Multi-seed and cross-task validation remain open.

AI.tldr: Muon optimizer significantly outperforms AdamW in sparse-reward agentic RL post-training on ALFWorld when applied to hidden weight matrices under GiGPO, achieving up to +88% validation success, with effects dependent on advantage estimator and learning rate.
AI.motivation: While Muon is competitive with AdamW in large-scale pre-training, its value for RL post-training (especially sparse-reward agentic settings) remains unexplored. This gap motivates the study.
AI.method: Matched single-seed comparisons of vanilla Muon vs. AdamW on ALFWorld using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Muon is applied only to hidden weight matrices under GiGPO. Investigated across two advantage estimators (GRPO, GraphGPO) and two learning rates (3e-5, 1e-5). Metrics: final-window validation success, normalized validation AUC, and updates-to-threshold.
AI.result: Under GiGPO, Muon raises final-window validation success from 0.290 to 0.546 (+88%); AdamW controls retain zero post-update success. At 3e-5, Muon improves GRPO from 0.161 to 0.268; GraphGPO gap narrows near saturation. At 1e-5, GraphGPO Muon reaches 0.901, normalized validation AUC rises from 0.399 to 0.556, and reaches 0.5/0.75 success 30 and 60 updates earlier, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Muon shows clear benefit for agentic RL post-training. The optimizer, advantage estimator, and learning rate must be studied jointly. Multi-seed and cross-task validation remain as future work.

title: Physics-enhanced reinforcement learning for real-time optimal control of dynamical systems
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising feedback control strategy for nonlinear and complex dynamical systems. However, RL algorithms are sample inefficient and require a large number of interaction with the environment to synthesize optimal control strategies. Consequently, applications of RL are typically limited to sparse sensors and actuators due to the curse of dimensionality entailed by the exploration-exploitation dilemma in high-dimensional spaces. In this work, we bridge RL and traditional optimal control for dynamical system with a novel Physics-EnhAnced Reinforcement Learning (PEARL) paradigm tailored to the control of high-dimensional and parametric dynamical systems, exploiting the differentibility of their dynamics. Specifically, PEARL employs an actor-adjoint algorithm that leverages automatic differentiation to compute policy gradients over short horizons and adjoint-based sensitivities of future returns approximated via neural networks, significantly reducing the number of environment interactions, while mitigating long-term gradient instabilities. Through two challenging parametric navigation problems in unsteady flows, we show that PEARL (i) effectively exploits differentiable environments to outperform state-of-the-art RL algorithms, (ii) is sample efficient, thanks to the physics-guided policy learning, (iii) generalizes across multiple scenarios, which is crucial when dealing with parametric systems, and (iv) enables scaling RL to high-dimensional state and action spaces, without requiring low-dimensional state representations or multi-agent strategies.

AI.tldr: PEARL is a novel RL paradigm that leverages differentiable physics to achieve sample-efficient policy learning for high-dimensional parametric dynamical systems, outperforming state-of-the-art RL in unsteady flow navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard RL algorithms suffer from sample inefficiency and the curse of dimensionality, limiting their applicability to systems with sparse sensors and actuators. There is a need to bridge RL with traditional optimal control to handle high-dimensional, parametric dynamical systems efficiently.
AI.method: PEARL uses an actor-adjoint algorithm combining automatic differentiation for short-horizon policy gradients with neural network-approximated adjoint sensitivities for long-horizon returns. This exploits differentiable environment dynamics to reduce environment interactions and mitigate gradient instabilities.
AI.result: On parametric navigation problems in unsteady flows, PEARL outperforms state-of-the-art RL algorithms, demonstrates sample efficiency via physics-guided learning, generalizes across scenarios, and scales to high-dimensional state/action spaces without low-dimensional representations or multi-agent strategies.
AI.conclusion: PEARL effectively bridges RL and optimal control by exploiting differentiable dynamics, enabling scalable, sample-efficient, and generalizable control of high-dimensional parametric systems.

title: A Blueprint for Equilibrium-Based Differentiable Continuous-Variable Thermodynamic Computing
summary: To address the escalating energy and latency demands of machine-learning workloads, we introduce a blueprint for an energy-efficient and fast thermodynamic computing stack that leverages stochastic analog processes in physical hardware. In this work, we focus on energy-based thermodynamic computing where the stochastic process is well described by Langevin dynamics with tunable energy potentials. The implementation of such potentials in physical hardware enables us to generate and sample from basic parameterized energy-based models. We demonstrate how to construct and train popular classes of machine learning models based on these hardware-native energy-based models, using the framework of probabilistic graphical models. We analyze the runtime and energy consumption of different models in this thermodynamic paradigm based on theoretical considerations and numerical studies. As a preliminary experimental realization of such hardware, we present our stochastic analog superconducting circuits driven by thermal noise. Together, these results outline a path toward energy-efficient thermodynamic hardware for probabilistic machine learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes a thermodynamic computing stack using stochastic analog hardware governed by Langevin dynamics to perform energy-efficient probabilistic machine learning via hardware-native energy-based models, with superconducting circuit prototypes demonstrated.
AI.motivation: Rising energy and latency costs of conventional ML workloads necessitate fundamentally new computing paradigms that exploit physical stochastic processes for inherent efficiency.
AI.method: Blueprints an energy-based thermodynamic computing framework where Langevin dynamics with tunable potentials are implemented in analog hardware; models are constructed as probabilistic graphical models and trained as energy-based models; runtime and energy are analyzed theoretically and numerically; preliminary hardware realization uses stochastic analog superconducting circuits driven by thermal noise.
AI.result: The thermodynamic paradigm supports construction and training of popular ML model classes; theoretical and numerical analyses quantify runtime/energy advantages; superconducting circuit prototypes provide initial experimental validation.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic computing hardware offers a viable path toward energy-efficient probabilistic machine learning by natively embodying energy-based sampling dynamics.

title: PagedWeight: Efficient MoE LLM Serving with Dynamic Quality-Aware Weight Quantization
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a popular class of large language models (LLMs), offering high efficiency and accuracy. However, in KV-cache-intensive serving scenarios, MoEs often exhibit a tension between the GPU memory requirements of the model weights and the growing KV cache. We propose PagedWeight, a novel management method for MoE LLM serving that dynamically quantizes MoE model's weights at runtime and balances expert-weight precision with the KV cache sizes. PagedWeight exposes and effectively navigates the complex tradeoff between the model's task accuracy, memory consumption, and throughput/latency. Across several memory-sensitive MoE serving scenarios, PagedWeight improves the quality-memory tradeoff over several existing quantization baselines. PagedWeight achieves FP16-equivalent accuracy with up to 72.0% GPU memory savings and 1.94$\times$ throughput improvement, and improves quality over quantization methods by up to 39.3% at a similar memory budget with at most 4.1% throughput loss.

AI.tldr: PagedWeight is a runtime dynamic weight quantization method for Mixture-of-Experts LLM serving that balances expert weight precision against KV cache sizes, achieving up to 72% GPU memory savings and 1.94× throughput improvement while maintaining FP16-equivalent accuracy.
AI.motivation: In KV-cache-intensive serving scenarios, MoE models face a tension between GPU memory consumed by model weights and the growing KV cache. Existing solutions fail to effectively navigate the tradeoff between accuracy, memory consumption, and throughput/latency.
AI.method: PagedWeight dynamically quantizes MoE model weights at runtime, managing the tradeoff between expert-weight precision and KV cache size. It exposes a precision–memory–throughput tradeoff space and navigates it to optimize serving under memory constraints.
AI.result: PagedWeight achieves FP16-equivalent accuracy with up to 72.0% GPU memory savings and 1.94× throughput improvement. At similar memory budgets, it improves quality over baseline quantization methods by up to 39.3%, with at most 4.1% throughput loss.
AI.conclusion: PagedWeight effectively resolves the weight–KV cache memory tension in MoE serving by enabling dynamic runtime quantization, significantly outperforming static quantization baselines in both memory efficiency and accuracy retention.

title: Beyond a Single Direction: Chain-of-Thought Disrupts Simple Steering of Refusal
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before producing final outputs, introducing a dynamic internal state that may complicate control mechanisms such as refusal. Unlike instruction-tuned LLMs, where refusal is mediated by a single directional subspace, refusal in large reasoning models (LRMs) additionally depends on the CoT. In DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, activation steering reverses refusal in only 39% of cases when the CoT is kept fixed, but removing the CoT entirely increases this to 70%, indicating that the CoT actively reinforces refusal. In a two-stage intervention where the model regenerates its CoT under activation steering, refusal is reversed in 94% of cases, while the resulting CoT alone retains 48% of this effect even after steering is removed. This suggests that the CoT can carry and reconstruct the compliance signal independently. These findings indicate that refusal in LRMs is jointly encoded in residual stream activations and CoT. This joint activation makes LRM more robust against activation-level interventions alone, but exposes CoT to a possible alternative surface attack.

AI.tldr: Refusal in large reasoning models is jointly encoded in both residual stream activations and chain-of-thought traces, making them more robust to activation steering alone but vulnerable to attacks targeting the CoT itself.
AI.motivation: LRMs introduce dynamic CoT traces that complicate refusal mechanisms compared to standard instruction-tuned LLMs. Understanding how refusal is distributed between activation subspaces and CoT is critical for both robustness and safety.
AI.method: The authors perform activation steering experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B under three conditions: (1) steering with fixed CoT, (2) steering after removing CoT entirely, and (3) a two-stage intervention where the model regenerates its CoT under steering, then tests the CoT's independent effect after removing steering.
AI.result: Steering with fixed CoT reverses refusal in only 39% of cases; removing CoT raises this to 70%. The two-stage intervention achieves 94% reversal, and the resulting CoT alone retains 48% reversal even without steering, demonstrating the CoT independently encodes compliance signals.
AI.conclusion: Refusal in LRMs is dually encoded across activations and CoT, conferring robustness against pure activation-level interventions but exposing a new attack surface via CoT manipulation.
